lessons.title: What Computation Is
lessons.content:
Think about the gate at a Dhaka metro rail station. You tap your card. The gate checks it and does exactly one of two things: it opens, or it stays shut and beeps. It never writes you a poem. It never asks how your day was. It just answers one question: "Is this card allowed in, yes or no?" That tiny gate is a great first picture of what this whole course is about. Theory of Computation asks: what kinds of yes/no questions can a machine answer, how much memory does it need, and are there questions no machine can ever answer?

What "computation" means: Computation is following fixed rules, step by step, to turn an input into an output, without needing any cleverness or guessing. Adding two numbers with pen and paper is computation. Sorting your cricket cards by player name is computation. Looking up a word in a dictionary is computation. The key word is "fixed rules". If a person with no special talent can follow the steps exactly and always get the right result, it is computation. A step that needs creativity, like "write a good song", is not one fixed rule, so it is not computation in this sense.

Why only yes/no questions: At first this sounds too small. Real programs print lists, draw pictures and send messages. But here is the trick: almost any task can be turned into a set of yes/no questions. "What is 23 times 7?" becomes "Is 23 times 7 equal to 161?" asked again and again for different answers, or "Is the first digit of the answer 1?", "Is the second digit 6?" and so on. A question whose answer is only yes or no is called a decision problem. Decision problems are the simplest kind of problem, so they are the easiest to study carefully. If we show that even a yes/no version is impossible, then the bigger version is impossible too.

Examples of decision problems: Is this bKash PIN exactly 5 digits long? Is this number prime? Does this sentence have balanced brackets? Does this Python program ever stop running? Does this road map have a route that visits every district exactly once? Each one has a clear input and a clear yes or no. Some of these are easy, some are hard, and one of them (does this program stop?) is proven impossible for any computer. By the end of the course you will know which is which, and why.

The problem with real computers: Why not just study laptops and phones? Because they are messy. A laptop has a certain amount of RAM, a certain speed, a certain processor, an operating system, drivers and a battery. Next year all of that changes. If we prove something about one laptop model, the proof is useless for the next model. Scientists wanted results that stay true forever, no matter what hardware is invented. So they needed something simpler.

Models, the pretend machines: A model of computation is a pretend machine described completely on paper by a few exact rules. It has no brand, no battery and no speed limit. Think of a model like the map of Dhaka on your phone. The map is not the city. It has no smell, no noise, no rickshaw bells. But it keeps exactly the part you need, the roads and how they connect, so you can plan a route. A model of computation keeps exactly the part we need: what the machine can remember, and how it moves from one step to the next. Because the rules are exact, we can prove things about the model with mathematics, and the proofs never go out of date.

Where the analogy breaks: A map is a picture of something real. Some of our models are bigger than anything real. The Turing machine, which you will meet later, has an endless tape of memory. No real computer has endless memory. That is on purpose. If a problem cannot be solved even with endless memory and endless time, then it can never be solved by any real computer, today or in a thousand years. So the model is sometimes stronger than reality, and that makes "impossible" results extra strong.

What people did before: Before the 1930s, "algorithm" had no exact meaning. People knew recipes for solving problems, like Euclid's method for the greatest common divisor, which is more than 2000 years old. But nobody had a mathematical definition of "a method that a machine could follow". Without a definition, you cannot prove that no method exists. You can only say "we have not found one yet". That was the big gap.

Hilbert's question: In 1928 the German mathematician David Hilbert asked a famous question, called the Entscheidungsproblem, which simply means "decision problem" in German. He asked: is there a mechanical method that takes any mathematical statement and decides, yes or no, whether it can be proved? Many people hoped the answer was yes. If it were yes, all of mathematics could, in principle, be handed to a machine.

Turing's answer, 1936: A young British mathematician, Alan Turing, attacked this question by first defining what a "mechanical method" is. He imagined a human clerk working with a pencil, a strip of paper divided into boxes, and a small rule book. The clerk looks at one box, checks his current "state of mind", writes a symbol, moves left or right, and changes state. That is the Turing machine. Using it, Turing proved that no such general method exists: the answer to Hilbert was no. Around the same time, the American Alonzo Church reached the same answer using a different system called lambda calculus. Later it was shown that Turing machines and lambda calculus can solve exactly the same problems, which strongly suggests both captured the true idea of "algorithm".

Chomsky and smaller machines, 1950s: In 1956 the linguist Noam Chomsky studied grammars, the rule systems that build sentences. He arranged grammars into levels of power, now called the Chomsky hierarchy. Around the same time, people studied machines with very little memory, called finite automata. Stephen Kleene showed in 1956 that the patterns we now write as regular expressions match exactly what finite automata can recognise, and Rabin and Scott in 1959 studied finite automata that can "guess". These small machines turned out to be exactly what is needed for searching text and for the first stage of a compiler.

The three big questions: The whole subject sits on three questions. Each one gives a part of the course.

Question 1, automata theory: What can simple machines do? An automaton (plural: automata) is a self-running machine that reads input and changes state by fixed rules. We start with the weakest machine, the finite automaton, which has only a fixed, small memory. Then we add a stack and get the pushdown automaton. Each step up gives more power. The big lesson is that memory decides power. A machine that can remember only "which of 5 situations am I in" cannot count to a million.

Question 2, computability theory: What can any machine do at all, given unlimited time and memory? Here we use the Turing machine. The shocking answer is that some yes/no questions can never be answered by any program, not because we are not smart enough, but because it is logically impossible. The most famous one is the halting problem: given a program and its input, will it stop or run forever? No program can answer this correctly for every case.

Question 3, complexity theory: Among the problems that can be solved, which can be solved fast? Some problems take a reasonable number of steps, like sorting a list. Others seem to need so many steps that the sun would burn out first, like checking every possible route for a delivery van visiting 60 places. This part of the course gives you the famous P versus NP question, which is still unsolved and has a one million dollar prize on it.

How the three fit together: Picture three circles, one inside the other. The biggest circle holds every yes/no question you could ever write down. Inside it is a smaller circle: questions some Turing machine can always answer. These are called decidable. Inside that is a smaller circle: questions that can be answered quickly. And deep inside are the questions a tiny finite automaton can answer. Most of this course is about finding which circle a problem lives in, and proving it.

A worked example of picking a machine: Take the question "Does this string of 0s and 1s have an even number of 1s?" A machine only needs to remember one bit: even so far, or odd so far. Read 1101: start even, read 1 to odd, read 1 to even, read 0 stay even, read 1 to odd. End odd, so the answer is no. Only two situations were ever needed, so a finite automaton is enough. Now take "Does the string have the same number of 0s as 1s?" To answer this the machine must count, and the count can grow without limit. Two situations, or 100 situations, are never enough for every string. So this question needs a stronger machine. You just did real theory of computation: you looked at what must be remembered and used it to decide which machine is needed.

Real-life example 1, the lift: An apartment lift controller is a small machine with states like "at floor 1, doors open" and "moving up". Buttons are inputs. Its rules are fixed. Engineers design such controllers using exactly the finite automata of this course, and they can check with a program that the lift can never move with its doors open, because the machine has only a fixed number of states to check.

Real-life example 2, the compiler: When you write a C program and compile it, the compiler first chops your code into words like "int", "x", "=" and "5". This stage, called the lexer, is a finite automaton. Next it checks the grammar, like whether brackets match, and this stage uses context-free grammars and pushdown automata, which come in the middle of this course. So every compiler you have ever used is built from ideas in this subject.

When to use this theory: Use it when you design a text matcher, a protocol, a parser, a game state system, or a controller. Use it when someone asks "can we write a tool that always finds every bug?" because the theory tells you that, in general, no. Use it when a problem looks slow and you need to know if a fast solution is even likely to exist.

When it is not the right tool: The theory does not tell you how many milliseconds your app takes, or which database is faster. For that you need real benchmarks. Also, "undecidable in general" does not mean "useless to try". Real bug finders still find many bugs. They just cannot be perfect on every possible program.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think a model is a real device you can buy; it is not, it is a mathematical object. Another mistake is thinking "impossible" means "too slow"; undecidable means no correct program exists at all, which is different from slow. Exams often ask you to define computation, state Hilbert's problem, name the three areas and give an example of each, and explain why we use abstract models.

Mental model: Picture a row of machines in a shop, from left to right getting more memory: a finite automaton with a few lights, a pushdown automaton with a stack of plates, and a Turing machine with an endless notebook. Every yes/no question walks along the row and stops at the first machine that can answer it. Some questions walk past all of them and fall off the end. Those are the undecidable ones. And for the questions that are answered, a stopwatch measures how long it takes; that stopwatch is complexity.

Recap and next: Computation is following fixed rules. We study yes/no questions using pretend machines so our results last forever. The three big areas are automata, computability and complexity. Next lesson we build the language every machine speaks: alphabets, strings and languages.
key_points: Computation means following fixed rules step by step to turn input into output, with no guessing or creativity.
A decision problem is a question with only a yes or no answer; most tasks can be rewritten as decision problems.
We study pretend machines (models) because real hardware changes, but results about exact models stay true forever.
Hilbert asked in 1928 for a mechanical method to decide any maths statement; Turing (and Church) showed in 1936 none exists.
Automata theory asks what simple machines can do, computability asks what any machine can do, complexity asks what can be done fast.
Memory decides power: a machine that remembers only a fixed number of situations cannot count without limit.
Undecidable means no correct program exists at all, which is different from a problem being merely slow.
lessons.tip: For every new machine in this course, ask one question first: what exactly can this machine remember? Almost every result follows from the answer.
lessons.task: Write down 5 everyday yes/no questions (for example, is this bKash PIN 5 digits, does this word read the same backwards). For each, write what a machine must remember while reading the input left to right, and guess whether a fixed small memory is enough.

quiz.q: Which of these is a decision problem?
quiz.explain: A decision problem has only a yes or no answer. 'Is 91 prime?' is exactly that (the answer is no, 91 = 7 x 13).

quiz.q: Why do we study abstract models instead of real laptops?
options: Results about exact models stay true no matter what hardware is invented
quiz.explain: Hardware keeps changing; a precise mathematical model lets us prove results that never go out of date.

quiz.q: Who answered Hilbert's decision problem in 1936 by defining a machine model?
quiz.explain: Turing defined the Turing machine and used it to show no general mechanical method exists. Church reached the same answer with lambda calculus.

quiz.q: Which area asks 'which solvable problems can be solved quickly'?
quiz.explain: Complexity theory measures the time and memory needed, and contains the P vs NP question.

quiz.q: A machine must answer 'does this string have equally many 0s and 1s?'. Why is a fixed small memory not enough?
options: Because the string has two symbols
Because the machine must keep a count that can grow without limit
Because the answer is always no
quiz.explain: The difference between 0s and 1s can become any size, so no fixed number of situations can track it for every string.

lessons.title: Alphabets, Strings and Languages
lessons.content:
Before you can play cricket, everyone must agree on the basics: what a ball is, what a run is, what counts as out. Before machines can answer questions, we need the same kind of agreement. What exactly does a machine read? What exactly is a "question"? This lesson builds that tiny vocabulary: alphabets, strings and languages. Every later lesson uses these words, so we build them carefully.

Why we need exact words: In everyday talk, "word" and "sentence" are fuzzy. Is "don't" one word or two? Is an empty message a message? A machine cannot handle fuzzy. If we want to prove things about machines, every object must have a definition with no wiggle room. So we strip input down to the simplest possible thing: a row of symbols.

Symbol and alphabet: A symbol is a single basic mark the machine can read, like 0, 1, a or b. An alphabet is a finite, non-empty set of symbols. We write it with the Greek letter Σ (sigma). Examples: Σ = {0, 1} is the binary alphabet. Σ = {a, b} is a small letter alphabet. Σ = {0, 1, 2, ..., 9} is the digit alphabet, which is what a bKash PIN uses. Finite means we can list all symbols and the list ends. Non-empty means it has at least one symbol. Why must it be finite? Because a machine with fixed rules must have a rule for each symbol it might see, and you cannot write infinitely many rules.

String: A string (also called a word) is a finite sequence of symbols from the alphabet, written one after another. Over Σ = {0, 1}, the strings 0110, 1, and 000 are all valid. Order matters: 01 and 10 are different strings. Repetition is allowed: 0000 is fine. The string "0120" is not a string over {0, 1}, because 2 is not in the alphabet.

Length: The length of a string w, written |w|, is how many symbols it has, counting repeats. |0110| = 4. |a| = 1. |aaa| = 3. Length counts positions, not different symbols. A very common slip is to say |aaa| = 1 because there is only one kind of letter. That is wrong; there are three positions.

The empty string: There is exactly one string with length 0. It has no symbols at all. We call it the empty string and write it ε (epsilon). Some books write λ (lambda). It is like an empty SMS: you pressed send but typed nothing. It is still a message, just with nothing inside. So |ε| = 0. The empty string is not "nothing exists"; it is a real string that happens to be empty. This difference becomes very important soon.

Concatenation: Concatenation means joining two strings end to end. If x = ab and y = ba, then xy = abba and yx = baab. Notice xy and yx are different, so the order matters. Lengths add up: |xy| = |x| + |y|. And the empty string does nothing when joined: wε = εw = w, just like adding 0 to a number. That is why ε is called the identity for concatenation.

Powers of a string: w to the power n, written w^n, means w joined with itself n times. If w = ab, then w^3 = ababab, w^1 = ab, and w^0 = ε. Why is w^0 the empty string? Because joining zero copies leaves you with nothing, and the "nothing string" is ε. It also keeps the rule w^m w^n = w^(m+n) true for m = 0. Similarly a^4 means aaaa. You will see notation like a^n b^n a lot: it means some a's followed by the same number of b's, for example a^2 b^2 = aabb.

Reversal: The reverse of w, written w^R, is w read backwards. (abb)^R = bba. (rickshaw)^R = wahskcir. A string equal to its own reverse is a palindrome, like aba, 0110, or "madam". The reverse of ε is ε. A neat rule you can check by hand: (xy)^R = y^R x^R. Try x = ab, y = c: xy = abc, reverse cba. And y^R x^R = c followed by ba = cba. Same. Like taking off socks and shoes: you put on socks then shoes, but take off shoes first, then socks.

Prefix, suffix and substring: A prefix of w is any starting piece. Prefixes of abc are ε, a, ab and abc. A suffix is any ending piece: ε, c, bc, abc. A substring is any unbroken piece from anywhere: for abc that is ε, a, b, c, ab, bc and abc. Note that ac is not a substring of abc, because a and c are not next to each other. Also, every string is a prefix, suffix and substring of itself, and ε is a prefix, suffix and substring of every string. A string of length n has exactly n + 1 prefixes, one for each place you can stop: after 0 symbols, after 1, and so on up to after n.

Σ^k, strings of one exact length: Σ^k is the set of all strings of length exactly k over Σ. For Σ = {0, 1}: Σ^0 = {ε}, Σ^1 = {0, 1}, Σ^2 = {00, 01, 10, 11}. How many are in Σ^3? Each of the 3 positions has 2 choices, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. In general, if the alphabet has m symbols, Σ^k has m^k strings. That is why a 5-digit PIN has 10^5 = 100,000 possible values: 10 choices for each of 5 positions.

Σ star and Σ plus: Σ* (read "sigma star") is the set of all strings of any finite length over Σ, including ε. It is Σ^0 together with Σ^1, Σ^2, Σ^3 and so on forever. Σ+ ("sigma plus") is the same but without ε: all strings of length 1 or more. So Σ* = Σ+ ∪ {ε}. Σ* is infinite, because there is no longest string; you can always add one more symbol. But every single string inside it is finite. Infinite set, finite members. Students mix these up all the time.

Language: Here is the key definition. A language over Σ is any set of strings from Σ*. That's it. Any collection, big or small, chosen by any rule. Examples over {0, 1}: L1 = {0, 01, 011} is a language with 3 strings. L2 = all strings with an even number of 1s is an infinite language. L3 = all binary numbers divisible by 3, like 0, 11, 110, 1001, is infinite. The word "language" is borrowed from linguistics. Think of English: from all possible letter rows, only some are real English words. That chosen set is the language.

Three special languages people confuse: ∅ (the empty set) is the language with no strings at all. {ε} is the language with exactly one string, the empty string. And ε itself is a string, not a language. Imagine a lunch box. ∅ is having no lunch box. {ε} is having a lunch box that is empty inside. Not the same! A machine for ∅ rejects everything. A machine for {ε} accepts only when the input is empty. Exams love this question.

Finite vs infinite languages: A finite language has a fixed count of strings, like the 64 districts of Bangladesh written as names. An infinite language never ends, like all even binary numbers. Finite languages are always easy for machines, because a machine can just store the whole list. All the interesting theory is about infinite languages: how can a finite set of rules describe infinitely many strings?

Union of languages: Languages are sets, so set operations work. The union L1 ∪ L2 contains every string in either one. If L1 = {a, ab} and L2 = {ab, b}, then L1 ∪ L2 = {a, ab, b}. Intersection L1 ∩ L2 = {ab}, strings in both. Complement of L means all strings in Σ* that are not in L. If L is "even number of 1s", its complement is "odd number of 1s".

Concatenation of languages: L1L2 is the set of strings you get by taking any string from L1 and gluing any string from L2 after it. If L1 = {a, b} and L2 = {c, cc}, then L1L2 = {ac, acc, bc, bcc}. Try every pair: 2 × 2 = 4 combos. Two traps: L∅ = ∅, because there is nothing to glue on, so no pair exists. But L{ε} = L, because gluing the empty string changes nothing. Again, ∅ and {ε} behave very differently.

Kleene star: The star of a language, L*, means "pick any number of strings from L, including zero, and glue them in a row". So L* = {ε} ∪ L ∪ LL ∪ LLL and so on. If L = {ab}, then L* = {ε, ab, abab, ababab, ...}. If L = {0, 1}, then L* is every binary string, which is exactly why Σ* has a star in its name. Two surprising facts: ∅* = {ε}, because choosing zero strings always gives ε, even when there is nothing to choose from. And {ε}* = {ε}. L+ is the same as L* but you must pick at least one string. The star is named after Stephen Kleene, and it is how finite rules describe infinite languages.

Decision problem = membership: Now the big link. Last lesson we said every problem can be a yes/no question. Here is how to write it formally. Take "Is this number prime?" Write numbers in binary. Let PRIME = {10, 11, 101, 111, 1011, ...}, the binary strings of all prime numbers. Then the question "is n prime?" becomes "is the string for n a member of the language PRIME?" Every decision problem becomes a membership question: given a string w, is w in L? A machine "solves" the problem if it says yes exactly for strings in L. We say the machine accepts the strings in L and rejects the rest, and that it recognises L.

Real-life example 1, the bKash PIN check: Alphabet Σ = {0, 1, ..., 9}. The language VALID_SHAPE = Σ^5, all 5-digit strings, which has 100,000 members. When you type 4 digits, the string has length 4, not in Σ^5, so the app does not accept it. When you type 12345, length 5, all digits, it is a member. Note this only checks the shape. Checking it is your actual PIN is a second language with just one member, chosen by you.

Real-life example 2, a mobile number: A Bangladeshi mobile number is written as 01 followed by 9 more digits, 11 digits in total, like 01712345678. As a language: L = {01} concatenated with Σ^9, where Σ is the digits. Using what you learned, how many strings are in L? The first two symbols are fixed, and each of the 9 others has 10 choices, so 10^9 strings. A form that checks this is a machine recognising L. Real operator rules (the third digit must be a valid operator code) make the language smaller, but the idea is the same.

When to use this view: Whenever you design a validator, a search pattern, a file format checker, or a protocol, first write the alphabet and describe the language of valid inputs. It forces you to think about edge cases like the empty input, which is where many bugs live.

When it is not enough: Some real inputs are not naturally strings, like a photo or a graph. We can always encode them as strings, for example a graph as a list of edges written in binary, but the encoding choice matters. Later in the course, we will be careful about this when talking about speed.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mixing up ε, {ε} and ∅. Saying Σ* is finite, or that it contains infinitely long strings (it does not, every string is finite). Forgetting that order matters in concatenation. Forgetting ε when listing prefixes. Exams ask: list Σ^2, count Σ^k, find L1L2 for small sets, find L* for a tiny L, show (xy)^R = y^R x^R on an example, and explain why a decision problem is a language.

Mental model: Picture a giant library with endless shelves. Σ* is the library: every finite string ever possible sits on a shelf, sorted by length, shortest first, with the thin empty book ε at the very start. A language is a highlighter: you mark some books yellow. A machine is a librarian who, given any one book, must say "yellow" or "not yellow". Our whole course is about which highlight patterns a given librarian can always judge correctly, and how much scratch paper the librarian needs.

Recap and next: An alphabet is a finite symbol set, a string is a finite row of symbols, a language is any set of strings, and a decision problem is asking whether a string is in a language. ε, {ε} and ∅ are three different things. Next lesson we sharpen our proof tools, including induction on strings and the pigeonhole principle, before we build our first real machine.
key_points: An alphabet Σ is a finite, non-empty set of symbols; a string is a finite sequence of symbols from it.
|w| counts positions; ε is the unique string of length 0 and acts like 0 in addition: wε = εw = w.
Σ^k has m^k strings for an m-symbol alphabet; Σ* is all finite strings including ε, Σ+ excludes ε.
A language is any set of strings over Σ; it can be finite or infinite.
∅ has no strings, {ε} has one (empty) string, and ε is a string, not a language.
L1L2 glues every string of L1 with every string of L2; L∅ = ∅ but L{ε} = L.
L* is zero or more strings of L glued together, so ∅* = {ε}.
Every decision problem is a membership question: given w, is w in L?
lessons.tip: Whenever you see ∅, {ε} or ε in a question, stop and picture the lunch box: no box, an empty box, or the emptiness itself. Most trick questions are right there.
lessons.task: Let Σ = {a, b}. On paper, list Σ^2 and Σ^3 and check the counts match 2^k. Then for L1 = {a, ab} and L2 = {b, ε} write L1L2 and L2L1 and see whether they are equal. Finally list all strings of length at most 4 in {ab}*.

quiz.q: What is |abba|?
quiz.explain: Length counts positions, including repeats: a, b, b, a gives 4.

quiz.q: For Σ = {0, 1}, how many strings are in Σ^4?
quiz.explain: Each of 4 positions has 2 choices, so 2^4 = 16.

quiz.q: If L1 = {a, b} and L2 = ∅, what is L1L2?
quiz.explain: Concatenation needs one string from each language. L2 has none, so no pair exists and the result is empty.

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
options: Σ* contains some infinitely long strings
quiz.explain: Star allows choosing zero strings, which always gives ε, even from an empty language. Σ* is infinite but every member is finite.

quiz.q: How is the problem 'is n a prime number?' expressed in this lesson's terms?
options: As the length of a string
As membership: is the binary string of n in the language PRIME?
As the reversal of a string
quiz.explain: A decision problem becomes the question of whether an input string belongs to a language.

lessons.title: Proof Tools for This Course
lessons.content:
In a cricket match, when the umpire is not sure, the third umpire checks the replay. Nobody accepts "I feel it was out". They want evidence that everyone can check. Theory of Computation works the same way. Our languages are usually infinite, so we can never test every string. Testing 1,000 strings and seeing they work proves nothing about string number 1,001. We need proofs: arguments that cover every case at once. This lesson packs your toolbox with the five proof tools this course uses again and again.

Set notation recap: A set is a collection of things with no order and no repeats. x ∈ A means "x is in A". A ⊆ B means every member of A is also in B. A ∪ B is everything in either, A ∩ B is everything in both, and A minus B is what is in A but not in B. We often build sets with a rule, called set-builder notation: {w | w has an even number of 1s} reads "all strings w such that w has an even number of 1s". |A| is the size of a finite set. The power set of A is the set of all subsets of A; if |A| = 3, it has 2^3 = 8 subsets, because each member is either in or out.

Pairs and functions: The Cartesian product A × B is all ordered pairs (a, b) with a from A and b from B. If Q = {q0, q1} and Σ = {0, 1}, then Q × Σ = {(q0,0), (q0,1), (q1,0), (q1,1)}, 4 pairs. A function f: A → B gives exactly one output in B for each input in A. Why recap this? Because next lesson a machine's rules will be a function δ: Q × Σ → Q, which means "for each pair (state, symbol), give exactly one next state". If you understand this line, you understand half of the next lesson.

Tool 1, proof by construction: To prove that something exists, build it and show it works. That is all. Claim: for every k ≥ 1 there is a binary string of length k with exactly one 1. Proof: build w = 1 followed by k - 1 zeros. Its length is 1 + (k - 1) = k, and it has exactly one 1. Done. In this course, the most common construction is building a machine. To prove "the language of strings ending in 01 is regular", you will construct a machine for it and argue it accepts exactly the right strings. Construction proofs are the friendliest kind, because you end with a real object you can test.

Tool 2, proof by contradiction: To prove a statement is true, assume it is false and follow the logic until something impossible appears. Since logic does not lie, the assumption must be wrong. Claim: Σ* has no longest string. Proof: suppose it does, call it w, with length n. Now take any symbol a from Σ and form wa. It is a finite string over Σ, so it is in Σ*, and its length is n + 1, longer than w. But w was supposed to be the longest. Impossible. So no longest string exists. Notice the shape: assume, derive nonsense, conclude. The pumping lemma proofs and the halting problem proof later in the course are both contradiction proofs, so get comfortable with this shape now.

Why contradiction is so useful here: Many of our big claims are "impossible" claims: no finite automaton accepts this language, no program solves this problem. You cannot construct "nothing". So instead, you imagine the thing does exist and show it would cause a crash in logic.

Tool 3, mathematical induction: Induction proves a statement for every natural number n = 0, 1, 2, ... in two steps. Base case: show it is true for the smallest n. Inductive step: show that if it is true for n, it must also be true for n + 1. Picture dominoes in a long line. The base case knocks over the first one. The inductive step guarantees each falling domino knocks over the next. Together, every domino falls, even though there are infinitely many. Both parts are needed: a perfect chain with no first push does nothing, and a first push with a broken chain stops early.

Induction example with counting: Claim: over Σ = {0, 1}, the set Σ^n has exactly 2^n strings, for every n ≥ 0. Base case n = 0: Σ^0 = {ε}, which has 1 string, and 2^0 = 1. True. Inductive step: assume Σ^n has 2^n strings. Every string of length n + 1 is a string of length n followed by one last symbol, which is 0 or 1. Different choices give different strings, and every length n + 1 string is made this way. So |Σ^(n+1)| = 2^n × 2 = 2^(n+1). True. So it holds for all n.

Induction on string length: In this course we usually do induction on the length of a string. We first need a definition built the same way. Reverse can be defined like this: ε^R = ε, and for a string w followed by one symbol a, (wa)^R = a w^R. In words: to reverse a string, take its last symbol to the front, then reverse the rest. Check: (ab)^R = b (a)^R = b a. Good.

Worked induction proof: Claim: for all strings x and y, (xy)^R = y^R x^R. We do induction on |y|. Base case, |y| = 0, so y = ε: (xε)^R = x^R, and y^R x^R = ε x^R = x^R. Equal. Inductive step: assume the claim holds for every y of length n. Take y of length n + 1 and write it as y = za, where z has length n and a is one symbol. Then (xy)^R = (xza)^R = a (xz)^R by the definition of reverse. By our assumption, (xz)^R = z^R x^R, so this is a z^R x^R. And y^R = (za)^R = a z^R. So y^R x^R = a z^R x^R. Both sides match. Done. This exact pattern, "split off the last symbol, use the definition, use the assumption", is how you will prove machines correct.

Preview, proving a machine correct: Next lesson we build a machine that tracks whether the number of 1s read so far is even. To prove it right, you claim: "after reading any string w, the machine is in state EVEN exactly when w has an even number of 1s". Base case: after reading ε, the machine is in its start state EVEN, and ε has zero 1s, which is even. Step: reading 0 keeps the count and keeps the state; reading 1 flips the count's parity and flips the state. So the claim survives every step. That is induction on length, applied to machines.

Tool 4, the pigeonhole principle: If you put more than n pigeons into n holes, at least one hole gets two or more pigeons. In a class of 13 students, two must share a birth month, because there are only 12 months. A stronger form: if you put N items into k boxes, some box has at least N divided by k, rounded up. 25 students and 12 months means some month has at least 3 birthdays.

Pigeonhole on machines: Here is why this principle is the heart of the pumping lemma. Imagine a machine with 3 states reading the string aaa. It starts in a state, then moves after each symbol. Count the states it visits: the start, after the first a, after the second a, after the third a. That is 4 visits but only 3 states. So by pigeonhole, some state is visited twice. Between those two visits, the machine read some piece of the input and came back to the same state. That piece is a loop. In general, a machine with n states reading any string of length n or more must repeat a state and therefore contains a loop. Lesson 11 builds the whole pumping lemma on this single fact.

Tool 5, countable and uncountable sets: A set is countable if you can list its members as first, second, third and so on, so that every member gets a finite position number, like roll numbers in a class. The natural numbers are countable. The even numbers are countable too: list 0, 2, 4, 6... and the even number 2n gets roll number n + 1.

Σ* is countable: List strings by length first, then in dictionary order within each length: ε, 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11, 000, 001 and so on. This is called shortlex order. Any string, say 1011, appears at some finite position because there are only finitely many shorter strings. Why not plain dictionary order? Because then the list goes 0, 00, 000, 0000 forever and never reaches 1. Since every machine and every program can be written down as a finite string, there are only countably many machines.

Uncountable, the diagonal trick: Now the set of all languages over {0, 1}. Suppose someone claims a complete list L1, L2, L3 and so on. Also list all strings s1 = ε, s2 = 0, s3 = 1, s4 = 00 and so on. Make a table: row i is language Li, column j is string sj, and the box says Yes if sj is in Li. Now build a new language D using the diagonal: put si into D exactly when si is NOT in Li. Say L1 contains s1: then D leaves s1 out. Say L2 does not contain s2: then D includes s2. D disagrees with L1 about s1, with L2 about s2, with every Li about si. So D is not anywhere in the list. That contradicts the claim that the list was complete. So the languages cannot be listed: there are uncountably many. This is Georg Cantor's diagonal argument from 1891.

The big consequence: Countably many machines, uncountably many languages. There are far more languages than machines, so some languages have no machine at all. It is like a school with roll numbers for every student but infinitely more seats to fill than roll numbers can name. This is our first glimpse that computing has hard limits. The argument does not tell us which language lacks a machine. In lesson 22, Turing's halting problem gives a real, natural example, using the same diagonal trick.

Real-life example 1, PINs and pigeonhole: A bKash PIN has 5 digits, so there are 10^5 = 100,000 possible PINs. bKash has many millions of users. By pigeonhole, many users must share the same PIN. That is fine, because the PIN is checked together with your phone number. It shows why a PIN alone is not an identity.

Real-life example 2, file fingerprints: Programs make short fingerprints of files, called hashes, often of a fixed length like 256 bits. There are infinitely many possible files but only 2^256 possible fingerprints. Pigeonhole says two different files must share a fingerprint. Such a pair is called a collision. Good hash functions do not avoid collisions; they only make them very hard to find.

Which tool when: Claim says "there exists"? Try construction. Claim says "for every string" or "for every n"? Try induction on length. Claim says "no machine can" or "it is impossible"? Try contradiction. Long input and a machine with few states? Think pigeonhole. Need to show something has no machine at all, by counting? Think countable versus uncountable and the diagonal.

Limits of these tools: Induction proves a pattern you already guessed; it does not find the pattern for you. A contradiction proof often tells you that something is impossible without explaining what would work instead. The counting argument proves some language has no machine but cannot point to one. Each tool is good for one job.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Skipping the base case in induction. Using in the step the very thing you want to prove for n + 1. In contradiction proofs, assuming something stronger than the plain opposite. In pigeonhole, counting states but forgetting the start state, which is why a string of length n gives n + 1 visits. Exams ask: prove a string identity by induction, apply pigeonhole to a DFA, show Σ* is countable, and outline the diagonal argument.

Mental model: Picture a toolbox with five tools. A hammer, construction, for building the thing. A mirror, contradiction, where you imagine the opposite and watch it break. A row of dominoes, induction, for "every length". A pigeon loft, pigeonhole, for "long inputs must repeat". And a grid with a red diagonal line, the diagonal trick, for "there are more problems than machines". Before every proof, open the box and ask which tool fits the shape of the claim.

Recap and next: We recapped sets, pairs and functions, then learned construction, contradiction, induction on string length, pigeonhole and diagonalization. Next lesson we use construction to build our first real machine, the deterministic finite automaton, and trace it on actual strings.
key_points: Languages are usually infinite, so testing examples is never enough; we need proofs that cover every case.
A function δ: Q × Σ → Q gives exactly one next state for every (state, symbol) pair; this is how machine rules are written.
Construction proves existence by building the object, such as a machine, and showing it works.
Contradiction assumes the opposite and derives something impossible; pumping lemma and halting proofs use it.
Induction on string length needs a base case (ε) and a step (from length n to n + 1, often by splitting off the last symbol).
Pigeonhole: a machine with n states reading n or more symbols makes at least n + 1 state visits, so some state repeats and a loop exists.
Σ* is countable (shortlex order), so there are countably many machines; the set of all languages is uncountable by Cantor's diagonal argument.
Therefore some languages have no machine at all, even before we know which ones.
lessons.tip: Before writing any proof, write one line saying which tool you are using and why. It keeps you from mixing an induction step into a contradiction and losing marks.
lessons.task: Write all binary strings of length up to 3 in shortlex order and number them 1, 2, 3 and so on. Then invent four small languages L1 to L4, fill a 4 by 4 Yes/No table against the first four strings, and build the diagonal language D by flipping the diagonal. Check that D differs from every row.

quiz.q: A DFA has 4 states and reads a string of length 4. Why must some state be visited twice?
options: Because there are 5 state visits (start plus one per symbol) but only 4 states
Because the string is too short
Because the start state is also accepting
quiz.explain: Counting the start, a string of length 4 gives 5 visits. Five visits into four states forces a repeat by pigeonhole.

quiz.q: Which proof tool best fits the claim 'for every string w, |w^R| = |w|'?
options: Induction on the length of w
quiz.explain: The claim is about every string, so induction on length (base ε, then add one symbol) is the natural fit.

quiz.q: Why is Σ* listed in shortlex order rather than plain dictionary order to show it is countable?
options: Dictionary order would list 0, 00, 000, ... forever and never reach 1
Shortlex order is shorter to write
Σ* is uncountable in dictionary order
quiz.explain: In plain dictionary order some strings never get a finite position. Shortlex gives every string a finite position because only finitely many strings are shorter.

quiz.q: What does the diagonal argument show about languages over {0, 1}?
options: They can be listed in shortlex order
They are uncountable, so they cannot all be listed
quiz.explain: The diagonal language D differs from every language in any proposed list, so no list is complete.

quiz.q: Since machines are countable and languages are uncountable, what follows?
options: Some languages have no machine at all
quiz.explain: There are more languages than machines, so some languages must be left without any machine.

lessons.title: Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA)
lessons.content:
Think of the push switch on a table lamp. Press it once, the light is on. Press again, off. Press again, on. The lamp does not remember how many times you pressed in total. It only remembers one thing: on or off right now. Yet from that one bit you can answer a question about your whole button history: "Did I press an odd number of times?" Just look at the light. That lamp is a tiny machine with two states, and it is exactly the kind of machine we build today: the deterministic finite automaton, or DFA.

What a DFA is: A DFA is the simplest model of computation. It reads an input string one symbol at a time, from left to right, and never goes back. It cannot write anything down. Its only memory is which state it is in right now. A state is one "situation" the machine can be in, like "light on". After each symbol, a fixed rule moves it to a new state. When the input ends, the machine looks at its current state: if it is an accepting state, the answer is yes (accept); otherwise no (reject).

Why such a weak machine: Before models like this, designers wrote ad hoc code or circuits full of flags and counters, and it was hard to be sure they were right. A DFA forces you to list every situation and every move, so nothing is hidden. Because the number of states is finite, a computer can check every one of them. And many real tasks, such as text search, input validation, and simple controllers, need only finite memory. The weakness is the point: it is the cheapest machine that does the job, and it runs in one step per symbol.

The five parts: A DFA is written as a 5-tuple M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F). Q is a finite set of states. Σ is the input alphabet. δ (delta) is the transition function, δ: Q × Σ → Q, which says: given the current state and the symbol just read, here is the next state. q0 is the start state, one member of Q. F is the set of accepting (final) states, a subset of Q; it may have many states or even none.

What "deterministic" means: For every state and every symbol, there is exactly one next state. Not zero, not two. So given the same input, the machine always takes the same path. No guessing, no choice. Remember δ is a function on Q × Σ, so if there are 3 states and 2 symbols, there must be exactly 3 × 2 = 6 rules. A missing rule means it is not a valid DFA.

Two ways to draw a DFA: A state diagram draws each state as a circle, each rule as an arrow labelled with a symbol, the start state with an arrow coming from nowhere, and accepting states as double circles. In text we write the arrows like q0 --1--> q1. A transition table lists one row per state and one column per symbol. Both hold the same information; the table is easier to check for missing rules, the diagram is easier to understand.

Example 1, even number of 1s: Σ = {0, 1}. L = strings with an even number of 1s. What must the machine remember? Only whether it has seen an even or odd number of 1s so far. So two states: q0 for even, q1 for odd. Start in q0, since zero 1s is even. Accept in q0. Rules: Row q0: on 0 go to q0, on 1 go to q1. Row q1: on 0 go to q1, on 1 go to q0. As arrows: q0 --0--> q0, q0 --1--> q1, q1 --0--> q1, q1 --1--> q0. Formally M = ({q0, q1}, {0, 1}, δ, q0, {q0}).

Tracing example 1: Input 1101: start q0, read 1 -> q1, read 1 -> q0, read 0 -> q0, read 1 -> q1. Ends in q1, not accepting, reject. Correct, 1101 has three 1s. Input 1001: start q0, read 1 -> q1, read 0 -> q1, read 0 -> q1, read 1 -> q0. Ends in q0, accept. Correct, two 1s. Input ε: the machine reads nothing and stays in q0, which is accepting, so ε is accepted. Zero 1s is even, so that is right too. Always check ε separately; it is the input people forget.

How it runs inside a computer: A DFA turns into a tiny program. state = q0. For each symbol c in the input: state = delta[state][c]. At the end: return state is in F. The table delta is just a 2D array. There are no other variables, no counters, no lists. That is why a DFA uses a fixed amount of memory no matter how long the input is, and takes exactly one step per symbol. A string of a million symbols takes a million table lookups and nothing more.

The language of a DFA: The set of all strings a DFA M accepts is called the language of M, written L(M). We say M recognises L(M). Example 1 recognises "even number of 1s". A language is called regular if some DFA recognises it. This word "regular" will follow us for the next eight lessons. Note that M recognises exactly one language: it must accept every string in it and reject every string outside it.

Example 2, strings ending in 01: Σ = {0, 1}. What must we remember? How much of the pattern 01 we have just seen at the end. Three situations: A, the end does not help us yet; B, the last symbol was 0, which could be the start of 01; C, the last two symbols were 01. Start in A, accept in C. Rules: Row A: on 0 go to B, on 1 go to A. Row B: on 0 go to B, on 1 go to C. Row C: on 0 go to B, on 1 go to A.

Why those rules: From B, reading another 0 keeps us in B, because the newest 0 can still start a 01. From C, reading 0 sends us to B, not A, because that fresh 0 is a new possible start. From C, reading 1 means the string now ends in 11, which helps nothing, so back to A. Each rule answers one question: after this symbol, what is the most useful thing I can say about the end of the string?

Tracing example 2: Input 1101: start A, read 1 -> A, read 1 -> A, read 0 -> B, read 1 -> C. Ends in C, accept. Correct, it ends in 01. Input 0110: start A, read 0 -> B, read 1 -> C, read 1 -> A, read 0 -> B. Ends in B, reject. Notice the machine passed through C in the middle, but that does not matter. Accepting is decided only at the very end. A machine does not stop early when it touches an accept state.

Example 3, binary numbers divisible by 3: Σ = {0, 1}, read the number from its most significant bit. First principles: if the number read so far has value v and we read one more bit b, the new value is 2v + b. For example, reading 110 goes 1, then 2 × 1 + 1 = 3, then 2 × 3 + 0 = 6. But the value can grow forever, so we cannot store it. Here is the trick: to know if the final value is divisible by 3, we only need the remainder after dividing by 3. And the new remainder depends only on the old remainder: new r = (2r + b) mod 3. Only three remainders exist, 0, 1 and 2, so three states r0, r1, r2.

The table for example 3: Start r0, accept r0. Row r0: on 0 go to r0, on 1 go to r1. Row r1: on 0 go to r2, on 1 go to r0. Row r2: on 0 go to r1, on 1 go to r2. Check one rule: from r1 reading 0, 2 × 1 + 0 = 2, so r2. From r2 reading 1, 2 × 2 + 1 = 5, and 5 mod 3 = 2, so r2. Each rule is just arithmetic, not magic.

Tracing example 3: Input 1001 (that is 9): start r0, read 1 -> r1, read 0 -> r2, read 0 -> r1, read 1 -> r0. Ends in r0, accept. 9 is divisible by 3. Input 111 (that is 7): start r0, read 1 -> r1, read 1 -> r0, read 1 -> r1. Ends in r1, reject; 7 leaves remainder 1, and the state name tells you so. A DFA with finite states handled numbers of any size, because it kept only what matters.

Dead or trap state: Language: strings over {a, b} that start with a. Start s. Row s: on a go to Y, on b go to D. Row Y: on a go to Y, on b go to Y. Row D: on a go to D, on b go to D. Accept Y only. D is a dead state, also called a trap: once you enter, you can never leave, and it is not accepting. Input bab: s, read b -> D, read a -> D, read b -> D, reject. As soon as the first symbol is b, the answer is decided. Many diagrams leave the trap out to keep the picture clean, with the rule "any missing arrow goes to an invisible trap". In an exam, draw it unless told otherwise, because a DFA must have a move for every symbol.

Real-life example 1, PIN shape check: Σ = the 10 digits. Language: exactly 5 digits. States p0 to p5 count digits typed, plus a trap T. Each digit moves p0 to p1, p1 to p2, up to p4 to p5. A digit in p5 goes to T, and T stays in T. Accept p5 only. Input 1234: p0, p1, p2, p3, p4. Ends in p4, reject, too short. Input 123456: reaches p5 after five digits, the sixth goes to T, reject, too long. 7 states handle every possible input.

Real-life example 2, a lexer reading numbers: When a compiler reads code like x = 250, part of it is a DFA that recognises an integer: from start, a digit goes to state NUM, more digits stay in NUM, and NUM is accepting. Anything else goes to a trap. Real lexers combine many such small DFAs, one for numbers, one for names, one for operators, into one big DFA that scans source code at high speed.

When to use a DFA: Whenever the answer depends on a fixed, bounded amount of information about what you have read: parity, remainders, the last few symbols, whether a pattern has appeared, a small fixed counter. DFAs are perfect for validation, lexers, protocols, and simple controllers.

When not to use a DFA: When the answer needs unbounded memory. Is the string a^n b^n, the same number of a's then b's? You must remember n, and n can be bigger than any fixed number of states. Balanced brackets with any depth, the same problem. Lesson 11 proves these are impossible for DFAs; lesson 16 gives a stronger machine with a stack.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Missing transitions, so the machine is not complete. Two arrows with the same symbol from one state, which breaks determinism. Forgetting to decide if the start state accepts, which decides ε. Thinking the machine accepts the moment it touches an accept state. Exams ask you to give the 5-tuple, draw the diagram and table, trace given strings, and design a DFA for a described language such as "contains 11", "length divisible by 3", or "ends with ab".

Mental model: Picture a board game. Each state is a square on the board, and you have one token. The input string is a deck of cards. You flip the cards one by one, and each card tells you exactly which square to move to from where you stand, according to the rule book (the table). You cannot peek at earlier cards and cannot write notes. When the deck runs out, look at your token: on a gold square you win, otherwise you lose. Designing a DFA means deciding what each square should mean, so that standing on it tells you everything you need to know about the cards already flipped.

Recap and next: A DFA is a 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) with exactly one move per state and symbol, accepts if it ends in F, and uses only its current state as memory. We designed DFAs for parity, endings, divisibility, and with a trap state. Next lesson we learn a reliable design method and how to combine and flip DFAs.
key_points: A DFA reads input left to right once, has only its current state as memory, and accepts if it ends in an accepting state.
Formally a DFA is a 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) with δ: Q × Σ → Q.
Deterministic means exactly one next state for every state and symbol, so |Q| × |Σ| rules in total.
The language L(M) is all strings M accepts; a language is regular if some DFA recognises it.
Design by asking what to remember: parity needs 2 states, 'ends in 01' needs 3, 'binary divisible by 3' needs 3 remainders using r -> (2r + b) mod 3.
A dead (trap) state is non-accepting and loops to itself on every symbol; it catches hopeless inputs.
Acceptance is decided only at the end of the input; passing through an accept state in the middle means nothing.
DFAs fail when unbounded memory is needed, such as a^n b^n or balanced brackets of any depth.
lessons.tip: When you finish a DFA, check three things: every state has exactly one arrow per symbol, you know whether ε is accepted, and you have traced at least one string that should be accepted and one that should be rejected.
lessons.task: Design a DFA over {a, b} for strings that contain the substring aa. Write its transition table, then trace baab and abab on paper. (Hint: remember 'no a pending', 'just saw one a', and 'found aa'.)

quiz.q: A DFA has 4 states and alphabet {0, 1, 2}. How many transitions must δ define?
quiz.explain: δ is defined on Q × Σ, so 4 × 3 = 12 pairs, each with exactly one next state.

quiz.q: Using the 'ends in 01' DFA (A start, C accept; A: 0->B, 1->A; B: 0->B, 1->C; C: 0->B, 1->A), which state is reached on 0110?
quiz.explain: A -0-> B -1-> C -1-> A -0-> B. B is not accepting, and indeed 0110 does not end in 01.

quiz.q: In the divisible-by-3 DFA, what is the next state from r2 on reading 0?
quiz.explain: New remainder = (2 × 2 + 0) mod 3 = 4 mod 3 = 1, so r1.

quiz.q: What is a dead (trap) state?
options: An accepting state with no outgoing arrows
A state that exists only in NFAs
A non-accepting state that every symbol keeps you in
quiz.explain: Once entered it is never left and never accepts, so the input is already rejected.

quiz.q: Why can no DFA recognise a^n b^n for all n?
options: DFAs cannot read the letter b
It would need to remember n, which can exceed any fixed number of states
quiz.explain: A DFA's only memory is its state, and there are finitely many states, but n can be arbitrarily large.

lessons.title: Designing DFAs Well
lessons.content:
Watch a cricket scorer during a T20 match. After 100 balls, does she remember every single ball? No. She keeps a short summary: runs, wickets, overs. From that summary she can answer any question the crowd cares about, and when the next ball is bowled, she can update it without looking back. A good DFA works the same way. Each state is a summary of everything read so far. Designing a DFA well means choosing the smallest summary that still lets you answer the question at the end and update after each new symbol. This lesson gives you a step by step method for that, then shows how to combine and flip DFAs.

The "what must I remember?" method: Step 1: imagine you are the machine, reading the string left to right, one symbol at a time, with no going back. Step 2: ask what is the least information about the part already read that you need for two jobs: deciding accept or reject if the input ended right now, and updating correctly after the next symbol. Step 3: list every possible value of that information; each value becomes one state. Step 4: for every state and every symbol, ask "if I knew this and then read that, what do I know now?"; that is your transition. Step 5: the start state is the value for the empty string; accepting states are the values where the answer is yes. Step 6: test ε, a string that should be accepted, and one that should be rejected.

Why both jobs matter: If your summary only answers the final question, you may not be able to update it. Example: for "binary number divisible by 3", storing only "divisible yes or no" is not enough. If the number so far is 4 (not divisible) or 5 (not divisible), both say "no", but after reading a 0 they become 8 (no) and 10 (no), and after a 1 they become 9 (yes) and 11 (no). So "no" alone cannot predict the future. The remainder 0, 1 or 2 can. A good summary must be closed under updating.

Worked design, contains 101: Σ = {0, 1}, accept strings that contain 101 somewhere. What to remember: how much of 101 we have matched at the end so far, or that we already found it. States: S, nothing useful; A, the end is 1; B, the end is 10; F, found 101 already. Start S, accept F. Now fill each row by asking "what do I know now?". Row S: on 0 stay S, on 1 go to A. Row A: on 0 go to B (now we have 10), on 1 stay A (the newest 1 can still start 101). Row B: on 0 go to S (100 kills the progress), on 1 go to F. Row F: on 0 or 1 stay F, because once found, always found.

Tracing the 101 machine: Input 0101: start S, read 0 -> S, read 1 -> A, read 0 -> B, read 1 -> F. Accept. Input 1001: start S, read 1 -> A, read 0 -> B, read 0 -> S, read 1 -> A. Ends in A, reject, and 1001 really has no 101. Input 11011: S, A, A, B, F, F. Accept. The tricky rule was A on 1 staying in A: in 11011, the first 1 fails, but the second 1 starts the match.

Combining two conditions: Often a language has two rules at once. "Even number of 1s AND ends with 0." You could design from scratch, but there is a neater way: build a small DFA for each rule, then run both at the same time. This is the product construction.

Product construction step by step: Machine 1, even 1s: states E (even) and O (odd); a 1 flips, a 0 keeps. Machine 2, ends with 0: states N (last symbol not 0, or nothing read yet) and Z (last symbol was 0); a 0 goes to Z, a 1 goes to N. The product machine's states are pairs: (E,N), (E,Z), (O,N), (O,Z). Start (E,N), the pair of both start states. On each symbol, both parts move by their own rules at the same time. On 0: (E,N) -> (E,Z), (E,Z) -> (E,Z), (O,N) -> (O,Z), (O,Z) -> (O,Z). On 1: (E,N) -> (O,N), (E,Z) -> (O,N), (O,N) -> (E,N), (O,Z) -> (E,N).

Choosing accepting pairs: For AND (intersection), accept a pair only when both parts accept: only (E,Z). For OR (union), accept when at least one part accepts: (E,N), (E,Z) and (O,Z). For "in L1 but not L2" (difference), accept (E,N). The states and arrows stay the same; only the accept set changes. That is the beauty: one construction, many operations.

Tracing the product: Input 1100: start (E,N), read 1 -> (O,N), read 1 -> (E,N), read 0 -> (E,Z), read 0 -> (E,Z). For AND, (E,Z) is accepting, accept. Check: two 1s (even) and ends with 0. Input 1000: (E,N), read 1 -> (O,N), read 0 -> (O,Z), read 0 -> (O,Z), read 0 -> (O,Z). For AND, reject (one 1 is odd). For OR, accept, because it ends with 0. Same run, different verdicts, depending only on the accept set.

Why the product works: After reading any string w, the first part of the pair is exactly where machine 1 would be, and the second part is exactly where machine 2 would be. You can prove this by induction on the length of w: true for ε (both start states), and each step updates each part by its own rule. So the pair knows both answers. The cost: if machine 1 has m states and machine 2 has n states, the product has m × n states. Two 10-state machines give 100 states. Fine on paper for small cases, but it grows fast when you combine many machines.

When to use the product, and when not: Use it when the language is clearly two simple rules joined by AND, OR or 'but not'; it is mechanical and hard to get wrong. Design from scratch when the rules are tangled together, or when combining many machines would blow up the state count. Joining ten 2-state machines by product gives 2^10 = 1024 pair states, while a direct design, or the minimisation of lesson 8, may need far fewer.

Complement by swapping: To accept exactly the strings a DFA rejects, keep everything and swap accepting with non-accepting states. Why does this work? Because a DFA, on any input, ends in exactly one state. That state is either in F or not. Swap F, and every answer flips. For "contains 101", the complement machine accepts S, A and B, and rejects F, so it recognises "does not contain 101". Input 1001 ends in A, now accepted, correct.

The two traps of complement: First, the DFA must be complete. If you left out a trap state and some string "falls off" with no arrow to follow, that string is rejected by the original and also by the swapped machine, which is wrong. Always add the trap before swapping. Second, the swap trick only works for DFAs. For the guessing machines of the next lesson (NFAs), swapping accept states does not give the complement. Many students lose marks here.

The extended transition function: δ tells you where one symbol takes you. We also want "where does a whole string take me?". That is δ* (delta star), defined by induction: δ*(q, ε) = q, since reading nothing moves you nowhere. And δ*(q, wa) = δ(δ*(q, w), a): to read w then a, first go wherever w takes you, then take one more step on a. Example with the "ends in 01" DFA from lesson 4 (A start; A: 0->B, 1->A; B: 0->B, 1->C; C: 0->B, 1->A): δ*(A, 01) = δ(δ*(A, 0), 1) = δ(B, 1) = C. Now we can write acceptance in one line: M accepts w exactly when δ*(q0, w) is in F.

Real use 1, a vending machine: A juice machine costs 15 taka and takes 5 and 10 taka coins. What must it remember? Only how much money is inside: 0, 5, 10, or at least 15. States c0, c5, c10 and PAID. Rows: c0: 5 -> c5, 10 -> c10. c5: 5 -> c10, 10 -> PAID. c10: 5 -> PAID, 10 -> PAID. PAID: any coin -> PAID. Accept PAID. Input 5, 5, 5: c0, c5, c10, PAID, accept and drop the juice. Input 10, 5: c10, PAID. Where the analogy breaks: a real machine also gives change (10 + 10 = 20, so 5 taka back) and resets after serving. Machines that produce output like this are Moore and Mealy machines, which come in lesson 12.

Real use 2, the metro rail gate: States LOCKED and UNLOCKED. Inputs: TAP (a valid card) and PUSH (someone walks through). LOCKED: TAP -> UNLOCKED, PUSH -> LOCKED (the bar stays firm). UNLOCKED: TAP -> UNLOCKED, PUSH -> LOCKED (one person passed, lock again). Trace TAP, PUSH, PUSH: LOCKED, UNLOCKED, LOCKED, LOCKED. The second person is blocked. The real gate also has timers, invalid cards and sensors, which add more inputs and states, but still a finite number, so it is still a finite automaton at heart.

Real use 3, keywords in a lexer: A lexer must tell the keyword "if" from a name like "ifty". A DFA reads i, then f, and is in a state meaning "so far exactly if". If the next character is a letter, it moves to an "identifier" state; if it is a space or bracket, the token was the keyword. Lexer generators such as lex and flex build DFAs like this from patterns automatically.

The limit, in your own reasoning: Why can't a DFA with k states recognise a^n b^n? Feed it a, aa, aaa, up to k + 1 a's. That is k + 1 strings but only k states, so by pigeonhole two of them, say a^i and a^j with i different from j, end in the same state. Now add b^i to both. From the same state, the same input leads to the same final state, so the machine gives the same answer for a^i b^i and a^j b^i. But the first should be accepted and the second rejected. Contradiction. Finite memory cannot keep apart infinitely many different counts. Lesson 11 turns this into the pumping lemma.

Fewer states is better, but not urgent: The method may give extra states that behave the same. That is not wrong, just wasteful. Lesson 8 shows how to minimise any DFA to the smallest possible one, and that this smallest DFA is unique.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Choosing a summary that cannot be updated. Forgetting that in "contains" patterns, a failed match can be partly reused (the A on 1 stays A rule). Swapping accept states on an incomplete DFA or on an NFA. Forgetting that the product's start state is the pair of start states. Exams ask: design DFAs for "contains", "ends with", "number of a's mod k" languages; build the product for an AND or OR; complement a given DFA; compute δ* on a string.

Mental model: Picture each state as a sticky note on the machine's forehead. The note holds the summary, nothing more. Each new symbol is read, the old note is thrown away, and a new note is written using only the old note and the symbol. For two rules, the machine wears two notes side by side. To flip the answer, you do not touch the notes at all; you just change which notes count as "yes".

Recap and next: Design a DFA by deciding the smallest summary that answers the question and can be updated. The product construction runs two DFAs at once, giving AND, OR and difference by choosing the accept set. Swapping accept states complements a complete DFA. δ* follows a whole string. Next lesson we relax the rule of exactly one move and meet the nondeterministic finite automaton.
key_points: Each DFA state is a summary of the input so far; pick the smallest summary that answers the question and can be updated after every symbol.
Method: imagine reading left to right, decide what to remember, make one state per value, fill rows by 'what do I know now?', then test ε and examples.
Product construction runs two DFAs at once with pair states; m and n states give m × n states.
In the product, AND accepts pairs where both accept, OR where either accepts, difference where the first accepts and the second does not.
Complement a DFA by swapping accepting and non-accepting states, but only on a complete DFA (trap included), and never on an NFA.
δ*(q, ε) = q and δ*(q, wa) = δ(δ*(q, w), a); M accepts w exactly when δ*(q0, w) is in F.
Vending machines, metro gates and lexers are finite automata at heart; machines with output are Moore and Mealy machines.
By pigeonhole, k states cannot keep apart k + 1 different counts, which is why a^n b^n is not regular.
lessons.tip: Write the meaning of each state in words next to it, like 'B = last symbol was 0'. If you cannot write a clear meaning, the state is probably wrong or unnecessary.
lessons.task: Build the product DFA for 'contains 101 AND has even length' over {0, 1}: take the 4-state 'contains 101' machine and a 2-state length-parity machine, write all 8 pair states, and trace 0101 and 10101 by hand.

quiz.q: Two DFAs have 3 and 5 states. How many states does their product construction have?
quiz.explain: Each product state is a pair, one from each machine, so 3 × 5 = 15.

quiz.q: In the product for 'even 1s' and 'ends with 0', which accept set gives the OR (union)?
quiz.explain: OR accepts when at least one part accepts: E (even) or Z (ends with 0). Only (O,N) fails both.

quiz.q: Why must you add the trap state before complementing a DFA by swapping?
options: Strings with no arrow to follow would be rejected by both machines
quiz.explain: A string that falls off an incomplete machine is rejected in the original and in the swapped one, so the swap would not flip its answer.

quiz.q: With the 'contains 101' DFA (S start; S: 0->S, 1->A; A: 0->B, 1->A; B: 0->S, 1->F; F loops), where does 1001 end?
quiz.explain: S -1-> A -0-> B -0-> S -1-> A. A is not accepting, and 1001 has no 101.

quiz.q: For the vending machine (15 taka; c0, c5, c10, PAID), what is a limitation of this plain DFA?
options: It cannot give change or other output, which needs a machine with output
quiz.explain: A plain DFA only accepts or rejects. Giving change is output, handled by Moore or Mealy machines.

lessons.title: Nondeterministic Finite Automata (NFA)
lessons.content:
Imagine a little boy is lost at the Boishakhi mela, and his family splits up to find him. At every fork in the crowd, one person goes left and another goes right. Some searchers hit dead ends and stop. If even one searcher finds him, the search is a success. Nobody needed to know the right path in advance; trying all paths at once did the job. This is the idea behind today's machine, the nondeterministic finite automaton, or NFA. It is allowed to have several choices, and it succeeds if any choice works.

The problem that NFAs solve: Try to design a DFA for "the third symbol from the end is 1" over {0, 1}. A DFA reads left to right and does not know where the end is. So at every moment it must remember the last three symbols it has read, just in case the string ends now. Three symbols have 2^3 = 8 combinations, so you need 8 states and 16 arrows, drawn carefully. It is doable but painful. Now imagine "the tenth symbol from the end": 2^10 = 1024 states. Designers wanted a way to describe such languages simply, the way a human thinks: "at some point, guess that this 1 is the third from the end, then check that exactly two more symbols follow".

What an NFA is: An NFA is like a DFA with three rule changes. First, from a state on a symbol, there may be several next states. Second, there may be zero next states; that path simply dies. Third, there may be ε-moves (epsilon moves): jumps to another state without reading any symbol. The NFA accepts a string if at least one possible path through the machine reads the whole string and ends in an accepting state. It rejects only if every path fails.

Nondeterministic does not mean random: This is the most common misunderstanding. A random machine flips a coin and might give different answers on different days. An NFA gives one fixed answer for every string: accept if some path works, reject if none does. "Nondeterministic" only means the rules do not pick a single next step. The answer itself is completely determined.

View 1, the perfect guesser: Picture the NFA as a lucky player who, at every choice, always guesses the move that leads to acceptance, if such a move exists. If the string is in the language, the lucky guesses find an accepting path. If it is not, no guess can help. This view makes NFAs easy to design: you just say "guess where the important part starts".

View 2, parallel copies: Picture the NFA cloning itself at every choice, like the family at the mela. Each copy follows one option. A copy with no move dies. After the last symbol, if any surviving copy is in an accepting state, accept. Instead of tracking copies, we just track the set of states the copies are in. This view is how computers actually run NFAs, and it is how you trace them by hand.

The formal definition: An NFA is a 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F), the same as a DFA except for δ. Now δ: Q × Σε → P(Q), where Σε means Σ plus the symbol ε, and P(Q) is the power set of Q, the set of all subsets (from lesson 3). So δ(q, a) is a set of states, which may be empty. The result is a set, not a single state; that is the whole difference.

Example, third-last symbol is 1: States q0, q1, q2, q3. Start q0, accept q3. Row q0: on 0 go to {q0}, on 1 go to {q0, q1}. Row q1: on 0 go to {q2}, on 1 go to {q2}. Row q2: on 0 go to {q3}, on 1 go to {q3}. Row q3: on 0 go to ∅, on 1 go to ∅. As arrows: q0 --0,1--> q0, q0 --1--> q1, q1 --0,1--> q2, q2 --0,1--> q3. In guessing words: wait in q0; when you see a 1, either keep waiting or guess "this is the third-last", and move to q1; then you must read exactly two more symbols to reach q3 just as the input ends. Only 4 states, built in a minute.

Tracing with sets, input 0100: Start with the set {q0}. Read 0: q0 on 0 gives {q0}. Set {q0}. Read 1: q0 on 1 gives {q0, q1}. Set {q0, q1}. Read 0: q0 gives {q0}, q1 gives {q2}. Set {q0, q2}. Read 0: q0 gives {q0}, q2 gives {q3}. Set {q0, q3}. The input ends, and the set contains q3, an accepting state. Accept. Check: in 0100, the third-last symbol is 1. Correct. The copy that guessed at the 1 won.

Tracing input 0011: Start {q0}. Read 0: {q0}. Read 0: {q0}. Read 1: {q0, q1}. Read 1: q0 gives {q0, q1}, q1 gives {q2}, set {q0, q1, q2}. The input ends. No q3 in the set. Reject. Check: the third-last symbol of 0011 is 0. Correct. The copy that guessed at the first 1 was in q2, still one symbol short. The copy that guessed at the last 1 was only in q1.

Tracing input 1011: Start {q0}. Read 1: {q0, q1}. Read 0: {q0, q2}. Read 1: q0 gives {q0, q1}, q2 gives {q3}, set {q0, q1, q3}. Read 1: q0 gives {q0, q1}, q1 gives {q2}, q3 gives nothing, set {q0, q1, q2}. Reject. Notice something important: the set contained q3 in the middle, but that copy died when one more symbol came. Like a DFA, an NFA only cares about where it is when the input ends. The third-last symbol of 1011 is 0, so rejecting is right.

Why the NFA is so much smaller: The NFA for "n-th symbol from the end is 1" needs n + 1 states. Any DFA for the same language needs at least 2^n states, because it must remember the last n symbols, and different endings must lead to different states. For n = 10 that is 11 states against 1024. NFAs can be exponentially smaller. That is their superpower for describing patterns.

Dying copies replace trap states: In a DFA, a hopeless input must go somewhere, so we add a trap. In an NFA, a missing move just means δ gives ∅ and that copy dies. q3 above has no moves at all, and that is perfectly legal. If every copy dies, the set becomes ∅ and stays ∅, and the string is rejected.

ε-moves, free jumps: An ε-move lets the machine change state without reading anything. Why would you want that? To glue small machines together. Language: strings over {a, b} that are all a's or all b's, that is a* ∪ b*. Build it like this: start state s, with s --ε--> p and s --ε--> r. p loops on a: p --a--> p. r loops on b: r --b--> r. Accept p and r. The start state just "chooses" which small machine to enter, for free.

ε-closure: The ε-closure of a state q, written ECLOSE(q), is the set of all states you can reach from q using only ε-moves, including q itself (zero jumps count). To compute it, start with {q}, then keep adding any state reachable by an ε-arrow from something in your set, until nothing new appears. Like water spreading through pipes. For the machine above, ECLOSE(s) = {s, p, r}, ECLOSE(p) = {p}, ECLOSE(r) = {r}. If there were a chain p --ε--> x --ε--> y, then y would also be in ECLOSE(p).

Tracing with ε-moves: The rule is: start with the ε-closure of the start state, and after every symbol, take the ε-closure again. Input aa: start ECLOSE(s) = {s, p, r}. Read a: s has no a-move, p goes to p, r has no a-move, giving {p}; closure {p}. Read a: {p}. Ends with p, accepting. Accept. Input ab: start {s, p, r}. Read a: {p}. Read b: p has no b-move, so ∅. All copies dead. Reject, correct, since ab mixes letters. Input ε: no symbols read, the set is {s, p, r}, which contains p, accepting. Accept, correct, since ε is in a*.

How a computer runs an NFA: current = ECLOSE(start). For each symbol c: next = the union of δ(q, c) for every q in current; current = ECLOSE(next). At the end, accept if current contains any accepting state. Each step may touch every state, so for an NFA with k states and an input of length n, the work is about n × k steps (times the arrows per state). That is slower per symbol than a DFA's single lookup, but there is no exponential blow-up. Ken Thompson used exactly this kind of simulation in 1968 for fast regular expression search, and many text-search tools still use the idea.

Are NFAs more powerful than DFAs? No. Every NFA can be turned into a DFA that accepts the same language. The trick is that the set of states an NFA can be in is itself just one of finitely many sets, at most 2^k for k states. So a DFA can use each set as one of its states. This is the subset construction of the next lesson. NFAs and DFAs recognise exactly the same languages, the regular languages. Nondeterminism buys convenience and size, not power. Careful: for the stack machines later in the course, nondeterminism really does add power, so do not generalise this fact.

Real-life example 1, text search: Searching a document for the word "ban" is the language Σ* ban, any text ending in ban as you scan. The NFA is tiny: q0 loops on every character and also, on b, guesses "the word starts here" and moves to q1; q1 --a--> q2; q2 --n--> q3, accepting. Every time you read a b, a new copy starts checking. Search tools do exactly this, often after converting parts to a DFA for speed.

Real-life example 2, joining patterns: A simple spam filter might flag messages containing "free" or containing "offer". Build a small NFA for each pattern, then add a new start state with ε-moves into both. The OR is done in one step, without the product construction from the last lesson, and the result has roughly the sum of the states, not the product.

When to use an NFA: For designing and describing patterns, for gluing machines (union, concatenation, star), and as the bridge between regular expressions and DFAs in lesson 10. When not: When you need the fastest possible matching on huge inputs, convert to a DFA first. And never complement an NFA by swapping accept states. Try it on the third-last machine: make q0, q1 and q2 accepting and q3 not. Input 0100 ends in {q0, q3}, which now contains q0, so it is accepted, but it was also accepted by the original. Both machines accept it, so the swap is not a complement. Convert to a DFA first, then swap.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Thinking nondeterministic means random. Requiring all paths to accept instead of at least one. Forgetting the ε-closure of the start state, or forgetting to close after each symbol. Thinking a set that touched an accepting state mid-way means accept. Exams ask: give the 5-tuple, explain the two views, design an NFA for "contains", "ends with" or "n-th from last" languages, trace a string with sets of states, and compute ε-closures.

Mental model: Picture a bag of glowing tokens on the state diagram instead of one token. Start by placing a token on the start state, then let tokens flow along every ε-arrow. For each symbol, every token moves along every arrow with that symbol; a token with nowhere to go vanishes, tokens can split into many, and tokens landing on the same state merge into one. Then let them flow along ε-arrows again. When the input ends, if any token sits on a double circle, the machine says yes.

Recap and next: An NFA may have many, one or zero moves per symbol, plus ε-moves, and accepts if some path ends in an accepting state. Trace it by tracking the set of current states with ε-closure. NFAs can be exponentially smaller than DFAs but recognise the same languages. Next lesson we prove that by turning any NFA into a DFA with the subset construction.
key_points: An NFA may have several, one or zero next states per symbol, plus ε-moves that read nothing.
An NFA accepts if at least one path reads the whole input and ends in an accepting state; it rejects only if every path fails.
Nondeterministic does not mean random: the answer for each string is fixed.
Two views: a perfect guesser, or parallel copies; in practice we track the set of current states.
Formally δ: Q × Σε → P(Q), so each move gives a set of states, possibly empty.
ECLOSE(q) is every state reachable from q by ε-moves alone, including q; take it at the start and after every symbol.
The NFA for 'n-th symbol from the end is 1' has n + 1 states, while any DFA needs 2^n.
