NFAs and DFAs recognise exactly the same languages; swapping accept states does not complement an NFA.
lessons.tip: When tracing an NFA, write one row per symbol with the full set of states, and redo the ε-closure every time. Most lost marks come from a forgotten closure, not from wrong arrows.
lessons.task: Draw an NFA over {a, b} for strings that end in ab (3 states are enough: wait, saw a, saw ab). Trace aab, abb and babab with sets of states and check each answer by just looking at the string's ending.

quiz.q: When does an NFA accept a string?
options: When every path ends in an accepting state
When at least one path reads the whole string and ends in an accepting state
When it passes through an accepting state at any time
When the set of states is empty
quiz.explain: One successful path is enough. Touching an accepting state mid-way does not count; only the end matters.

quiz.q: Third-last-is-1 NFA (q0: 0->{q0}, 1->{q0,q1}; q1 -> q2; q2 -> q3; q3 has no moves; accept q3). What is the set after reading 010?
In the machine s --ε--> p, s --ε--> r, p loops on a, r loops on b, what is ECLOSE(s)?
quiz.explain: The closure includes s itself (zero jumps) and every state reached by ε-moves: p and r.

quiz.q: Why can an NFA for 'the 10th symbol from the end is 1' be much smaller than any DFA for it?
options: NFAs ignore the end of the input
The NFA guesses where the 10th-last symbol is, while a DFA must remember the last 10 symbols, needing 2^10 states
quiz.explain: The NFA needs 11 states; a DFA must keep every possible 10-symbol ending apart.

quiz.q: Which statement about NFAs and DFAs is true?
options: NFAs recognise more languages than DFAs
Every NFA has a DFA recognising the same language
Swapping accept states always complements an NFA
quiz.explain: The subset construction turns any NFA into an equivalent DFA, so they recognise the same languages.

lessons.title: NFA to DFA: The Subset Construction
lessons.content:
Imagine your cousin got on the Dhaka metro rail, and you are tracking him by phone. He says "I changed trains" or "I got off" but never tells you exactly where he is. So you do something clever: you keep a written list of every station he could possibly be at right now. Each time he sends a new message, you cross out stations and add new ones. Your list is always exact, even though he never tells you one single place. That list-keeping trick is the whole secret of this lesson. It turns a guessing machine (NFA) into a normal, no-guessing machine (DFA).

Quick recap of the two machines: A DFA (deterministic finite automaton) is a pretend machine with a fixed set of states. A state is just a memory box like "I have seen an odd number of 1s so far". The machine reads an input string one symbol at a time. For every state and every symbol there is exactly ONE arrow to follow. When the string ends, if the machine stands on an accept state, it says yes. An NFA (nondeterministic finite automaton) relaxes the rule: from a state, a symbol may lead to many states, or to none, and there can be ε-moves (ε is the empty string), which are free jumps that read nothing. An NFA accepts a string if at least ONE possible path ends in an accept state.

The problem this lesson solves: NFAs are easy for humans to design, as you saw with "third-last symbol is 1". But a real computer cannot magically guess. Hardware chips, lexers inside compilers and fast text search tools want one fixed next step for every symbol, with no backtracking. So we ask: can every NFA be turned into a DFA that accepts exactly the same language? If yes, NFAs are just a design shortcut, not a more powerful machine. The answer is yes, and the method is called the subset construction (also called the powerset construction). It was published by Michael Rabin and Dana Scott in 1959.

What people did before: You could try one path, and if it fails, go back and try another. That is called backtracking, and on a long string the number of paths can explode. Or you could design the DFA by hand, which is painful and error-prone. The subset construction does the bookkeeping once, in advance, and gives a DFA that never backtracks.

The key idea from first principles: Let us think about what an NFA really "knows" after reading some input. It does not know one state. It knows a SET of states, all the places where some path could be right now. Fact one: the NFA has a finite number of states, say n. Fact two: a set of states is just a subset of those n states. Fact three: there are only 2^n possible subsets, which is a finite number. So "the set of states I could be in" is a finite piece of memory. A DFA is exactly a machine with finite memory. So we let each DFA state stand for one subset of NFA states. That is the whole proof idea, in four small steps.

The recipe in plain words: The DFA start state is the set of NFA states you can be in before reading anything: the NFA start state plus anything reachable from it by ε-moves. For any DFA state S (a set) and a symbol a, the next DFA state is: take every NFA state in S, follow all its a-arrows, collect all the landing places into one set, then add everything reachable from those by ε-moves. A DFA state is accepting if its set contains at least one NFA accept state, because that means at least one path could be accepting. If the set becomes empty, that is the dead state: no path survives, so no future input can lead to acceptance.

Why the accept rule is correct: The subset tracks ALL paths at once. If any member of the final set is an accept state, some path accepted; if none is, every path failed. So the NFA's "OR over all paths" rule becomes the DFA's "does the set contain an accept state" rule.

Worked example 1, the NFA: Our language is all binary strings that end with 01. The NFA has three states q0, q1, q2. Start is q0. Accept is q2. Arrows: q0 --0--> q0, q0 --1--> q0 (stay in q0 on anything), q0 --0--> q1 (guess "this 0 is the start of the final 01"), q1 --1--> q2. No arrows leave q2, and q1 has no arrow on 0. The NFA "guesses" when the last 01 begins.

Building the DFA table, one row at a time: We only build rows for subsets we actually reach, starting from the start set. Row {q0}: on 0, q0 can go to q0 or q1, so we get {q0,q1}. On 1, q0 goes only to q0, so {q0}. New set found: {q0,q1}. Row {q0,q1}: on 0, q0 gives {q0,q1} and q1 gives nothing, so {q0,q1}. On 1, q0 gives {q0} and q1 gives {q2}, so {q0,q2}. New set found: {q0,q2}. Row {q0,q2}: on 0, q0 gives {q0,q1}, q2 gives nothing, so {q0,q1}. On 1, q0 gives {q0}, q2 gives nothing, so {q0}. No new sets. We stop. The DFA has just three states. Only {q0,q2} contains q2, so it is the only accept state.

Rename and read the DFA: Call {q0} = A, {q0,q1} = B, {q0,q2} = C. The arrows are A --0--> B, A --1--> A, B --0--> B, B --1--> C, C --0--> B, C --1--> A. Read the meaning: A means "does not end in 0 or 01", B means "ends in 0", C means "ends in 01". It is the DFA you might design by hand, but it fell out of a recipe.

Tracing 1101: Start in A = {q0}. Read 1: A --1--> A, still {q0}. Read 1: still A. Read 0: A --0--> B = {q0,q1}. Read 1: B --1--> C = {q0,q2}. The string ended in C, which contains q2, so accept. Check: 1101 really ends with 01. Now trace 0010: A --0--> B, B --0--> B, B --1--> C, C --0--> B. We end in B = {q0,q1}, which has no q2, so reject. Correct, because 0010 ends with 10.

Unreachable subsets: Three NFA states give 2^3 = 8 possible subsets: {}, {q0}, {q1}, {q2}, {q0,q1}, {q0,q2}, {q1,q2}, {q0,q1,q2}. Our DFA used only 3 of them. The other 5 can never be reached from the start, so we never draw them. That is why the "lazy" method, building rows only for sets you actually reach, is the smart way. Writing all 2^n rows is not wrong, but it wastes time and clutters the diagram.

ε-closure, the tool for ε-moves: The ε-closure of a state is the set of all states you can reach from it using only ε-moves, including the state itself (zero moves is allowed). Think of a free lift: once you stand at its door, you are effectively on every floor it can take you to. Whenever we compute a DFA state, we always close it under ε, both for the start state and after every symbol.

Worked example 2, with ε-moves: Language a*b*c*, meaning some a's, then some b's, then some c's, any count including zero. The ε-NFA: q0 --a--> q0, q0 --ε--> q1, q1 --b--> q1, q1 --ε--> q2, q2 --c--> q2. Start q0, accept q2. Step one: the DFA start is the ε-closure of q0, which is {q0,q1,q2}, because q0 can slide freely to q1 and then to q2. Since it contains q2, the start is accepting, which makes sense: the empty string is in a*b*c*.

Building the rows: Row {q0,q1,q2}: on a, only q0 moves, to q0, and the closure of {q0} is {q0,q1,q2}. On b, only q1 moves, to q1, closure {q1,q2}. On c, only q2 moves, closure {q2}. Row {q1,q2}: on a, nobody moves, so the empty set {}. On b, closure of {q1} is {q1,q2}. On c, {q2}. Row {q2}: on a, {}. On b, {}. On c, {q2}. Row {}: every symbol leads back to {}. This is the dead state. Final DFA: 4 states. Accepting: {q0,q1,q2}, {q1,q2}, {q2}, since each contains q2. The dead state {} is not accepting.

Trace aabcc and aba: For aabcc: start {q0,q1,q2}, a stays there, a stays there, b goes to {q1,q2}, c goes to {q2}, c stays {q2}. Accept. For aba: {q0,q1,q2}, a stays, b goes to {q1,q2}, a goes to {}. Once in the dead state you never come back, so reject. That matches the rule: you cannot write an a after a b.

The exponential blow-up: The subset construction can create up to 2^n DFA states from an n-state NFA. Sometimes this really happens. Take the language "the third symbol from the end is 1" from the last lesson. The NFA needs only 4 states: it guesses which 1 is third from the end, then counts two more symbols. But any DFA must remember the last three symbols, since any of them may become "third from the end" later. There are 2^3 = 8 combinations of three bits, and two different combinations can always be told apart by some future input, so the DFA needs 8 states. In general, "the k-th symbol from the end is 1" needs k+1 NFA states but 2^k DFA states. For k = 20 that is 21 versus about one million.

Why both machines still have equal power: We showed every NFA can be converted to a DFA that accepts the same language. And every DFA already is an NFA (one that just happens to have exactly one arrow each time). So the set of languages DFAs recognise and the set NFAs recognise are the same: the regular languages. Nondeterminism adds convenience and compactness, not power, for finite automata. Careful: for pushdown automata (later lessons), nondeterminism does add power.

Real life example 1, the lexer: When a compiler reads your C or Java code, the first stage, the lexer, splits text into tokens like keywords, numbers and names. Tool writers describe each token with a pattern, turn the patterns into one big NFA, then run the subset construction to get a DFA table. The DFA reads every character exactly once with a single table lookup, which is very fast. Tools like lex and flex work this way.

Real life example 2, a bKash-style menu: Picture a phone USSD menu sketched with "this key could mean either option" branches, which is an NFA. Before coding it, a designer merges the possibilities into combined states like "user is either in Send Money or in Payment", which is exactly subset thinking. Where the analogy breaks: real menus usually are designed to be deterministic from the start, and they store extra data like amounts, which a finite automaton does not.

When to use it and when not: Use the subset construction when you need speed on many inputs, for example a search tool scanning gigabytes of logs, because each character then costs one lookup. Do not blindly use it when the NFA is large and the blow-up is real: a 40-state NFA might need billions of DFA states. In that case, tools simulate the NFA directly by keeping the current set of states during the run (the same idea, but computed on the fly), or they build DFA states lazily, only when an input actually needs them. That is a classic trade-off: memory for the table versus time per character.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting the ε-closure of the start state is the number one mistake. Second, forgetting the dead state {} when a set becomes empty, which leaves the DFA incomplete. Third, marking a subset as accepting only when it contains ALL accept states; the rule is "contains at least one". Fourth, treating {q0,q1} and {q1,q0} as different states; they are the same set. Exams give a small NFA to convert, draw and trace, or ask for the maximum number of DFA states (2^n).

Mental model: Picture the NFA as a board game where one coin can split into many coins. At every step, each coin moves along all its allowed arrows, coins on the same square merge, and coins with no arrow vanish. The DFA state is simply a photo of which squares have coins. Since the board has finitely many squares, there are finitely many possible photos, and the DFA is just the list of photos with "after symbol a, photo X becomes photo Y". Accept if any coin sits on an accept square.

Recap and what is next: Subset construction turns any NFA into an equivalent DFA by using sets of NFA states as DFA states, closing under ε-moves, and building only reachable sets. It proves DFAs and NFAs recognise the same languages, at the possible cost of 2^n states. But the DFA we get is not always the smallest possible. In the next lesson we learn DFA minimization: how to merge states that behave identically, and why the smallest DFA for a language is unique.
key_points: Subset construction: each DFA state is a set of NFA states, the places the NFA could be right now.
DFA start = ε-closure of the NFA start state; next set = ε-closure of all a-moves from the current set.
A DFA state accepts if its set contains at least one NFA accept state.
The empty set is the dead state; build rows only for reachable sets.
An n-state NFA can need up to 2^n DFA states; 'k-th symbol from the end is 1' really needs 2^k.
DFAs and NFAs recognise exactly the same languages: the regular languages.
Trade-off: a DFA table gives one lookup per character but may need huge memory; NFA simulation saves memory but costs more per character.
lessons.tip: Always work from a queue: write the start set first, and each time a new set appears in a row, add it to the bottom of your list. When the list has no unprocessed sets, you are done. This stops you from missing or duplicating rows.
lessons.task: On paper, convert the NFA for 'third symbol from the end is 1' (q0 loops on 0 and 1, q0 --1--> q1, q1 --0,1--> q2, q2 --0,1--> q3, accept q3) into a DFA. Count the reachable sets; you should get exactly 8. Then trace the string 0100 on your DFA and check the answer by hand.

quiz.q: An NFA has 5 states. What is the maximum number of states its subset-construction DFA can have?
quiz.explain: Each DFA state is a subset of the 5 NFA states, and there are 2^5 = 32 subsets, including the empty dead state.

quiz.q: When is a DFA state produced by subset construction an accept state?
options: When its set contains at least one NFA accept state
When its set contains all NFA accept states
When its set is the start set
quiz.explain: The NFA accepts if any path ends in an accept state, so one accept member in the set is enough.

quiz.q: For the ε-NFA q0 --ε--> q1 --ε--> q2, what is the ε-closure of q0?
quiz.explain: The ε-closure includes the state itself plus everything reachable by free ε-moves: q1 and then q2.

quiz.q: In the 'ends with 01' DFA built from {q0}, {q0,q1}, {q0,q2}, where does the string 0010 finish?
What does the subset construction prove about NFAs and DFAs?
options: NFAs recognise more languages than DFAs
They recognise exactly the same languages
DFAs are always bigger than NFAs
quiz.explain: Every NFA converts to an equivalent DFA and every DFA is already an NFA, so both recognise the regular languages.

lessons.title: DFA Minimization: Table-Filling and Myhill-Nerode
lessons.content:
Think about two shopkeepers at Karwan Bazar who sell the same rice at the same price, give the same discount and close at the same time. For a customer, they are the same shop, even if their signboards are different. If you were making a list of "shops that behave differently", you would write them down as one. DFA minimization does exactly this with states: it finds states that behave the same for every possible future input and merges them, until no two remaining states behave alike.

Why we need it: In the last lesson, the subset construction gave us DFAs, but nothing promised they were small. DFAs built by hand also often have extra states, because a designer remembers more than needed. Extra states cost memory in hardware circuits, make lexer tables bigger, and make it harder to check whether two machines are the same. A smaller DFA for the same language is simply better. The question is: how do we know which states are extra, and how small can we go?

The core question, from first principles: When are two states "the same"? A state is useful only for what happens next. So imagine putting a coin on state p and another coin on state q, and then feeding both the same leftover input string w. If, for EVERY possible w, both coins end up either both accepting or both rejecting, then no experiment can ever tell p and q apart. They are called equivalent (or indistinguishable). If there is even ONE string w where one coin ends in an accept state and the other does not, then p and q are distinguishable, and w is called a distinguishing string. Equivalent states can be merged safely, because the merged machine gives the same answer on every input.

A small but important fact: The empty string ε is also a possible future input. Feeding ε means "stop right now". So an accept state and a non-accept state are always distinguishable, by ε. This gives the starting point of every minimization algorithm: first separate accepting from non-accepting.

The second fact, which makes the algorithm work: Suppose on symbol a, state p goes to p' and state q goes to q'. If p' and q' are distinguishable by some string w, then p and q are distinguishable by the string aw. Why? Reading a moves the two coins to p' and q', and then w separates them. So distinguishability spreads backwards along arrows. The table-filling algorithm is just this fact repeated until nothing new happens.

Step zero, remove unreachable states: A state that cannot be reached from the start state by any input is useless; no string ever visits it. To find them, start from the start state and follow all arrows (a simple graph search, like BFS from your Data Structures course). Any state never visited gets deleted, along with its arrows. Do this first, because an unreachable state may look equivalent or not, and it only wastes table space.

Our example DFA: Alphabet {0,1}. Six states A to F. Start is A. Only D accepts. Arrows: A --0--> B, A --1--> C; B --0--> E, B --1--> D; C --0--> B, C --1--> C; D --0--> E, D --1--> C; E --0--> E, E --1--> D; F --0--> D, F --1--> F. This machine accepts binary strings ending in 01, but it was designed carelessly. Look: no arrow from any state goes into F. Starting from A we reach B and C, from them E and D, and then nothing new. So F is unreachable. Delete it. Five states remain: A, B, C, D, E.

The table: Draw a triangle table with one cell for each pair of states: (A,B), (A,C), (A,D), (A,E), (B,C), (B,D), (B,E), (C,D), (C,E), (D,E). That is 10 pairs, because 5 states give 5 times 4 divided by 2 = 10 pairs. We will put an X in a cell when we prove that pair is distinguishable.

Round 1, accept versus non-accept: D accepts and the others do not. So mark every pair containing D exactly once: (A,D), (B,D), (C,D), (D,E). The string ε distinguishes each of them. Four X's so far.

Round 2, look one step ahead: For each unmarked pair, check both symbols. If they lead to a marked pair, mark this one. Pair (A,B): on 0, A goes to B and B goes to E, giving (B,E), not marked yet. On 1, A goes to C and B goes to D, giving (C,D), which IS marked. So mark (A,B). Its distinguishing string is 1 followed by ε, just "1": from A, reading 1 lands in C (reject), from B it lands in D (accept). Pair (A,C): on 0 both go to B, the same state. On 1 both go to C, the same state. Not marked. Pair (A,E): on 1, A goes to C and E goes to D, (C,D) is marked, so mark (A,E). Pair (B,C): on 1, B goes to D and C goes to C, marked pair, so mark (B,C). Pair (B,E): on 0, B goes to E and E goes to E, the same state. On 1, both go to D. Not marked. Pair (C,E): on 1, C goes to C and E goes to D, marked, so mark (C,E).

Round 3, repeat until no change: Only (A,C) and (B,E) are still unmarked. Check (A,C) again: its successors are (B,B) and (C,C), which are not pairs of different states at all, so they can never be marked. The same is true for (B,E): successors (E,E) and (D,D). Nothing new is marked in this round, so we stop. Rule: stop when a whole round adds no new X.

Reading the answer: Unmarked pairs are equivalent. So A is equivalent to C, and B is equivalent to E. The groups are {A,C}, {B,E}, {D}. Merge each group into one state. Call them P = {A,C}, Q = {B,E}, R = {D}. New arrows come from any member, since all members agree: P --0--> Q, P --1--> P; Q --0--> Q, Q --1--> R; R --0--> Q, R --1--> P. Start is P because it contains A. Accept is R because it contains D. Six states became three. This is the same three-state DFA we got from the subset construction in the last lesson, which is a nice cross-check.

Trace to check: Take 1001. In the old machine: A --1--> C --0--> B --0--> E --1--> D, accept. In the new machine: P --1--> P --0--> Q --0--> Q --1--> R, accept. Take 0110. Old: A --0--> B --1--> D --1--> C --0--> B, reject. New: P --0--> Q --1--> R --1--> P --0--> Q, reject. The answers agree, as they must.

Why the algorithm is correct: Every X we place is backed by a real distinguishing string, built backwards from ε, so we never wrongly separate two states. And if two states are distinguishable, the shortest distinguishing string has some length k, and it will be found in round k+1 at the latest, because each round finds strings one symbol longer. So when a round adds nothing, every distinguishable pair has been found. A round that continues must mark at least one new pair, and there are finitely many pairs, so the algorithm always stops.

Partition refinement, the other common method: Instead of pairs, think in groups. Start with two groups: accepting {D} and non-accepting {A,B,C,E}. Now, inside each group, check where each state goes, in terms of groups. In {A,B,C,E}: on 1, A goes to C (non-accept group), B goes to D (accept group), C goes to C (non-accept), E goes to D (accept). States that point to different groups must be split. So split into {A,C} and {B,E}. Check again with the new groups: {A,C} both go to {B,E} on 0 and to {A,C} on 1. {B,E} both go to {B,E} on 0 and to {D} on 1. Nothing splits, so we are done, with the same answer. This is Moore's algorithm. A smarter version by John Hopcroft (1971) runs in O(n log n) time, which is what fast tools use.

Uniqueness of the minimal DFA: Here is a surprising and very useful fact: for every regular language, the minimal DFA is unique, apart from the names of its states. Whatever DFA you start with, if you remove unreachable states and merge equivalent ones, you get the same shape. This gives a clean test for whether two DFAs accept the same language: minimize both and check if they are the same machine with renamed states.

The Myhill-Nerode idea: Now flip the view from states to strings. Call two strings x and y equivalent for a language L if, for every suffix z, xz is in L exactly when yz is in L. In plain words, after reading x or y, the future looks the same. For "ends with 01", there are exactly three classes: strings that end in 01, strings that end in 0, and all the rest. These match our states R, Q, P. The Myhill-Nerode theorem says: L is regular if and only if the number of such classes is finite, and that number is exactly the number of states in the minimal DFA. Bonus: it also proves a language is NOT regular. For {a^n b^n}, the strings a, aa, aaa, ... are all in different classes, because the suffix b^i accepts a^i but rejects a^j for j not equal to i. Infinitely many classes means no DFA can exist. Lesson 11 shows another tool for this, the pumping lemma.

Real life example 1, the metro rail gate: An engineer designs a gate controller with states like "locked, no card", "locked, card was rejected", "locked, after alarm reset". If all three react the same way to every future event (card tap, push, timeout), minimization merges them into one "locked" state. The circuit needs fewer flip-flops, each flip-flop being a tiny one-bit memory cell. Fewer states, less hardware, lower cost.

Real life example 2, text search tools: A regex engine compiles a pattern to an NFA, converts to a DFA, and then minimizes it. Smaller tables fit better in the CPU cache, which is the small, very fast memory close to the processor, so scanning big files runs faster. Where the analogy with shops breaks: shops can behave the same today and differently tomorrow, but DFA states never change; equivalence is checked against all futures at once.

When not to bother: For a tiny DFA used once, minimization is not worth the effort. Also, minimization only applies to DFAs. Minimizing an NFA is a much harder problem in general, and the table-filling method does not work on NFAs, because NFA states do not have one fixed next state.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting to remove unreachable states first, which leaves extra states that the table cannot always detect as useless. Stopping after one pass instead of repeating rounds until nothing changes. Marking (p,q) because p and q go to DIFFERENT states; the rule is that they go to a MARKED pair, and going to different but equivalent states is fine. Using a DFA that is missing arrows; add a dead state first so every state has every arrow. Exams give a 6 to 8 state DFA and ask for the table, the final groups, and the minimized diagram, or ask you to state Myhill-Nerode.

Mental model: Picture every state as a person who will answer "yes" or "no" to every possible future story you could tell. Two people are the same if their answers agree for every story. You find disagreements cheaply: accept versus reject disagree on the empty story, and if two people step to two disagreeing people after one word, they disagree too. Keep spreading disagreements backwards; whoever never disagrees is merged. The final machine has one person per "kind of future".

Recap and next: Remove unreachable states, separate accept from non-accept, then keep marking pairs that lead into marked pairs until nothing changes; unmarked pairs merge. The minimal DFA is unique, and Myhill-Nerode ties its size to the number of string classes. Next lesson moves from machines to a compact way of writing languages as text: regular expressions.
key_points: Two states are equivalent if every future string leads both to accept or both to reject; otherwise some distinguishing string exists.
Always remove unreachable states first using a graph search from the start state.
Table-filling: mark all (accept, non-accept) pairs, then mark any pair whose successors on some symbol form a marked pair; repeat until a round adds nothing.
Unmarked pairs are equivalent; merge each group into one state.
Partition refinement (Moore) splits groups whose members point to different groups; Hopcroft's version runs in O(n log n).
The minimal DFA of a regular language is unique up to renaming states, which gives an equivalence test.
Myhill-Nerode: L is regular exactly when it has finitely many string classes, and that count equals the minimal DFA size.
lessons.tip: Write the distinguishing string next to every X in your table. It costs a few seconds, catches wrong marks, and many examiners give extra marks for it.
lessons.task: Draw a DFA over {a,b} for 'even number of a's' but use four states: E1, O1, E2, O2, where E1 --a--> O1 --a--> E2 --a--> O2 --a--> E1 and every state loops on b; E1 and E2 accept. Run the table-filling algorithm and check that you get exactly two groups.

quiz.q: Why is every pair (accept state, non-accept state) marked in the first round?
options: Because the empty string ε already distinguishes them
Because they have different numbers of arrows
quiz.explain: Feeding ε means stopping now: one accepts and the other rejects, so they can never be merged.

quiz.q: In the example, A --1--> C and B --1--> D, and (C,D) is marked. What follows?
options: (A,B) must be marked, distinguished by the string 1
quiz.explain: If the successors are distinguishable by w, then the pair is distinguishable by 1w; here w = ε.

quiz.q: When does the table-filling algorithm stop?
options: When a whole round marks no new pair
When the start state is marked
quiz.explain: Each round finds distinguishing strings one symbol longer; a round with no new marks means nothing more can be found.

quiz.q: What does the Myhill-Nerode theorem say about {a^n b^n}?
options: It has infinitely many classes, so it is not regular
It has 2 classes, so it is regular
Its minimal DFA has n states
quiz.explain: The strings a, aa, aaa, ... are pairwise distinguishable, so there are infinitely many classes and no DFA can exist.

quiz.q: Which statement about minimal DFAs is true?
options: Every language has many different minimal DFAs
Minimizing an NFA uses the same table method
The minimal DFA of a regular language is unique up to renaming states
quiz.explain: Uniqueness is why comparing minimized DFAs is a correct test for equal languages.

lessons.title: Regular Expressions
lessons.content:
Every mobile number in Bangladesh looks like 01XXXXXXXXX: it starts with 01, then an operator digit like 7 or 8, then eight more digits, eleven digits in total. You understood that rule from one short pattern, without anyone drawing you a machine with states and arrows. A regular expression is exactly that: a short line of text that describes a whole language, often an infinite one. In this lesson we learn the theory version, how to build them, the algebra rules they obey, and how they differ from the "regex" you type in Python or in an editor.

What problem it solves: So far we described languages in two ways. One was English sentences, like "all strings that end with 01", which are clear to humans but vague for computers. The other was drawing DFAs and NFAs, which are exact but slow to draw and hard to type into a program. We want something exact, short, and typeable. Regular expressions are that middle ground. The mathematician Stephen Kleene introduced them in the early 1950s to describe what simple "nerve net" machines can recognise. Ken Thompson later put them into text editors and Unix tools, which is why every programmer uses them today.

The building blocks: A regular expression (regex for short) is built from three kinds of basic pieces. The symbol ∅ describes the empty language, which contains no strings at all. The symbol ε describes the language containing only the empty string. Any single alphabet symbol, like a, describes the language {a}. That is all the base material. Everything else is built by combining smaller regexes with three operations.

The three operations: Union, written R + S (programmers write R|S), means "a string from R or a string from S". So a + b describes {a, b}. Concatenation, written RS, means "a string from R followed by a string from S". So ab describes {ab}, and (a + b)c describes {ac, bc}. Star, written R*, means "zero or more strings from R glued together". So a* describes {ε, a, aa, aaa, ...}. Notice zero copies is allowed, which is why ε is always in R*. These three are the same operations on languages you met in lesson 02, now written as a formula.

Why only these three: From first principles, think about what a finite automaton can do. It can choose between paths (union), go through one part then another (concatenation), and loop back (star). These are exactly the three shapes of path in a graph. That is the deep reason regexes and finite automata describe the same languages, which is the topic of the next lesson.

Handy shorthands: R+ (written as a superscript plus) means "one or more", and equals RR*. R? means "zero or one" and equals R + ε. (0 + 1 + ... + 9) is often shortened to [0-9]. These do not add any new power; they are just abbreviations of the three operations.

Precedence, the order of operations: Just like in arithmetic, where multiplication binds tighter than addition, regexes have an order: star first, then concatenation, then union. So ab* + c means (a(b*)) + c, which describes {c, a, ab, abb, ...}. It does NOT mean (ab)* + c, and it does not mean a(b* + c). When in doubt, add brackets. Writing (ab)* when you mean ab* is one of the most common mistakes, and they are very different: (ab)* gives {ε, ab, abab, ...}, while ab* gives {a, ab, abb, ...}.

Reading a regex aloud: Read (0 + 1)*01 as "any string of 0s and 1s, then 01". The part (0 + 1)* is the "anything" block over alphabet {0,1}: each round of the star picks a 0 or a 1, so any string can be built. That is why (a + b)* over alphabet {a,b} describes ALL strings, which we call Σ*.

Building regexes, method: Do not try to guess the regex in one shot. Ask: what is the fixed part, what is the free part, and what is forbidden? Then build from small pieces and test with a few strings that should be in and a few that should be out. Let us work through six examples.

Example 1, ends with 01: The fixed part is 01 at the end. Before it, anything. Answer: (0 + 1)*01. Test: 1101 is in (1 and 1 from the star, then 01). 0110 is not, because it does not end in 01.

Example 2, contains aa somewhere: Fixed part aa, anything before, anything after: (a + b)*aa(a + b)*. Test: baab is in. abab is not, because two a's are never next to each other.

Example 3, even length: An even-length string is a sequence of blocks of two symbols. One block is (a + b)(a + b). So the answer is ((a + b)(a + b))*. Zero blocks gives ε, whose length 0 is even, which is correct.

Example 4, at most one a over {a,b}: Some b's, then maybe one a, then some b's: b*(a + ε)b*. Test: bbabb is in, bab is in, bbb is in (choose ε), aba is out.

Example 5, number of a's divisible by 3: Think of "chunks": each chunk contains exactly three a's, with b's allowed anywhere around them. One chunk is ab*ab*ab*. Before the first chunk there may be b's. Answer: b*(ab*ab*ab*)*. Test: babbaba has three a's. Split it as b, then one chunk a, bb, a, b, a. In. The string aab has two a's, so it must be out, and indeed no split works.

Example 6, no two 1s next to each other: Here we think about what is forbidden: "11". So every 1 must be followed by a 0, except maybe a 1 at the very end. Build the string from blocks "0" and "10", then allow an optional final 1: (0 + 10)*(ε + 1). Test 0101: blocks 0, 10, then a final 1. In. Test 110: the first 1 must start a "10" block, but the next symbol is 1. No block fits, so out. Correct.

Going the other way, regex to words: Exams also hand you a regex and ask what it means. Take (0 + 1)*1(0 + 1). Read it from the right: the last symbol is anything, the symbol before it must be 1, and anything can come before that. So it describes "binary strings whose second-last symbol is 1". Check with examples: 10 is in, 011 is in, 01 is out (its second-last symbol is 0), and 1 is out because it has no second-last symbol at all. A good habit: generate the three or four shortest strings the regex allows, and the pattern usually jumps out. For this one they are 10, 11, 010, 011, 110 and 111.

The algebra of regexes: Two regexes are equal if they describe the same language. Many rules follow directly from the meaning, so you do not need to memorise them. R + ∅ = R, because adding no strings changes nothing. Rε = εR = R, because gluing the empty string adds nothing. R∅ = ∅R = ∅, because concatenation needs one string from each side, and ∅ has none to give. This one surprises people: ∅ behaves like zero in multiplication, ε behaves like one. ∅* = ε, because the star always includes zero copies, which is ε. ε* = ε. R + R = R, since a set union with itself is itself. (R*)* = R*, and R*R* = R*. Also R(S + T) = RS + RT, like opening brackets in algebra.

Rules that look true but are not: (RS)* is not R*S*. Counterexample: abab is in (ab)* but not in a*b*, because in a*b* all a's come before all b's. (R + S)* is not R* + S*: ab is in (a + b)* but not in a* + b*. However, (a + b)* = (a*b*)* is true: each round of the outer star can pick any run of a's then b's, so every string can be built. When you suspect a rule, find a short string that breaks it. That is how you test, instead of trusting memory.

Theory regex versus real-world regex: In Python, JavaScript or grep, the pattern ^01[3-9][0-9]{8}$ means: ^ is the start of the line, 01 is literal, [3-9] is one digit from 3 to 9, [0-9]{8} is exactly eight digits, and $ is the end. In theory notation it is 01(3 + 4 + ... + 9)(0 + 1 + ... + 9) written 8 times in a row. Every piece is still union, concatenation or star, so this pattern is a true regular expression. You could run grep -E '^01[3-9][0-9]{8}$' contacts.txt to list the valid numbers in a file.

Where real regex goes beyond theory: Many programming engines support backreferences, like ^(.*)\1$, where \1 means "the same text the first group matched". This matches strings of the form ww, like abcabc. The language {ww} is NOT regular, so no DFA exists for it. In other words, these "regex" engines are more powerful than regular expressions, and they pay for it: they use backtracking, and some patterns like (a+)+$ can take exponential time on a long string of a's ending in a wrong character. That is a real cause of website outages. Engines like Google's RE2 and Go's regexp package refuse backreferences and use automata, so they always run in time proportional to the input length.

Real life example, email check: A simple pattern like [a-z0-9.]+@[a-z]+\.[a-z]+ accepts rahim.k@gmail.com and rejects rahim@gmail. It is useful for catching typing mistakes in a form. Where it breaks: real email rules are much more complicated, so no short regex matches exactly all valid emails. The honest approach is a loose regex plus sending a confirmation email.

When not to use regexes: Regexes cannot count without limit. Balanced brackets like (()()), nested HTML tags, or a^n b^n need memory that grows, which a finite automaton does not have. For those, you need a grammar and a parser, coming in lesson 13. Also, a huge clever regex is hard to read and debug; sometimes ten lines of normal code are better engineering.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mixing up ∅ and ε: ∅ is "no strings", ε is "one string, the empty one". Forgetting that star includes zero copies. Wrong precedence, like writing ab* for (ab)*. Writing a* + b* when the question wants (a + b)*. Forgetting the case where the string is empty or very short. Exams ask: "write a regex for strings with at least two a's", "describe L((0 + 1)*1(0 + 1))", or "prove or disprove (a + b)* = a*(ba*)*". That last one is true: after the first run of a's, every b starts a new block followed by a's.

Mental model: Think of a regex as a recipe for a train of carriages. Concatenation couples carriages in order. Union is a junction where you choose one track. Star is a loop track you can go around zero or more times. Any string the train can spell while following the tracks is in the language. This picture is almost exactly an NFA, which is no accident.

Recap and next: A regex is built from ∅, ε and symbols using union, concatenation and star, with star binding tightest. Build regexes from fixed parts, free parts and forbidden patterns, and always test with strings. Equalities follow from meaning; disprove fake ones with a counterexample. Real-world regex adds shorthands and sometimes extra non-regular power. Next lesson proves that regexes and finite automata are equally powerful, by converting in both directions.
key_points: A regex is built from ∅, ε and single symbols using union (+), concatenation and star (*).
Precedence: star first, then concatenation, then union; ab* is not (ab)*.
R* always contains ε because zero copies are allowed; (a+b)* means all strings over {a,b}.
Build a regex from the fixed part, the free part and what is forbidden, then test with in and out strings.
Identities follow from meaning: R∅ = ∅, Rε = R, ∅* = ε, (R*)* = R*; (RS)* is not R*S*.
Real regex adds shorthands like [0-9], {8}, ^ and $; backreferences go beyond regular languages.
Regexes cannot match unbounded nesting like balanced brackets; use a grammar and parser instead.
lessons.tip: After writing any regex, test it with at least three strings that should match and three that should not, including the empty string. Most wrong answers fail on ε or on a very short string.
lessons.task: Write theory regexes over {a,b} for: (1) strings starting and ending with the same symbol, (2) strings with at least two a's, (3) strings where every a is immediately followed by b. Then test each with five strings of your choice. If you have a computer, check them with Python's re.fullmatch, writing + as |.

quiz.q: Which language does ab* + c describe?
quiz.explain: Star binds first, then concatenation, then union: (a(b*)) + c.

quiz.q: What is R∅ equal to, for any regex R?
quiz.explain: Concatenation needs a string from both sides, and ∅ has none, so nothing can be formed.

quiz.q: Which regex describes binary strings with no two 1s next to each other?
quiz.explain: Every 1 except a final one must be followed by 0, so build from blocks 0 and 10 plus an optional last 1.

quiz.q: Why is (ab)* not equal to a*b*?
options: Because abab is in (ab)* but not in a*b*
Because ε is in a*b* only
quiz.explain: In a*b* all a's come before all b's, so abab cannot be formed.

quiz.q: Why is the Python pattern ^(.*)\1$ not a regular expression in the theory sense?
options: The backreference matches ww, which is not a regular language
quiz.explain: {ww} needs unbounded memory to compare the halves, so no DFA can recognise it.

lessons.title: Regex and Automata: Thompson, State Elimination and Arden
lessons.content:
Think of a recipe and a cooked dish. The recipe is a short text; the dish is the real thing. A good cook can turn any recipe into a dish, and a good food expert can taste any dish and write down its recipe. In this course, a regular expression is the recipe and a finite automaton is the dish. This lesson shows both directions: regex to machine (Thompson's construction) and machine to regex (state elimination and Arden's theorem). Together they prove Kleene's theorem: regexes and finite automata describe exactly the same languages.

Why we need both directions: Humans like writing regexes because they are short. Computers like running automata because each input symbol is one simple step. So a tool like grep must turn your regex into a machine. Going the other way is useful too: if an engineer designed a DFA, for example for a metro card reader, turning it into a regex gives a compact description for documentation or for a test generator. And for theory, the two directions together prove that nothing is lost when you switch between the two views.

Quick recap: An ε-NFA is an NFA that may also have ε-moves, free jumps that read no symbol. The ε-closure of a set of states is everything reachable from it by ε-moves alone, including the states themselves. A regex is built from ∅, ε and single symbols using union (+), concatenation and star (*).

Thompson's construction, the idea: Ken Thompson described this method in 1968 for a text search program. From first principles: a regex is built from tiny pieces by three operations, so if we can build a machine for each tiny piece, and a way to glue machines for each operation, we can build a machine for ANY regex, following the same steps that built the regex. Every machine we build has exactly one start state and exactly one accept state, with no arrows leaving the accept state. This "one door in, one door out" shape is what makes gluing easy.

The base pieces: For the symbol a, make two states: s --a--> f. For ε, make s --ε--> f. For ∅, make two states with no arrow between them; nothing can ever be accepted.

Gluing for union R + S: Add a new start state and a new accept state. From the new start, put ε-arrows to the start of R's machine and to the start of S's machine. From the accept of R and the accept of S, put ε-arrows to the new accept. The old accept states stop being accepting. Meaning: at the start, the machine freely chooses which branch to try, just like the union "R or S".

Gluing for concatenation RS: Put an ε-arrow from the accept state of R's machine to the start state of S's machine. R's accept stops being accepting. Meaning: first finish a string of R, then continue with a string of S. (Some textbooks merge the two states instead of using an ε-arrow; both are correct.)

Gluing for star R*: Add a new start and a new accept. Arrows: new start --ε--> R's start (go into the loop), new start --ε--> new accept (zero copies, so ε is accepted), R's accept --ε--> R's start (go around again), R's accept --ε--> new accept (stop looping). This is a roundabout: you may skip it, go around once, or go around many times.

Worked example, (a + b)*a: Build from the inside out. Machine for a: 3 --a--> 4. Machine for b: 5 --b--> 6. Union a + b: new start 2 and new accept 7, with 2 --ε--> 3, 2 --ε--> 5, 4 --ε--> 7, 6 --ε--> 7. Star (a + b)*: new start 1 and new accept 8, with 1 --ε--> 2, 1 --ε--> 8, 7 --ε--> 2, 7 --ε--> 8. Machine for the last a: 9 --a--> 10. Concatenation: 8 --ε--> 9. Final machine: start 1, accept 10, ten states in total. Notice it is mechanical; you never had to think about what the language means, which is exactly why a program can do it.

Tracing ba on the Thompson machine: Start set is the ε-closure of state 1: from 1 we can slide to 2 and 8; from 2 to 3 and 5; from 8 to 9. So {1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9}. Read b: only state 5 has a b-arrow, to 6. Closure of {6}: 6 to 7, 7 to 2 and 8, 2 to 3 and 5, 8 to 9. So {2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9}. Read a: state 3 goes to 4 and state 9 goes to 10. Closure gives {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10}. It contains 10, so ba is accepted. Correct, since ba ends with a. Now trace ab: after a we get the same big set {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10}; after b only 5 moves, to 6, giving {2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9}. No 10, so reject. Correct, ab ends with b.

Why Thompson's construction is a good engineering choice: Each regex symbol or operator adds at most two states, so the machine size grows only linearly with the regex length. Each state has at most two arrows leaving it, which makes simulation simple. The cost is many ε-moves, which is why tools then either simulate the NFA with state sets, or apply the subset construction from lesson 07 to get a fast DFA.

The other direction, DFA to regex: Now we go from a machine back to a recipe. The trick is a new kind of machine called a generalized NFA (GNFA), whose arrows are labelled with whole regexes instead of single symbols. An arrow labelled ab* means "you may cross this arrow by reading any string in ab*". Then we remove states one by one, each time repairing the arrows so the language stays the same, until only a start and an accept state remain. The label on the last arrow is the answer.

The repair rule, from first principles: Suppose we remove a state X. Any path that went through X looked like: come in from P with label R1, loop at X some number of times with label R2, then leave to Q with label R3. So the new direct arrow from P to Q must carry R1(R2)*R3. If there was already an arrow from P to Q with label R4, combine them with union: R1(R2)*R3 + R4. Do this for every pair (P, Q) of an incoming and an outgoing neighbour. Nothing else changes.

Worked example: Take the DFA for "strings over {a,b} that end with b": q0 --a--> q0, q0 --b--> q1, q1 --a--> q0, q1 --b--> q1. Start q0, accept q1. Step one: add a new start S with S --ε--> q0, and a new accept F with q1 --ε--> F. Now the start has no incoming arrows and there is one accept with no outgoing arrows, the same tidy shape as Thompson's machines.

Remove q0: Incoming to q0: from S with ε, from q1 with a. Loop on q0: a. Outgoing from q0: to q1 with b. Pair (S, q1): new label ε a* b, which is a*b. Pair (q1, q1): new label a a* b, combined with the existing loop b gives b + aa*b. Remaining machine: S --a*b--> q1, q1 loops on (b + aa*b), q1 --ε--> F.

Remove q1: Incoming from S with a*b, loop b + aa*b, outgoing to F with ε. New arrow: S --a*b(b + aa*b)*--> F. Answer: a*b(b + aa*b)*. Sanity check by meaning: a*b reaches the first b; then each block is either another b, or some a's followed by a b. So the string always ends with b, and any such string can be built. It equals the simpler (a + b)*b, which shows an important fact: elimination gives a correct regex, not always the prettiest one. Removing states in a different order can give a different-looking but equal regex.

Arden's theorem, the algebra method: Here is another way, using equations like in school algebra. Arden's theorem says: if P and Q are regexes and P does not contain ε, then the equation R = Q + RP has exactly one solution, R = QP*. Why is it true? Unroll it: R = Q + RP = Q + (Q + RP)P = Q + QP + RPP, and keep going: R = Q(ε + P + PP + ...) = QP*. The condition "P has no ε" stops fake extra solutions.

Using Arden on the same DFA: For each state, write "the strings that reach this state" as an equation from its incoming arrows. q0 = ε + q0 a + q1 a (ε because q0 is the start). q1 = q0 b + q1 b. Solve q1 first: it has the form R = Q + RP with Q = q0 b and P = b, so q1 = q0 b b*. Substitute into q0: q0 = ε + q0 a + q0 b b* a = ε + q0(a + bb*a). Arden again: q0 = (a + bb*a)*. So q1 = (a + bb*a)* bb*. Since q1 is the accept state, that is the language. It looks different from a*b(b + aa*b)* but describes the same strings, all strings ending in b. Different routes, same language.

Kleene's theorem, closing the circle: Thompson shows regex to ε-NFA. Lesson 07 shows ε-NFA to DFA. State elimination or Arden shows DFA to regex. So: a language is regular (some DFA accepts it) if and only if some regex describes it. Stephen Kleene proved this in the 1950s, and the regular languages got their name from his "regular events".

Real life example 1, grep: When you type grep -E 'ab+c' log.txt, the tool parses your pattern, builds an automaton in a Thompson-like way, and runs it over every line, keeping a set of current states or building DFA states as needed. That is why the search time grows with the file size, not with the number of possible matches.

Real life example 2, a validator from a diagram: Imagine an engineer drew a DFA for valid Bangladeshi mobile numbers: states for "read 0", "read 01", "read operator digit", then a counter state for each of the eight remaining digits. To put this rule into a web form, she converts the diagram to a regex, 01[3-9][0-9]{8}, a single line any developer can read. Where the "recipe and dish" analogy breaks: a real recipe loses detail, but here no information is lost at all; the conversions are exact.

When to use which: Use Thompson when a program must turn user-written patterns into machines quickly and safely; its linear size is a big plus. Use state elimination or Arden mainly on paper and in proofs; on large DFAs the resulting regex can become huge, in the worst case exponentially longer than the DFA, so it is rarely done in production.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In Thompson's star, forgetting the new start --ε--> new accept arrow, which wrongly rejects ε. In state elimination, forgetting the loop at the removed state, or forgetting to union with an already existing direct arrow. Forgetting to add the new start and new accept first, so the start or accept gets eliminated. Using Arden when P contains ε. Exams typically ask: "Construct an ε-NFA for (ab + a)* using Thompson's method", "Find a regex for this 3-state DFA using state elimination", or "State and prove Arden's theorem".

Mental model: Picture two translators sitting at a table. One reads a regex from left to right and builds a pipe network: plain pipes for symbols, a fork for union, a joint for concatenation, a roundabout for star. The other takes a pipe network and starts removing junction boxes one by one, each time writing on the new direct pipe "what used to happen through this box": in, loop, out. When only start and end remain, the writing on the last pipe is the regex.

Recap and next: Thompson's construction builds an ε-NFA from any regex using one gadget per operator. State elimination removes states, relabelling with R1(R2)*R3 + R4, until one arrow is left. Arden's theorem solves R = Q + RP as R = QP*. Together with the subset construction, they prove Kleene's theorem. Next lesson asks the opposite question: how do we prove a language is NOT regular? The tool is the pumping lemma.
key_points: Kleene's theorem: a language is regular exactly when some regex describes it.
Thompson's construction builds an ε-NFA with one start and one accept state, using a gadget for symbol, union, concatenation and star.
Thompson's machine size grows linearly with the regex, at the cost of many ε-moves.
State elimination turns a DFA into a regex by removing states; new label = R1(R2)*R3 + R4.
Always add a new start and a new accept state before eliminating.
Arden's theorem: if ε is not in P, then R = Q + RP has the unique solution R = QP*.
Different elimination orders give different-looking but equal regexes; DFA to regex can blow up in size.
lessons.tip: In state elimination, before removing a state, list its incoming arrows, its loop and its outgoing arrows in three columns. Then fill one new label for every in-out pair. This simple table prevents the two classic mistakes: forgetting the loop and forgetting an existing direct arrow.
lessons.task: Draw the Thompson ε-NFA for (ab + a)* on paper and number its states. Trace the strings aba and b, writing the set of states after each symbol. Then take the 3-state 'ends with 01' DFA from lesson 07 and find a regex for it by state elimination.

quiz.q: In Thompson's star gadget for R*, which arrow lets the machine accept ε?
quiz.explain: Skipping the loop entirely means zero copies of R, which is exactly ε.

quiz.q: When removing state X with incoming label R1, loop R2, outgoing R3, and an existing direct arrow R4, what is the new label?
quiz.explain: A path through X comes in, loops any number of times, then leaves; the old direct route is kept by union.

quiz.q: By Arden's theorem, what solves R = Q + RP when ε is not in P?
quiz.explain: Unrolling gives Q + QP + QPP + ..., which is QP*.

quiz.q: What does Kleene's theorem state?
options: Every NFA is smaller than its DFA
Regex and finite automata describe exactly the same languages
quiz.explain: Thompson gives regex to NFA; subset construction and state elimination complete the circle.

quiz.q: Why do real tools use Thompson's construction rather than state elimination when processing user patterns?
options: State elimination does not work on DFAs
Thompson's machine grows only linearly with the pattern
quiz.explain: Linear size makes building the machine cheap and safe, while DFA-to-regex can blow up.

lessons.title: The Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages
lessons.content:
Imagine a small neighbourhood in Mirpur with only 5 street corners. A rickshaw starts at one corner and takes a ride that passes through 6 corners, one after another. Here is a guaranteed fact: at least one corner was visited twice. Why? There are only 5 different corners, so 6 visits cannot all be different. And if the rickshaw came back to a corner, the part of the ride between the two visits is a loop. The rickshaw could skip that loop or go around it many times, and it would still finish at the same place. This simple fact, called the pigeonhole principle, is the whole engine behind the pumping lemma.

The problem we want to solve: So far we proved languages ARE regular by building a DFA, NFA or regex. But some languages, like {a^n b^n : n ≥ 0}, meaning some a's followed by the same number of b's, seem to need counting without limit. How do we PROVE that no DFA exists? We cannot try every DFA one by one, there are infinitely many. We need an argument that works for all DFAs at once. The pumping lemma, published by Bar-Hillel, Perles and Shamir in 1961, gives exactly that. (Lesson 08's Myhill-Nerode idea is another tool for the same job.)

Recap of the pigeonhole principle: If you put more than k pigeons into k holes, some hole gets at least two pigeons. Here, the holes are the states of a DFA and the pigeons are the moments during a run.

Building the lemma from first principles: Suppose a DFA has p states. Feed it a string s of length at least p. While reading the first p symbols, the machine is in p + 1 states: the start one, and one after each symbol. Since there are only p different states, some state appears twice among those p + 1 moments. Call the first repeated state R. Now cut s into three parts. x is the part read before the first visit to R. y is the part read between the first and second visit to R, which is the loop. z is everything after. Since the repeat happened within the first p symbols, x and y together have length at most p. And the loop read at least one symbol, so y is not empty.

Why pumping works: After reading x, the machine is at R. Reading y brings it back to R. So reading y twice brings it back to R again, and reading y zero times leaves it at R too. In every case, the machine then reads z from R and ends in the same final state as before. So if s = xyz was accepted, then xz, xyyz, xyyyz and so on are all accepted too. "Pumping" means repeating y any number of times, including zero.

A concrete example with real numbers: Take the DFA for "the number of a's is divisible by 3" over {a,b}, with states r0, r1, r2 (remainder 0, 1 or 2). Arrows: r0 --a--> r1, r1 --a--> r2, r2 --a--> r0, and every state loops to itself on b. Start and accept: r0. Here p = 3. Take s = aaab, which is in the language. Trace: r0, after a r1, after a r2, after a r0. The state r0 repeats after 3 symbols. So x = ε (empty), y = aaa, z = b. Pump down, i = 0: the string is b, with 0 a's, accepted. Pump up, i = 2: aaaaaab, with 6 a's, accepted. Exactly as promised.

The formal statement: If L is a regular language, then there is a number p ≥ 1 (the pumping length) such that every string s in L with length at least p can be split into s = xyz satisfying three conditions. One: |y| > 0, the loop is not empty. Two: |xy| ≤ p, the loop happens early. Three: for every i ≥ 0, the string x y^i z is in L. Each condition comes straight from the story above, so there is nothing to memorise without reason.

How we use it, the contrapositive: The lemma says "regular implies pumpable". So if a language is NOT pumpable, it is NOT regular. To prove non-regularity, we show that for some long string, every legal split fails to pump. It is cleanest to think of it as a game against an opponent who claims L is regular. Step 1: the opponent picks p; you do not know its value, so you treat it as a symbol. Step 2: you pick a string s in L with |s| ≥ p, and you choose it cleverly. Step 3: the opponent picks ANY split xyz obeying |y| > 0 and |xy| ≤ p. Step 4: you pick an i such that x y^i z is NOT in L. If you can always win, whatever the opponent does in steps 1 and 3, L is not regular.

Proof 1, {a^n b^n : n ≥ 0}: Assume L is regular with pumping length p. Choose s = a^p b^p. It is in L and has length 2p ≥ p. Now the opponent splits s. Because |xy| ≤ p and the first p symbols are all a's, both x and y consist only of a's. So y = a^k for some k ≥ 1. Choose i = 2. The new string is a^(p+k) b^p: it has more a's than b's, so it is not in L. Every legal split fails, so L is not regular. With real numbers: if p were 3, s = aaabbb. Say y = a: pumping gives aaaabbb, 4 a's and 3 b's, out. Say y = aa: aaaaabbb, out. Say y = aaa: aaaaaabbb, out. The opponent cannot escape, because the first p symbols are all a's. That is why we put p a's first: it traps y.

Proof 2, palindromes over {0,1}: A palindrome reads the same backwards, like 0110 or 101. Choose s = 0^p 1 0^p. It is a palindrome of length 2p + 1. Since |xy| ≤ p, y lies inside the first block of 0s, so y = 0^k with k ≥ 1. Choose i = 0: we get 0^(p-k) 1 0^p. The 1 is no longer in the middle; there are fewer 0s on the left than on the right, so it is not a palindrome. Not regular. Notice the choice of s: if you chose s = 0^(2p), all 0s, every pumped string is still all 0s, which is still a palindrome, and you lose. Choosing s is where the thinking happens: make a string where breaking the early part destroys the structure.

Proof 3, {a^(n²) : n ≥ 0}, strings whose length is a perfect square: Choose s = a^(p²). Its length p² is at least p. Any split has y = a^k with 1 ≤ k ≤ p, because |y| ≥ 1 and |y| ≤ |xy| ≤ p. Choose i = 2: the length becomes p² + k. Now some arithmetic: p² < p² + k ≤ p² + p < p² + 2p + 1 = (p + 1)². So the new length lies strictly between two neighbouring perfect squares, p² and (p + 1)², and therefore is not a perfect square. Not regular. Example: with p = 3, the length 9 + k is 10, 11 or 12, all strictly between 9 and 16.

Pumping down, a useful trick: Sometimes pumping up does not break anything, and i = 0 does. Take L = {a^n b^m : n > m}. Choose s = a^(p+1) b^p. Again y = a^k with k ≥ 1. Pumping up only adds more a's, which keeps n > m, so it stays in L. But i = 0 removes k a's, giving a^(p+1-k) b^p, where p + 1 - k ≤ p. Now the a's are not more than the b's, so it is out of L. Not regular. Lesson: try both i = 0 and i = 2.

What it means in real life: A compiler must check that brackets in your code are balanced, like ((a + b) * c). Balanced brackets contain the pattern "(^n )^n", n opening brackets followed by n closing ones, which pumps exactly like a^n b^n. So no regex, and no finite automaton, can check nested brackets for every depth. That is why compilers use grammars and stack-based parsers (lessons 13 to 17) for syntax and use regexes only for simple tokens. A second example: a bKash-style app may validate a phone number with a regex, because the set of 11-digit numbers is finite and regular, but it cannot use a pure regex to check "the deposit and withdrawal counts in this log match", which needs unbounded counting.

Where the rickshaw analogy fits and breaks: It fits: few corners, long ride, a repeat is forced, and the loop can be skipped or repeated. It breaks: a real rickshaw loop costs time and money, while a DFA does not care how many times it goes around; it only cares where it ends.

Common mistake 1, using it to prove regularity: The lemma says regular implies pumpable. It does NOT say pumpable implies regular. There exist non-regular languages that pass the pumping test. So "this language can be pumped, therefore it is regular" is a wrong proof. To prove regularity, build a DFA, NFA or regex, or use closure properties (next lesson).

Common mistake 2, choosing p yourself: Writing "let p = 5" and showing one example is not a proof. The opponent picks p, so your argument must work for any p, which is why we write p as a symbol.

Common mistake 3, choosing the split yourself: You must defeat EVERY legal split, not just the one you like. A good choice of s, like a^p b^p, reduces all splits to one case. If your s allows y to fall in different places, you must handle each case separately.

Other mistakes: picking s that is not in L, or shorter than p; forgetting the condition |xy| ≤ p, which is often the key that traps y; and forgetting that i = 0 is allowed. Also remember that every finite language is regular, so you can never prove a finite language non-regular; the lemma holds there trivially, by choosing p larger than the longest string.

What exams ask: State the pumping lemma precisely; prove that a^n b^n, ww^R, ww, a^n b^n c^n, a^(n²) or a^p with p prime is not regular; explain why it cannot prove regularity; find the mistake in a wrong proof.

Mental model: Picture the DFA as a small town with p corners and a long ride s. In the first p blocks of the ride, the rickshaw must revisit a corner, so there is an early loop y. A regular language must survive the loop being skipped or repeated. Your job as the prover is to choose a ride where any early loop carries something that must be balanced against the rest, like the a's against the b's, so skipping or repeating it breaks the balance.

Recap and next: The pumping lemma comes from the pigeonhole principle: a long accepted string forces a loop within the first p symbols, and the loop can be pumped. To prove non-regularity, play the game: the opponent picks p and the split, you pick s and i. Choose s to trap y, and try both i = 0 and i = 2. It only proves non-regularity, never regularity. Next lesson: closure properties, which let you prove regularity or non-regularity by combining languages, plus decision questions and automata with output.
key_points: Pigeonhole: a DFA with p states reading p symbols visits p+1 states, so some state repeats, creating a loop.
Lemma: if L is regular, there is p such that every s in L with |s| ≥ p splits as xyz with |y| > 0, |xy| ≤ p, and xy^iz in L for all i ≥ 0.
Use the contrapositive as a game: opponent picks p and the split, you pick s and i.
Choose s so that |xy| ≤ p traps y in a useful block, as in a^p b^p.
Try both pumping up (i = 2) and pumping down (i = 0).
a^n b^n, palindromes and a^(n²) are not regular; balanced brackets are not regular either.
The lemma can never prove a language IS regular; build a machine or use closure for that.
lessons.tip: Before writing a pumping proof, write your chosen s and draw a line after the first p symbols. Everything left of the line is where y can live. If that region is all one symbol, your proof will be short.
lessons.task: Prove with the pumping lemma that L = {0^n 1 0^n : n ≥ 0} is not regular. Then explain in two sentences why choosing s = 0^p would not work for the palindrome language. Finally, take the 'a's divisible by 3' DFA, pick s = baaab, and find x, y, z by tracing.

quiz.q: Why must a DFA with p states repeat a state while reading the first p symbols?
options: Because it visits p+1 states but has only p distinct ones
Because the alphabet has p symbols
Because the string is a palindrome
quiz.explain: Start plus one state per symbol gives p+1 visits; with only p states, the pigeonhole principle forces a repeat.

quiz.q: In the proof that a^n b^n is not regular with s = a^p b^p, why does y contain only a's?
options: Because |xy| ≤ p and the first p symbols are all a's
Because the opponent chooses y = a
quiz.explain: The condition |xy| ≤ p puts x and y inside the first p symbols, which are all a's.

quiz.q: For L = {a^n b^m : n > m} with s = a^(p+1) b^p, which i breaks the string?
quiz.explain: Pumping up keeps n > m; removing y leaves at most p a's against p b's, so the string leaves L.

quiz.q: A student shows a language satisfies the pumping conditions and concludes it is regular. What is wrong?
options: Pumpable does not imply regular; some non-regular languages pass the test
quiz.explain: The lemma only says regular implies pumpable; the reverse is false.

quiz.q: In the a^(n²) proof, after pumping with i = 2 the length is p² + k with 1 ≤ k ≤ p. Why is it not a square?
options: Because it lies strictly between p² and (p+1)²
quiz.explain: p² < p² + k ≤ p² + p < (p+1)², and no square lies strictly between two consecutive squares.

lessons.title: Closure and Decision Properties, Moore and Mealy Machines
lessons.content:
Think of LEGO. If you snap two LEGO pieces together, you always get a LEGO object, never a wooden one. Mathematicians call this "closure": a family of things is closed under an operation if applying the operation to members of the family always gives another member. Regular languages are like LEGO: union, intersection, complement and several other operations on regular languages always give regular languages. This lesson shows why each one is true, how to use closure to prove that a language is not regular, which questions about regular languages a computer can always answer, and finally two kinds of automata that produce output instead of only saying yes or no.

Why closure matters: First, it lets you build complicated machines from simple ones, the way an engineer builds a filter "valid phone number AND not on the block list" from two simple rules. Second, it is a powerful proof tool. Third, every closure proof is a construction, so it tells you exactly how to build the machine, not just that it exists.

Recap: A language is regular if some DFA (or NFA, or regex) recognises it. A complete DFA has exactly one arrow for every state and every symbol. Kleene's theorem from lesson 10 says we may use whichever form, DFA, NFA or regex, is most convenient for each proof.

Union: If R1 and R2 are regexes for L1 and L2, then R1 + R2 is a regex for L1 ∪ L2. Done. With machines: add a new start state with ε-arrows to both old start states, and the NFA accepts if either branch does.

Intersection, the product construction: There is no regex operator for "and", so we use machines. Run two DFAs side by side, like two cashiers checking the same customer. A state of the new DFA is a pair (state of M1, state of M2). On a symbol, both parts move at the same time. A pair accepts only if both parts accept. Example: M1 checks "even number of a's" with states E and O: E --a--> O, O --a--> E, and both loop on b. M2 checks "ends with b" with states N and B: N --a--> N, N --b--> B, B --a--> N, B --b--> B. Start pair (E, N). Trace abab: (E, N) --a--> (O, N) --b--> (O, B) --a--> (E, N) --b--> (E, B). Both parts accept, so abab is accepted: it has two a's and ends with b. The product of an m-state and an n-state DFA has m times n states, here 2 times 2 = 4. For union, the same product works with "either part accepts".

Complement, swap accept and non-accept: Take a complete DFA for L. Make every accept state non-accepting and every non-accept state accepting. Each string ends in exactly one state, so it is accepted by the new machine exactly when the old one rejected it. Two warnings. One: the DFA must be complete. If arrows are missing, there is a hidden dead state; you must draw it before swapping, because after the swap it must become accepting. Two: this does NOT work on an NFA. Example: an NFA with q0 --a--> q1 and q0 --a--> q2, where only q1 accepts, accepts "a". After swapping, q2 accepts, so "a" is still accepted through q2. An NFA accepts when SOME path accepts, and swapping gives "some path rejects", which is not the complement. Convert to a DFA first.

Difference: L1 − L2 means strings in L1 but not in L2. It equals L1 ∩ (complement of L2), and both of those are closed, so difference is closed too. This is how "valid number but not blocked" filters are built.

Concatenation and star: With regexes it is immediate: R1R2 and R1*. With NFAs: for L1L2, add ε-arrows from every accept state of M1 to the start of M2, and keep only M2's accept states. For L*, add a new start state that is also accepting (so ε is in L*), with an ε-arrow to the old start, and ε-arrows from old accept states back to the old start. These are the same gadgets as Thompson's construction.

Reversal: The reverse of a string writes it backwards: the reverse of abb is bba. To recognise reversed strings, flip every arrow of an NFA for L, make the old start state the only accept state, and add a new start state with ε-arrows to all old accept states. A path that spelled w forwards now spells w backwards. Example: "ends with 01" reversed becomes "starts with 10".

Homomorphism: A homomorphism h replaces each symbol by a fixed string, for example h(0) = a and h(1) = bb. Apply it to every string of L. If L has regex R, just replace each symbol in R by its string: L(0*1) becomes L(a*bb). So regular languages are closed under homomorphism. They are also closed under inverse homomorphism, which is often useful in harder proofs.

Proving non-regularity with closure: This is often shorter than the pumping lemma. Example 1: L = all strings over {a,b} with equally many a's and b's. Suppose L were regular. The language a*b* is regular. Regular languages are closed under intersection, so L ∩ a*b* would be regular. But L ∩ a*b* is exactly {a^n b^n}, which lesson 11 proved is not regular. Contradiction, so L is not regular. Example 2: L = {a^n b^m : n ≠ m}. Suppose L were regular. Then its complement is regular, and the complement intersected with a*b* is regular. But that intersection is exactly {a^n b^n}: the strings of the form a*b* that are NOT in L, meaning n = m. Contradiction again. Notice the pumping lemma would be awkward here, since pumping a^p b^q with p ≠ q can easily stay unequal.

Closure does not run backwards: If L1 ∪ L2 is regular, that does not mean L1 and L2 are. Take any non-regular L; L ∪ (complement of L) is Σ*, which is regular. Also, a part of a regular language can be non-regular: {a^n b^n} sits inside the regular a*b*. So never argue "it is inside a regular language, so it is regular".

Decision properties, which questions always have answers: A decision problem is a yes/no question. For regular languages given as DFAs, these can all be answered by an algorithm that always finishes. Membership: is w in L? Run the DFA on w; it takes |w| steps. Emptiness: is L empty? Do a graph search from the start state; L is empty exactly when no accept state is reachable. Finiteness: is L finite? First delete states that are unreachable from the start or cannot reach an accept state. Then L is infinite exactly when what remains has a cycle. Why: a cycle on a path to acceptance can be pumped as often as you like, giving infinitely many strings; with no cycle, every accepted string has length less than the number of states, so there are finitely many. Equivalence: is L1 = L2? Build the symmetric difference (L1 − L2) ∪ (L2 − L1) with the closure constructions and test it for emptiness; or minimize both DFAs and compare, as in lesson 08.

Why decision properties matter: These algorithms are what make regular languages safe in tools. A compiler can check that two token rules never clash, a network filter can check that a rule set blocks nothing valid. Later you will see that for Turing machines the same questions, like emptiness and equivalence, have no algorithm at all. Regular languages are the friendly end of the spectrum.

Automata with output: So far our machines only say accept or reject at the end. Many real devices instead produce an output at each step: a traffic light shows a colour, a vending machine drops a product. Two classic models do this. A Moore machine gives an output for each STATE. A Mealy machine gives an output for each TRANSITION, depending on the state and the symbol just read. Both have no accept states; their job is the output sequence.

Moore example, remainder modulo 3: Read a binary number from the left, and after each bit output the remainder of the number so far when divided by 3. States r0, r1, r2 with outputs 0, 1 and 2. Rule: reading bit b in state r goes to state (2r + b) mod 3, because adding a bit doubles the number and adds b. Trace 1101: start r0, output 0. Read 1: (0 + 1) mod 3 = 1, go to r1, output 1. Read 1: (2 + 1) mod 3 = 0, r0, output 0. Read 0: 0, r0, output 0. Read 1: 1, r1, output 1. Output sequence 0 1 0 0 1. Check: 1 is 1, 11 is 3, 110 is 6, 1101 is 13, and their remainders are 1, 0, 0, 1. Notice a Moore machine gives n + 1 outputs for n inputs, because the start state outputs before anything is read.

Mealy example, detect two 1s in a row: Output 1 whenever the current bit and the previous bit are both 1. States A (last bit was not 1) and B (last bit was 1). Arrows written as input/output: A --0/0--> A, A --1/0--> B, B --0/0--> A, B --1/1--> B. Trace 0111: A --0/0--> A --1/0--> B --1/1--> B --1/1--> B. Output 0 0 1 1. Correct: only the third and fourth bits have a 1 before them. A Mealy machine gives exactly n outputs for n inputs.

Moore versus Mealy, trade-offs: Mealy machines often need fewer states, because the output can depend on the input directly, and they react in the same step. Moore outputs depend only on the state, so they stay steady while the input changes, which hardware designers like because it avoids short output glitches. The two models are equally powerful: a Moore machine converts to Mealy by moving each state's output onto its incoming arrows, and a Mealy machine converts to Moore by splitting each state into copies, one per output arriving there, which can add states. The only difference is that Moore's extra first output.

Real life: A traffic signal at a Dhaka intersection is naturally a Moore machine: each state, like "north-south green", has one fixed output, the light colours. A metro rail ticket gate or vending machine is naturally Mealy: the output "open the gate" or "drop a drink" happens on the transition caused by a valid card tap or the last coin. Where the analogy breaks: real controllers also use timers and counters with large values, which go beyond a pure finite machine in practice, even though engineers still model the core logic as Moore or Mealy machines.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Swapping accept states on an NFA or on an incomplete DFA. Thinking intersection can be written directly as a regex operator. Arguing "subset of a regular language, so regular". In closure proofs, intersecting with a language that is not regular, which proves nothing. Mixing up Moore (output on states) and Mealy (output on arrows), or forgetting Moore's extra first output. Exams ask: build the product DFA for two small DFAs; prove a language non-regular using closure; give an algorithm for emptiness or finiteness; design a Moore or Mealy machine for a sequence detector and convert between them.

Mental model: Picture regular languages as a walled garden. Union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation, star, reversal and homomorphism are gates that only lead back into the garden. If you start inside the garden and end up at a language known to be outside, like a^n b^n, then your starting language was never inside. Inside the garden, every basic question has a simple answer by graph search. Moore and Mealy machines are the same garden machines, given a voice: one speaks in every room, the other speaks on every door.

Recap and next: Regular languages are closed under union, intersection (product construction), complement (swap on a complete DFA), difference, concatenation, star, reversal and homomorphism. Closure plus a known non-regular language gives quick non-regularity proofs. Membership, emptiness, finiteness and equivalence are all decidable by simple algorithms. Moore and Mealy machines add output to finite automata. Next lesson leaves regular languages behind: context-free grammars, which can finally describe nesting like balanced brackets.
key_points: Regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation, star, reversal and homomorphism.
Intersection uses the product construction: pair states, move both together, accept when both accept.
Complement swaps accept states, but only on a complete DFA, never on an NFA.
To prove non-regularity: assume regular, combine with regular languages by closed operations, and reach a known non-regular language like a^n b^n.
Closure does not run backwards: a subset of a regular language can be non-regular.
