Membership, emptiness, finiteness (cycle on a useful path) and equivalence are decidable for regular languages.
Moore machines output per state (n+1 outputs); Mealy machines output per transition (n outputs); both are equally powerful.
lessons.tip: For every closure proof, say which form you are using: regex for union, concatenation and star; complete DFA for complement; product DFA for intersection. Picking the easiest form for each operation makes the proof two lines long.
lessons.task: Build the 4-state product DFA for 'even number of a's AND ends with b' and trace aab and abb. Then design a Mealy machine over {0,1} that outputs 1 exactly when the last three bits read are 101, trace it on 10101, and write down the output sequence.

quiz.q: Why does swapping accept states fail to complement an NFA?
options: An NFA accepts if some path accepts, so after swapping a string can still be accepted by another path
quiz.explain: In the example, 'a' is accepted before the swap via q1 and after the swap via q2.

quiz.q: How many states does the product DFA of a 3-state DFA and a 4-state DFA have?
quiz.explain: Each product state is a pair, so there are 3 × 4 = 12 pairs.

quiz.q: L has equally many a's and b's. Which step shows L is not regular?
options: L ∩ a*b* = {a^n b^n}, which is not regular
quiz.explain: If L were regular, intersecting with regular a*b* would give a regular language, but a^n b^n is not.

quiz.q: When is the language of a DFA infinite?
options: When it has more than 10 states
When it has a dead state
When a cycle lies on some path from the start to an accept state
quiz.explain: Such a cycle can be pumped any number of times, giving infinitely many accepted strings.

quiz.q: In a Mealy machine, the output depends on what?
options: Only the number of symbols read
The current state and the input symbol, written on the transition
quiz.explain: Mealy outputs sit on arrows; Moore outputs sit on states.

lessons.title: Context-Free Grammars
lessons.content:
Open your class 6 math khata and look at this: {2 x [3 + (4 - 1)]}. Your teacher's rule: every bracket you open must be closed, and the last one opened is the first one closed. Strange fact: none of the machines we have built so far can check this rule for brackets nested as deep as anyone likes. Today we meet a new tool that can describe it easily. It is called a context-free grammar, and it is the tool that describes the shape of every programming language you will ever use. Quick recap of where we are: A finite automaton (DFA or NFA) reads a string one symbol at a time, moving between a fixed, finite set of states. The languages it recognises are the regular languages. Lesson 11 showed that a^n b^n (some a's, then the same number of b's) is not regular: to check it you must count the a's, and a 10-state machine cannot tell 11 a's from 12. It runs out of memory. Why this matters, nesting: a^n b^n looks like a toy, but it is the skeleton of nesting. Replace a with "(" and b with ")" and a^n b^n becomes ((( ))). Replace them with "begin" and "end", or "{" and "}", or "
" and "
", and you get real code. Every programming language has things inside things inside things: a loop inside an if inside a function. Regular expressions cannot describe this, so we need something stronger. That something must still be simple and precise, because compilers have to follow it exactly. What people did before: In the 1950s, languages like FORTRAN were described in plain English, and each compiler writer read the English slightly differently. In 1956 the linguist Noam Chomsky was studying how human sentences are built, and he wrote down sentence structure as rewriting rules. A few years later John Backus and Peter Naur used the same idea to define the language ALGOL 60 precisely. Their notation is BNF (Backus-Naur Form): a language's shape as a short list of rules, not pages of English. The idea from first principles: How would you describe balanced brackets to a friend? You cannot list them all, there are infinitely many. You would say: "the empty string is balanced; if X is balanced then (X) is balanced; if X and Y are balanced then XY is balanced." That is a recursive description: big things are built out of smaller things of the same kind. A grammar is exactly this kind of description, written as rewriting rules. "Recursive" means defined using a smaller copy of itself, like a tiffin carrier built from identical boxes stacked on each other. The four parts of a CFG: A context-free grammar G is written as a 4-tuple (V, Σ, R, S). V is a finite set of variables (also called non-terminals). A variable is a placeholder name like S or E that stands for "some piece of the string, not decided yet". Σ is the alphabet of terminals, the real symbols that appear in the final string, like a, b, ( or ). R is a finite set of rules, also called productions, each of the form A -> w, where A is one variable and w is a string of variables and terminals (w may be empty, written ε). S is the start variable, where every derivation begins. Reading a production: The rule A -> w means "wherever you see A, you may replace it with w". If a variable has several rules, we join them with a vertical bar: S -> aSb | ε is short for two rules, S -> aSb and S -> ε. Terminals are the end of the road: no rule changes them. Variables must be replaced until none are left. Derivation, step by step: A derivation is a chain of replacements starting from S and ending in a string of only terminals. We write one step as u => v, meaning v came from u by using one rule once. Take G1 with the rules S -> aSb | ε. Here is how we get aabb: S => aSb (used S -> aSb) => aaSbb (used S -> aSb again on the middle S) => aabb (used S -> ε). Notice what happened: every time we added an a on the left, the same rule added a b on the right at the same moment. The grammar never counts. It simply makes the pairs together, so they can never get out of balance. That is the trick that finite automata could not do. The language of a grammar: The language of G, written L(G), is the set of all terminal strings that can be derived from S. A language is called context-free (a CFL) if some context-free grammar generates it. For G1, every derivation uses S -> aSb some number of times n and then S -> ε once, so L(G1) = { a^n b^n : n >= 0 } = {ε, ab, aabb, aaabbb, ...}. Could G1 make abab? No: in every half-finished string (called a sentential form, like aaSbb) all a's sit left of S and all b's right of S. Why "context-free": The left side of every rule is a single variable, alone. So the rule A -> w can be used on A no matter what symbols surround it, its neighbours (its context) do not matter. Grammars that allow rules like aAb -> aab, where replacing A depends on the neighbours, are called context-sensitive; they are stronger and come in lesson 24. Cricket version: context-free is "a wide always adds one run"; context-sensitive would be "a wide adds a run only if the previous ball was a four". Example 2, palindromes: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like madam, or "রমা কামার". Over {a, b}, the grammar is S -> aSa | bSb | a | b | ε. The idea: a palindrome is either tiny (empty, or one letter), or it is a palindrome with the same letter added on both ends. Derive abbba: S => aSa => abSba => abbba (last step S -> b). For even-length ones like abba: S => aSa => abSba => abba (S -> ε). The outside pair is built first, then the inside. Example 3, balanced brackets: The grammar is S -> (S) | SS | ε. Rule one wraps a balanced string in a pair. Rule two puts two balanced strings side by side. Rule three is the empty string. Let us derive (()()): S => (S) => (SS) => ((S)S) => (()S) => (()(S)) => (()()). Check each step: we wrapped, split into two, wrapped the first, emptied it, wrapped the second, emptied it. This is precisely the "last opened, first closed" rule of your math homework, and the grammar captured it in three short lines. Example 4, arithmetic expressions: Let E stand for an expression. E -> E + E | E * E | ( E ) | id, where id means any number or variable name, like x or 5. Derive (x + 5) * y, writing id for each name: E => E * E => ( E ) * E => ( E + E ) * E => ( id + E ) * E => ( id + id ) * E => ( id + id ) * id. This grammar works, but some strings can be built in two different ways. That problem, ambiguity, is lesson 14. Designing a grammar yourself: A method that usually works: write example strings and find an outside layer to peel off; what is left is usually a smaller string of the same kind, so the variable calls itself; then add the smallest string, the base case. Try { a^n b^(2n) }: every a is matched by two b's, so peel one a from the left and two b's from the right: S -> aSbb | ε. Check: S => aSbb => aaSbbbb => aabbbb, two a's and four b's. Gluing parts together: Take { a^n b^n c^m : n, m >= 0 }, matched a's and b's, then any number of c's. Two independent parts get their own variables: S -> AC, A -> aAb | ε, C -> cC | ε. Derive aabbc: S => AC => aAbC => aaAbbC => aabbC => aabbcC => aabbc. In fact every regular language is context-free: you can turn any DFA into a grammar by making one variable per state and a rule like Q -> aR for each transition from Q to R on a, plus Q -> ε for each accept state. So CFLs are a bigger family that contains all regular languages. Real life example 1, Bangla sentence grammar: In school you learned that a simple Bangla sentence is kortа + kormo + kriya, subject, object, verb. As grammar rules: Sentence -> Subject Object Verb, Subject -> আমি | রহিম, Object -> ভাত | বই, Verb -> খাই | পড়ে. Derive: Sentence => Subject Object Verb => আমি Object Verb => আমি ভাত Verb => আমি ভাত খাই. The match: variables are grammar categories, terminals are words. Where it breaks: this grammar also makes "রহিম বই খাই", right in shape but wrong in meaning and verb agreement. A CFG checks structure only, never meaning. Real life example 2, BNF in real programming languages: The official definitions of languages like C, Java and Python are written as grammars. A simplified piece looks like this: ::= | | ; and ::= if ( ) . In BNF, names in angle brackets are variables, "::=" means "->", and the bar means "or". Notice appears inside its own definition through . That is what lets you write an if inside an if inside a while. A missing closing brace gives "syntax error" because no derivation of the grammar can produce your code. How a compiler uses it: The compiler's parser (the part that checks structure) is built from the grammar, sometimes automatically by tools like yacc, Bison or ANTLR. The structure is defined once, exactly, instead of every compiler writer guessing from English. How a machine actually checks a string against a grammar comes in lessons 16 and 17. When to use a CFG: Use a grammar when your strings have nesting or matching pairs: brackets, tags, blocks, expressions, JSON, HTML-like structure, sentence structure. When NOT to use one: If the pattern has no nesting, like a phone number, an email shape or a date, a regular expression is simpler and its matcher is faster (a DFA reads each symbol once with no extra memory). And CFGs have limits too: they cannot describe a^n b^n c^n, where three counts must be equal, or the rule "every variable must be declared before it is used". Compilers check those things in a separate step after parsing. Lesson 18 proves the first limit. Common mistakes: First, mixing up variables and terminals. If a capital letter has no rule, it is not a variable you can expand, and a lowercase letter can never be replaced. Second, forgetting the base case: S -> aSb alone generates nothing, since S never disappears. Third, writing S -> aS | Sb | ε and expecting a^n b^n. It gives a*b*, no matching, because the two rules are used independently. Produce the matched pair in one rule instead. Fourth, claiming a grammar is correct after testing two strings. You must argue both directions: everything it makes is in the language, and everything in the language can be made. What exams ask: Typical questions are: write a CFG for a given language (a^n b^n, a^n b^(n+1), palindromes, equal numbers of a's and b's, balanced brackets); give the 4-tuple of a grammar; derive a given string step by step; describe in words the language a given grammar generates; and show that every regular language is context-free. For "describe the language", derive the first few short strings and spot the pattern. Mental model: Picture a grammar as a recipe book in a biye bari kitchen. The start variable S is the order "make the full feast". Each production is a recipe card that says how one dish can be made from smaller dishes and raw ingredients. Variables are dishes still to be cooked, terminals are raw ingredients that go straight onto the plate. A derivation is the cooking: you keep picking an unfinished dish and following one of its cards until only raw ingredients remain. A card can call for the same dish inside itself, so the feast nests as deep as you like, and each matching pair is placed by one card at one moment, so balance is never lost. Recap and what is next: A CFG is (V, Σ, R, S); productions rewrite one variable at a time, ignoring neighbours; derivations go from S to terminal strings, and those strings form a context-free language, a family that contains every regular language and also nesting. In the next lesson we draw derivations as trees, called parse trees, and see what goes wrong when one string has two different trees.
key_points: Regular languages cannot do unbounded nesting like a^n b^n, because a finite automaton cannot count without limit.
A CFG is a 4-tuple (V, Σ, R, S): variables, terminals, productions of the form A -> w, and a start variable.
A derivation replaces one variable at a time using a rule, from S until only terminals remain.
Context-free means a variable can be replaced whatever symbols surround it.
S -> aSb | ε makes a^n b^n by producing each a and its matching b in the same step.
Classic grammars: palindromes S -> aSa | bSb | a | b | ε, brackets S -> (S) | SS | ε.
Every regular language is context-free; BNF is the CFG notation used to define programming languages.
CFGs check structure, not meaning, and cannot describe a^n b^n c^n.
lessons.tip: When designing a grammar, always ask: what is the outside layer I can peel off, and what is left inside? Then write the base case before anything else.
lessons.task: On paper, write a grammar for { a^n b^(n+1) : n >= 0 }. Derive the strings b, abb and aabbb step by step, then try to derive abab and explain why it is impossible.

quiz.q: Why can no DFA recognise a^n b^n?
options: It cannot read the letter b
It would need to remember an unbounded count of a's with finitely many states
quiz.explain: A DFA has a fixed number of states, so it cannot tell apart arbitrarily many different counts of a's.

quiz.q: In the grammar S -> aSb | ε, which derivation is correct for aabb?
quiz.explain: Use S -> aSb twice, then S -> ε.

quiz.q: What does 'context-free' mean for a rule A -> w?
options: A can be replaced regardless of the symbols around it
The rule can only be used at the start
quiz.explain: The left side is a single variable, so its neighbours never affect whether the rule can be used.

quiz.q: Which grammar generates balanced brackets?
quiz.explain: Wrapping and placing side by side plus the empty string give all balanced strings; (S) | ε alone misses ()().

quiz.q: Which language is context-free but not regular?
quiz.explain: a^n b^n needs matching counts; the others are regular, and regular languages are also context-free.

lessons.title: Derivations, Parse Trees and Ambiguity
lessons.content:
Type 2 + 3 * 4 into your phone calculator. It says 14. But a careless person reading left to right would say 2 + 3 = 5, then 5 * 4 = 20. Same string, two meanings, two answers. In a compiler, that is a bug in every program. Today we learn how a grammar gives a string its structure, using trees, and what happens when a grammar allows two different structures for the same string.

Recap: A context-free grammar (lesson 13) has variables (placeholders like S or E), terminals (real symbols), productions like A -> w, and a start variable. A derivation starts at the start variable and keeps replacing one variable using one rule until only terminals remain. For S -> aSb | ε we had S => aSb => aaSbb => aabb.

The problem of order: When a half-finished string has two or more variables, which one do we replace first? Take G with rules S -> AB, A -> aA | a, B -> b, and derive aab. Option 1: S => AB => aAB => aaB => aab. Option 2: S => AB => Ab => aAb => aab. Both are correct derivations of aab. They used the same rules on the same variables, only in a different order. One string, many derivations that mean the same thing.

Leftmost and rightmost derivations: To remove this freedom, we fix a habit. In a leftmost derivation, every step replaces the leftmost variable. Option 1 above is leftmost. In a rightmost derivation, every step replaces the rightmost variable. Option 2 is rightmost. Note the word "leftmost" is about which variable you pick, not which rule. You still choose the rule. Top-down parsers (LL) build leftmost derivations; bottom-up parsers (LR) build rightmost ones in reverse.

Parse tree: A parse tree is a picture of a derivation that forgets the order. Rules for drawing it: the root is the start variable; every inner node is a variable; when a rule A -> X1 X2 ... Xk is used, node A gets children X1 to Xk from left to right; if the rule is A -> ε, A gets a single child ε; leaves are terminals or ε. Reading the leaves from left to right, skipping ε, gives the yield of the tree, which is the derived string.

Building a tree level by level: Grammar S -> aSb | ε, string aabb. Level 0: root S. Level 1: S used S -> aSb, so it has three children: a, S, b. Level 2: the middle S also used S -> aSb, so it has children a, S, b. Level 3: the innermost S used S -> ε, so it has one child, ε. Reading leaves left to right: a, a, ε, b, b, which gives aabb. The tree shows the nesting directly: the outer a and the last b are siblings, they were made as a pair.

Why trees beat derivations: For the grammar S -> AB, A -> aA | a, B -> b, both derivations of aab (leftmost and rightmost) draw exactly the same tree: S with children A and B; A with children a and A; the lower A with child a; B with child b. Different order, same structure. In fact, every parse tree matches exactly one leftmost derivation (walk the tree, always expanding the leftmost unfinished node) and exactly one rightmost derivation. So counting trees, counting leftmost derivations and counting rightmost derivations always give the same number.

Why structure matters: A compiler does not only ask "is this code valid?". It builds the parse tree (or a trimmed version, the abstract syntax tree) and then uses the tree to decide what to compute. Each inner node is an operation applied to the values of its children. So the tree is the meaning. If one string had two trees, the compiler would not know which program you wrote.

Ambiguity defined: A grammar is ambiguous if some string in its language has two or more different parse trees. Equivalently, two different leftmost derivations, or two different rightmost derivations. Careful: two different derivations alone prove nothing; we just saw a leftmost and a rightmost derivation drawing one tree.

The classic example: Grammar E -> E + E | E * E | id, string id + id * id. Leftmost derivation 1: E => E + E => id + E => id + E * E => id + id * E => id + id * id. Its tree: root E with children E, +, E; the right E has children E, *, E. So the * is lower in the tree, done first: id + (id * id). Leftmost derivation 2: E => E * E => E + E * E => id + E * E => id + id * E => id + id * id. Its tree: root E with children E, *, E; the left E has children E, +, E. Now + is lower, done first: (id + id) * id. Two leftmost derivations, two trees, so the grammar is ambiguous.

Cause and effect: Put numbers in: 2 + 3 * 4. Tree 1 computes 3 * 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14. Tree 2 computes 2 + 3 = 5, then 5 * 4 = 20. The rule is simple: the lower an operator sits in the tree, the earlier it is done, because a node needs its children's values first. A second problem hides in the same grammar. With minus, E -> E - E | id, the string 5 - 3 - 1 has tree (5 - 3) - 1 = 1 and tree 5 - (3 - 1) = 3. That is a question of associativity: which way equal operators group.

What people did before fixing grammars: Early language manuals wrote the grammar loosely and added English notes like "multiplication binds tighter than addition". The cleaner idea is to put precedence (which operator binds tighter) and associativity into the grammar itself, so the grammar allows only one tree.

Removing ambiguity with levels: Use one variable per precedence level. E -> E + T | T, T -> T * F | F, F -> ( E ) | id. Read it as: an expression (E) is a sum of terms; a term (T) is a product of factors; a factor (F) is an id or a bracketed expression. Why it works: a + can only be created by E, and E sits above T in every tree. A * is created by T, below. So inside a term, a + can appear only inside brackets. The grammar has no way to put + below * without brackets. Precedence is forced by the shape of the rules, not by an English note.

The single tree: Leftmost derivation of id + id * id in the new grammar: E => E + T => T + T => F + T => id + T => id + T * F => id + F * F => id + id * F => id + id * id. At the first step we had to choose E -> E + T, because E -> T would make a single term, and a term cannot contain a + outside brackets. So there is only one tree: root E with children E, +, T, and the multiplication lives under T. The answer for 2 + 3 * 4 is always 14.

Associativity from recursion: In E -> E + T the recursion is on the left. For a - b - c with E -> E - T | T, the leftmost E must hold a - b, so the tree is (a - b) - c, left associative, which is how arithmetic works: 5 - 3 - 1 = 1. If we wrote E -> T - E, the recursion would be on the right and we would get 5 - (3 - 1) = 3. Right recursion is correct for operators that group to the right, like the power operator in maths: 2^3^2 means 2^(3^2) = 512.

The dangling else: Grammar: S -> if C then S | if C then S else S | other. String: if C1 then if C2 then s1 else s2. Tree 1: the else belongs to the inner if, if C1 then (if C2 then s1 else s2). Tree 2: the else belongs to the outer if, if C1 then (if C2 then s1) else s2. If C1 is true and C2 is false, tree 1 runs s2 and tree 2 runs nothing; if C1 is false, it is the other way round. Different programs. C and Java settle it with the rule "an else matches the nearest unmatched if", and that rule can also be written into the grammar using two variables, one for fully matched statements and one for unmatched ones.

Inherently ambiguous languages: Usually ambiguity belongs to the grammar, not the language, and a better grammar fixes it. But some context-free languages have no unambiguous grammar at all. They are called inherently ambiguous. The standard example is { a^i b^j c^k : i = j or j = k }. Strings like a^n b^n c^n satisfy both conditions, and it has been proved that every grammar for this language gives some of them two trees, one built from the "a's match b's" part and one from the "b's match c's" part.

A hard limit: There is no algorithm that takes any CFG and always correctly answers "is it ambiguous?". This is an undecidable problem, a kind of result you will meet in lessons 22 and 23. In practice we argue from a grammar's structure, as with E, T, F, or let a parser generator report conflicts.

Real life example 1, Bangla phrases: Take "পুরনো বই আর খাতা". Tree 1: পুরনো (বই আর খাতা), both are old. Tree 2: (পুরনো বই) আর খাতা, only the books are old. If your mother says "পুরনো বই আর খাতা বিক্রি করে দাও", one tree sells your new khata too. Where it matches: same words, two groupings, two meanings, exactly like 2 + 3 * 4. Where it breaks: people use context and tone to pick the right meaning. A parser has no context; it only has the grammar, so the grammar must leave just one choice.

Real life example 2, spreadsheets and calculators: In Excel, =2+3*4 gives 14, but =2^3^2 gives 64, because Excel groups ^ from the left, unlike maths. Same symbols, a different grammar choice, a different answer. This is why every programming language manual has a precedence and associativity table, and why careful programmers add brackets when unsure: brackets force one tree in every language.

When to use an ambiguous grammar anyway: Parser generators like yacc and Bison accept the short ambiguous grammar E -> E + E | E * E | id together with declarations like "%left '+'" and "%left '*'" that pick one tree. When not: for a hand-written parser or a precise specification, use the layered grammar; no side rules to forget. And for a language like the one above that is inherently ambiguous, no fix exists, so you resolve choices outside the grammar.

Common mistakes: First, saying a grammar is ambiguous because a string has a leftmost and a rightmost derivation. You need two different trees (or two leftmost derivations). Second, thinking leftmost means "use the first rule"; it means expand the leftmost variable. Third, drawing a parse tree with terminals as inner nodes; terminals are always leaves. Fourth, believing every ambiguous language can be fixed; inherently ambiguous ones cannot. Fifth, forgetting that the fixed grammar must generate the same language; check that brackets and single ids still work.

What exams ask: Show that a grammar is ambiguous (give one string and two parse trees or two leftmost derivations); draw a parse tree and state its yield; give leftmost and rightmost derivations of a string; rewrite E -> E + E | E * E | id as an unambiguous grammar with correct precedence and associativity; explain the dangling else; give an example of an inherently ambiguous language.

Mental model: Picture a family tree drawn for a string. The start variable is the great-grandparent at the top, rules are the moments each parent had children, and the string is the row of youngest children read left to right. A derivation is just one possible order of telling the family story; the tree is the family itself. A grammar is unambiguous when every string has exactly one family tree. An operator's position in the tree is its job order: deeper means earlier.

Recap and what is next: Leftmost and rightmost derivations fix the order of expansion; a parse tree shows the structure and forgets order; the yield is the leaves read left to right; a grammar is ambiguous if one string has two trees; precedence levels and left or right recursion remove ambiguity in expressions; some languages are inherently ambiguous. Next lesson we clean grammars up: remove useless parts, ε-rules and unit rules, and convert to Chomsky Normal Form.
key_points: A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost variable; a rightmost one expands the rightmost.
A parse tree has the start variable at the root, variables inside, terminals or ε at the leaves; its yield is the leaves read left to right.
Each parse tree matches exactly one leftmost and one rightmost derivation.
A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two different parse trees (equivalently two leftmost derivations).
E -> E + E | E * E | id is ambiguous: id + id * id has two trees, giving 14 or 20 for 2 + 3 * 4.
The layered grammar E -> E + T | T, T -> T * F | F, F -> (E) | id fixes precedence and left associativity.
Some languages, like { a^i b^j c^k : i = j or j = k }, are inherently ambiguous.
Checking whether an arbitrary CFG is ambiguous is undecidable.
lessons.tip: To test a grammar for ambiguity, try short strings that mix two operators or nest two structures, like id + id * id or if-if-else. Ambiguity usually hides where two rules compete for the same piece.
lessons.task: Using E -> E - E | E / E | id, draw both parse trees for 8 - 4 - 2 and for 8 / 4 / 2 and compute each value. Then write a layered grammar that gives the normal maths answers.

quiz.q: What makes a grammar ambiguous?
options: A string with a leftmost and a rightmost derivation
A string with two different parse trees
A grammar with more than one variable
quiz.explain: Two trees (or two leftmost derivations) for one string; a leftmost plus a rightmost derivation can draw the same tree.

quiz.q: In E -> E + E | E * E | id, the tree with * at the root for 2 + 3 * 4 gives:
quiz.explain: * at the root means 2 + 3 is computed first, then 5 * 4 = 20.

quiz.q: Why does E -> E + T | T, T -> T * F | F, F -> (E) | id give * higher precedence?
options: Because * appears in T, below E, so + cannot sit under * without brackets
Because the grammar is right recursive
quiz.explain: The level structure forces every + to be above every unbracketed *, so * is done first.

quiz.q: Which language is inherently ambiguous?
options: { a^i b^j c^k : i = j or j = k }
quiz.explain: Strings a^n b^n c^n meet both conditions and every grammar gives some of them two trees.

quiz.q: The rule E -> E - T | T makes 10 - 4 - 3 equal to:
quiz.explain: Left recursion groups to the left: (10 - 4) - 3 = 3.

lessons.title: Simplifying Grammars and Normal Forms
lessons.content:
Before exams your mother says: clean your table first. Throw out the pens that do not write, the notes from a subject you dropped, and stop keeping a note that only says "see the other note". After cleaning, nothing on the table is useless and everything is easy to find. Grammars need the same cleaning. Today we remove the junk from a grammar and then press it into a strict standard shape called Chomsky Normal Form.

Why bother: Different people write different grammars for the same language, with all kinds of rule shapes. Algorithms and proofs hate variety. The CYK membership algorithm (lesson 17) and the pumping lemma for context-free languages (lesson 18) both need every rule in a fixed small shape. So we need a guaranteed recipe that takes any context-free grammar and produces an equivalent one, meaning one that generates exactly the same language, in the standard shape. Chomsky described this normal form in 1959, and Sheila Greibach gave another one in 1965.

Three kinds of junk: First, useless symbols: variables that can never finish into terminals, or that can never be reached from the start. Second, ε-productions: rules A -> ε that make a variable vanish. Third, unit productions: rules A -> B, where one variable just becomes another, like a note saying "see the other note". We remove them one kind at a time.

Useless symbols, two tests: A variable is generating if it can derive some string of terminals. A variable is reachable if the start variable can derive a string containing it. A variable is useful only if it passes both tests. To find generating ones, start with the terminals, then repeatedly mark a variable if it has a rule whose right side is made only of marked symbols, until nothing changes. To find reachable ones, start with S and repeatedly mark every variable that appears on the right side of a rule of a marked variable.

Worked example: S -> AB | a, A -> a, B -> Bb. Generating: A (A -> a), S (S -> a). B is not: its only rule needs B again, so it never ends, like a story that always says "to be continued". Remove B and every rule containing B: we get S -> a, A -> a. Now test reachability: from S we only reach a. A is unreachable, so remove it. Final grammar: S -> a.

Order matters here: If you test reachability first, all of S, A, B are reachable (S -> AB), so nothing is removed. Then removing non-generating B also deletes S -> AB, and A becomes unreachable, but you already did that test, so A stays as junk. The cause: removing non-generating symbols can create new unreachable ones, but not the other way round. So always remove non-generating first, then unreachable.

ε-productions, the idea: A variable is nullable if it can derive ε (the empty string). If some rule uses a nullable variable, then in real derivations that variable might vanish. To remove A -> ε without losing strings, we add copies of every rule with nullable variables left out in every possible way. For example, if A is nullable, the rule S -> aAb gets a partner S -> ab. Then delete all ε-rules. If ε itself was in the language, we keep exactly one rule: start -> ε.

Why remove ε-rules: Without them, a derivation can never make the string shorter. Each step keeps or grows the length. That makes derivations easy to bound and is the base of the 2n - 1 fact we will see soon. With ε-rules, a sentential form could grow huge and then shrink, so you can never be sure when to stop searching.

Unit productions: A rule A -> B does no real work. It is like an office file that goes from desk A to desk B without anyone writing on it. Worse, chains like A -> B, B -> A form loops that go nowhere. Removal: for every pair where A can reach B using only unit rules (including A itself), copy each non-unit rule of B to A. Then delete all unit rules. Example: A -> B | a, B -> bb. A reaches B, so A gets B's rule: A -> bb | a.

Chomsky Normal Form: A grammar is in CNF if every rule has one of two shapes: A -> BC (exactly two variables) or A -> a (exactly one terminal). One exception: the start variable S0 may have S0 -> ε if ε is in the language, and then S0 must not appear on the right side of any rule. Notice what CNF forbids: ε-rules elsewhere, unit rules, terminals mixed with variables, and right sides longer than two.

The conversion recipe: Step 1, START: add a new start variable S0 -> S, so the start never appears on a right side. Step 2, DEL: remove ε-rules. Step 3, UNIT: remove unit rules. Step 4, clean out useless symbols if any appeared. Step 5, TERM: in every right side of length two or more, replace each terminal a with a new variable Ta and add Ta -> a. Step 6, BIN: break every right side longer than two into a chain of pairs, so A -> BCD becomes A -> BX, X -> CD. Why this order: removing ε-rules can create new unit rules (S -> AB with B nullable gives S -> A), so UNIT must come after DEL.

Worked conversion, the grammar: S -> aSb | A, A -> cA | ε. This makes a^n c^m b^n: matched a's and b's around any number of c's. For example S => aSb => aAb => acAb => acb.

Steps 1 and 2: START: add S0 -> S. DEL: A is nullable (A -> ε). S is nullable too, because S -> A. And S0 is nullable because S0 -> S. Now add versions with nullable variables dropped. A -> cA gives A -> cA | c. S -> aSb gives S -> aSb | ab. S -> A dropped to nothing would be ε, which we do not add. S0 -> S gives S0 -> S | ε, and we keep S0 -> ε because ε is in the language. Delete A -> ε. Now: S0 -> S | ε, S -> aSb | ab | A, A -> cA | c.

Steps 3 to 6: UNIT: S -> A is a unit rule, so S gets A's rules: S -> aSb | ab | cA | c. S0 -> S is a unit rule, so S0 gets all of S's rules. Now S0 -> aSb | ab | cA | c | ε, S -> aSb | ab | cA | c, A -> cA | c. No useless symbols. TERM: add Ta -> a, Tb -> b, Tc -> c, giving S -> Ta S Tb | Ta Tb | Tc A | c. Note S -> c stays as it is, it is already a legal single terminal. BIN: S -> Ta S Tb is too long, so make X -> S Tb and S -> Ta X. Same for S0.

The final CNF grammar: S0 -> Ta X | Ta Tb | Tc A | c | ε; S -> Ta X | Ta Tb | Tc A | c; A -> Tc A | c; X -> S Tb; Ta -> a; Tb -> b; Tc -> c. Every rule is two variables or one terminal, and S0 -> ε is the one allowed exception. I checked by listing all strings up to length 7 from both grammars: the sets are identical. You can do a small check by hand: derive acb in the new grammar: S0 => Ta X => a X => a S Tb => a c Tb => a c b.

The 2n - 1 rule: In CNF, any string of length n >= 1 takes exactly 2n - 1 derivation steps. Why: a rule A -> BC turns one symbol into two, so it raises the number of symbols by one. Going from 1 symbol (S0) to n symbols needs exactly n - 1 such steps. Then each of the n positions needs one A -> a step to become a terminal. Total (n - 1) + n = 2n - 1. Check with acb: n = 3, and the derivation above had 5 steps. This also means every parse tree is a binary tree, which makes height arguments easy in lesson 18.

The cost, trade-off: CNF grammars are bigger and harder to read. Our 4 friendly rules became more than a dozen. Removing ε-rules can blow up badly: a rule with k nullable variables can turn into up to 2^k rules, so some books run BIN before DEL to keep this small. Also the parse tree changes shape: the CNF tree for a string is not the tree of the original grammar, so if the tree carries meaning, as in a compiler, you must map back.

Greibach Normal Form, the idea: In GNF, every rule looks like A -> a B1 B2 ... Bk: one terminal first, then zero or more variables. Example for { a^n b^n : n >= 1 }: S -> aSB | aB, B -> b. Derive aabb: S => aSB => aaBB => aabB => aabb. Each step produces exactly one terminal at the front, so a string of length n takes exactly n steps. That matches a machine that reads one input symbol per move, which helps when building a pushdown automaton from a grammar. GNF also has no left recursion (rules like A -> A...), which would make a top-down parser call itself forever without reading input. Every CFG without ε can be converted to GNF, but the steps are long, so here we keep only the idea.

Real life example 1, a government office: A file goes from Desk A to Desk B to Desk C, and only Desk C actually signs it. Unit-rule removal is like letting Desk A sign directly with Desk C's stamp: same result, no empty hops. Useless symbols are desks that no file ever reaches, or desks that never let a file out. Where the analogy breaks: in an office, removing desks changes jobs. In a grammar, the cleaned version is guaranteed to generate exactly the same language, nothing gained and nothing lost.

Real life example 2, parsers in practice: Parsers for human languages, trained on large sets of tagged sentences, often convert their grammars into a binary form like CNF so they can run CYK-style table algorithms. Compiler tools also transform grammars: top-down parser generators require left recursion to be removed first, and tools may do it for you. Even when nobody uses strict CNF, the same cleaning moves appear everywhere.

When to use, when not: Use CNF when you need an algorithm or proof: CYK, the pumping lemma, deciding whether a string is generated by checking all derivations of length 2n - 1. Use GNF ideas when building top-down or one-symbol-per-step machines. Do not use CNF as your main written grammar for a programming language; humans must read it, and the readable layered grammar from lesson 14 is better for that.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the new start variable, so S appears on a right side and S -> ε breaks the rules. Losing ε from the language by deleting S0 -> ε. Missing some combinations when dropping nullable variables (a rule with two nullable variables needs three new versions, not one). Doing UNIT before DEL. Leaving mixed rules like A -> aB, which are not CNF. Forgetting that A -> a is fine and should not be replaced by Ta.

What exams ask: Remove useless symbols from a given grammar and explain the order; find nullable variables and remove ε-productions; remove unit productions; convert a grammar to CNF step by step; prove that a CNF derivation of a length-n string takes 2n - 1 steps; state the form of GNF.

Mental model: Picture a factory line that builds strings. In CNF, every machine on the line does one of two jobs only: split one box into exactly two boxes, or stamp one box into a finished letter. No machine passes a box along unchanged (no unit rules), and no machine makes a box disappear (no ε-rules), except the one at the gate that may send out an empty order. Because each split adds exactly one box and each stamp finishes exactly one box, you can predict the work: 2n - 1 moves for n letters.

Recap and what is next: Remove non-generating then unreachable symbols; remove ε-rules by adding versions without nullable variables; remove unit rules by copying; then TERM and BIN give CNF, where every rule is A -> BC or A -> a. CNF derivations take 2n - 1 steps, and GNF puts one terminal first in every rule. Next lesson we meet the machine for context-free languages: a finite automaton with a stack, the pushdown automaton.
key_points: A useful variable must be generating (derives a terminal string) and reachable from the start.
Remove non-generating symbols first, then unreachable ones; the other order can leave junk.
Remove ε-rules by adding copies of rules with nullable variables dropped; keep S0 -> ε only if ε is in the language.
Remove unit rules A -> B by copying B's non-unit rules to A, after ε-removal.
CNF allows only A -> BC and A -> a, plus S0 -> ε with S0 never on a right side.
Conversion order: START, DEL, UNIT, (useless), TERM, BIN.
In CNF a string of length n needs exactly 2n - 1 derivation steps, and parse trees are binary.
GNF rules look like A -> a B1...Bk; each step makes one terminal and there is no left recursion.
lessons.tip: Write the grammar again in full after every step of the conversion. Most exam mistakes come from changing several things at once and losing a rule along the way.
lessons.task: Convert S -> ASB | ε, A -> aA | a, B -> b to Chomsky Normal Form step by step on paper. Then derive aab in your final grammar and count the steps; check that it equals 2n - 1.

quiz.q: In S -> AB | a, A -> a, B -> Bb, which symbols are useless?
quiz.explain: B never finishes (non-generating); after removing it and S -> AB, A becomes unreachable.

quiz.q: Which rule is allowed in Chomsky Normal Form?
quiz.explain: CNF allows only two variables or one terminal on the right side.

quiz.q: A CNF derivation of a string of length 6 takes how many steps?
quiz.explain: 2n - 1 = 11: five binary splits plus six terminal steps.

quiz.q: Why must unit-rule removal come after ε-rule removal?
options: Removing ε-rules can create new unit rules
ε-rules cannot exist with unit rules
quiz.explain: S -> AB with B nullable produces S -> A, a new unit rule.

quiz.q: If A and B are nullable, how many rules replace S -> AB (not counting ε)?
quiz.explain: Drop any subset except all: AB, A, B. Dropping both would give ε, which is not added.

lessons.title: Pushdown Automata
lessons.content:
At a biye bari, the clean plates sit in a tall stack near the food table. The helper puts each washed plate on top, and every guest takes the top plate. Nobody pulls a plate from the middle. That simple rule, last in, first out, is exactly the memory a finite automaton was missing. Give a finite automaton a stack of plates and it can suddenly check a^n b^n, balanced brackets and every other context-free language. This new machine is called a pushdown automaton, or PDA.

The gap we are filling: A finite automaton has only its current state as memory, so it cannot count without limit. Grammars (lessons 13 to 15) can describe nesting, but a grammar is a generator, it makes strings. We also want a recogniser: a machine that reads a given string and says yes or no. For regular languages, regex (generator) and DFA (recogniser) matched. For context-free languages, CFG is the generator and the PDA is the recogniser. Lesson 17 proves they match exactly.

What a stack is: A stack (from Data Structures) is a list where you can only touch one end, the top. Push puts a symbol on top. Pop removes the top symbol. You can look at the top, but not below it. Because the last thing pushed is the first thing popped, a stack naturally matches nested things: the last bracket opened is the first one closed. The stack can grow as tall as needed, which gives unlimited memory, but only in this restricted, top-only way.

Before PDAs: Programmers in the 1950s already used stacks inside programs to evaluate expressions and parse code. In the early 1960s, people building the first parsers described this "pushdown store" as part of an abstract machine. The clean question became: what can a finite control plus one stack recognise? Exactly the context-free languages.

The parts of a PDA: A PDA has a finite control (states, like a DFA), an input tape read left to right once, and a stack. In one move it looks at three things: the current state, the next input symbol (or it may choose not to read, an ε-move), and the symbol on top of the stack. Then it does three things: goes to a new state, pops the top symbol, and pushes a string of zero or more symbols in its place. Pushing zero symbols means a plain pop. Pushing back the same symbol means "leave the stack alone".

The 7-tuple: A PDA is P = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F). Q is the finite set of states. Σ is the input alphabet. Γ (gamma) is the stack alphabet, the symbols allowed on the stack, which may differ from the input. δ is the transition function. q0 is the start state. Z0 is the start stack symbol, sitting at the bottom at the beginning, so the machine can tell when the stack is "empty". F is the set of accepting states. δ takes (state, input symbol or ε, top of stack) and returns a set of choices, each a pair (new state, string to push). Because it returns a set, a PDA is nondeterministic by default, like an NFA.

Reading a transition: We write δ(q0, a, A) = {(q0, AA)}, or on a diagram an arrow labelled "a, A -> AA": read a, pop A, push AA. When a string is pushed, its leftmost symbol ends up on top. So "a, Z -> AZ" pops Z and pushes Z back with A on top of it. "b, A -> ε" reads b and simply pops an A.

Instantaneous description: To trace a PDA we write its full situation as a triple (state, remaining input, stack), with the top of the stack written on the left. This is called an instantaneous description, or ID. One move is written with the turnstile symbol: ID1 |- ID2. Many moves are written |-*. A trace is a chain of IDs, like a scorecard updated ball by ball.

Designing a PDA for a^n b^n, n >= 1: The plan in plain words: while reading a's, push one A for each a. When the first b comes, switch to "matching mode" and pop one A for each b. If the A's run out exactly when the input ends, accept. States: q0 (reading a's), q1 (reading b's), q2 (accept). Transitions: δ(q0, a, Z) = (q0, AZ); δ(q0, a, A) = (q0, AA); δ(q0, b, A) = (q1, ε); δ(q1, b, A) = (q1, ε); δ(q1, ε, Z) = (q2, Z). F = {q2}. The stack is the counter; Z is the floor that tells us the count reached zero.

Trace on aabb: (q0, aabb, Z) |- (q0, abb, AZ) |- (q0, bb, AAZ) |- (q1, b, AZ) |- (q1, ε, Z) |- (q2, ε, Z). First a: push A. Second a: push another A, stack AAZ. First b: pop, go to q1, stack AZ. Second b: pop, stack Z. The input is used up and Z is on top, so the ε-move goes to q2. Input finished in an accepting state: accept.

Traces that fail: aab: (q0, aab, Z) |- (q0, ab, AZ) |- (q0, b, AAZ) |- (q1, ε, AZ). The input is finished but an A is still on top, and there is no move for (q1, ε, A). The machine stops in q1, not accepting, so reject: too many a's. abb: (q0, abb, Z) |- (q0, bb, AZ) |- (q1, b, Z). Now there is no move reading b with Z on top. The ε-move to q2 is possible, but then the last b is still unread and q2 has no moves, so this path also fails. Too many b's. aba: after (q1, a, Z) there is no move that reads an a in q1, so reject: the order is wrong. Z guards the floor, so the machine never pops an empty stack.

Acceptance means: A PDA accepts a string if at least one sequence of moves reads the whole input and ends in an accepting state. Stopping early, getting stuck, or ending in a non-accepting state on every path means reject. With nondeterminism, one good path is enough, exactly as with NFAs.

Where nondeterminism matters, ww^R: Let L = { w w^R : w in {a, b}* }, even-length palindromes, like abba or baab. w^R means w reversed. The plan: push the first half, then pop while matching the second half. The problem: while reading, the machine cannot know where the middle is. Nothing in abba says "middle here". So the PDA guesses. Transitions: δ(q0, a, X) = (q0, aX) and δ(q0, b, X) = (q0, bX) for any top X (push what you read); δ(q0, ε, X) = (q1, X) (guess "this is the middle"); δ(q1, a, a) = (q1, ε) and δ(q1, b, b) = (q1, ε) (pop on match); δ(q1, ε, Z0) = (q2, Z0) (accept). Here the stack symbols are a, b and Z0.

Trace of ww^R on abba: The good guess, middle after two symbols: (q0, abba, Z) |- (q0, bba, aZ) |- (q0, ba, baZ) |- (q1, ba, baZ) |- (q1, a, aZ) |- (q1, ε, Z) |- (q2, ε, Z). Accept. The wrong guesses simply die. Guess after one symbol: (q1, bba, aZ), but the input says b and the top is a: no move, dead. Guess after three: (q1, a, bbaZ), input a, top b: dead. Guess at the very start: (q1, abba, Z) can only go to q2 with abba unread: dead. Guess at the end: (q1, ε, abbaZ), stuck with a on top: dead. One path accepts, so abba is accepted.

Two ways to accept: The version above is acceptance by final state: the input is finished and the machine is in a state of F, whatever is left on the stack. Another version is acceptance by empty stack: the input is finished and the stack is completely empty, including Z0, and states do not matter. For the a^n b^n machine, replace the last move with δ(q1, ε, Z) = (q1, ε), popping the floor. For nondeterministic PDAs both styles recognise exactly the same family of languages, because each can simulate the other: to go from empty stack to final state, put a new bottom marker below Z0 and jump to an accept state when you see it; to go the other way, from any accepting state, empty the stack with ε-moves.

Real life example 1, a code editor's bracket matcher: When you type code in VS Code and click a "{", the editor highlights its partner "}". Inside, it does what our PDA does: scan left to right, push every opening bracket, and pop when a closing bracket arrives, checking that it is the same kind. If you close ")" when "[" is on top, that is the red squiggle. If brackets remain on the stack at the end of the file, something was never closed. Where it breaks: a real editor also uses line numbers, colours and error recovery, and its stack size is limited by memory, while a PDA's stack is unlimited.

Real life example 2, the call stack: When function main calls f, and f calls g, your computer pushes a frame for each call onto the call stack. When g returns, its frame is popped and control goes back to f. Function calls nest exactly like brackets, which is why a stack is the natural memory for them. When recursion never stops, frames are pushed forever and the program crashes with a "stack overflow": the real stack is finite, unlike the PDA's.

Limits of one stack: A stack can only be read from the top, and popping destroys information. For a^n b^n c^n, you could push a's and pop them against b's, but then the count is gone when the c's arrive. No PDA can recognise this language (lesson 18 proves it). Interestingly, a finite control with two stacks is as powerful as a Turing machine, the most powerful model in this course, so the jump from one stack to two is huge.

When to use a PDA, and when not: Use a PDA (or code that behaves like one) when input has nesting: brackets, tags, expressions, recursive structures. When not: if the pattern is regular, a DFA is simpler and needs no stack. And if you need to compare three or more counts, or check copies like ww (a string followed by an exact copy of itself, not reversed), one stack is not enough, because the copy must be checked in the same order it was stored, but a stack gives things back in reverse.

PDA versus DFA, side by side: Memory: DFA only its state; PDA state plus an unbounded stack. Moves: DFA must read one symbol per move; PDA may also make ε-moves. Determinism: an NFA is no stronger than a DFA, but a nondeterministic PDA is strictly stronger than a deterministic PDA; ww^R needs the guess. Languages: DFA, regular; PDA, context-free.

Common mistakes: Writing the pushed string in the wrong order (remember: leftmost symbol becomes the top). Forgetting the bottom marker Z0, so the machine cannot tell when the count is zero. Accepting before the whole input is read. Thinking a PDA needs an empty stack to accept in final-state mode. Making a transition that pops when the stack top is not what you think, because each move must name the exact top symbol it expects. Trying to build a deterministic PDA for ww^R; it cannot be done.

What exams ask: Give the 7-tuple of a PDA; design a PDA for a^n b^n, a^n b^(2n), balanced brackets, ww^R, wcw^R or equal numbers of a's and b's; trace a PDA on a string using IDs; explain acceptance by final state versus empty stack and prove they are equivalent; explain why nondeterminism is needed for ww^R.

Mental model: Picture a ticket checker at a bus with a stack of tokens in his pocket. He reads passengers one by one, never going back (the input). His mood, "boarding" or "getting off", is the state. For each person boarding he drops a token on top of the stack; for each person getting off he removes the top token. He can only feel the top token. At the last stop, if the tokens are back to just the bottom marker and he is in the right mood, the trip was fine: accept. For tricky routes where he does not know where the turning point is, imagine him splitting into copies at every stop, each copy guessing differently, and the trip is fine if any copy ends happy.

Recap and what is next: A PDA is a finite automaton plus a stack, defined by the 7-tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F). Each move reads a symbol or ε, pops the top, and pushes a string. We trace with IDs (state, input, stack). A PDA for a^n b^n pushes on a and pops on b; the PDA for ww^R must guess the middle. Final-state and empty-stack acceptance are equally powerful. Next lesson we prove that PDAs and CFGs describe the same languages, meet deterministic PDAs, and test membership with the CYK algorithm.
key_points: A PDA is a finite automaton plus an unbounded stack used last in, first out.
7-tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F); each move reads a symbol or ε, pops the top, and pushes a string.
In a push, the leftmost symbol of the string becomes the new top.
An ID (state, remaining input, stack) is a snapshot; traces are chains of IDs joined by |-.
For a^n b^n: push A on each a, pop A on each b, accept when Z0 is back on top and the input is finished.
ww^R needs nondeterminism: the PDA guesses the middle and wrong guesses die.
Acceptance by final state and by empty stack are equally powerful for nondeterministic PDAs.
One stack cannot handle a^n b^n c^n; two stacks would be as powerful as a Turing machine.
lessons.tip: When designing a PDA, first write the plan in plain words: what do I push, when do I switch mode, what do I pop, how do I know I am done. Then turn each sentence into one or two transitions.
lessons.task: Design a PDA for { a^n b^(2n) : n >= 1 } (hint: push two symbols for each a). Trace it with IDs on abb and on aabbbb, and then on aabbb to see it reject.

quiz.q: What does the transition 'a, A -> AA' do?
options: Reads a, pops A, pushes AA, so one more A is on the stack
quiz.explain: Pop A and push AA leaves one extra A: the count goes up by one.

quiz.q: In the a^n b^n PDA, why do we keep Z0 at the bottom?
options: To know when the count has returned to zero
Because the stack must never be empty
quiz.explain: Seeing Z0 on top means all pushed A's have been matched.

quiz.q: Trace (q0, aab, Z) in the a^n b^n PDA. What happens?
options: It ends in q1 with A still on the stack, so it rejects
quiz.explain: After aab the stack is AZ in q1 with no input left, and there is no move: reject.

quiz.q: Why does the PDA for ww^R need nondeterminism?
options: It cannot know where the middle of the input is, so it must guess
It must read the input twice
quiz.explain: Nothing marks the middle; the PDA tries every split and one correct guess accepts.

quiz.q: Acceptance by final state and by empty stack for nondeterministic PDAs are:
options: Equal in power: each can be converted to the other
quiz.explain: Each style can simulate the other, so they recognise the same languages.

lessons.title: CFG and PDA Equivalence, Deterministic PDAs and CYK
lessons.content:
Your mother has a recipe book for pitha, and your nani can taste any pitha and say "yes, this was made the proper way" or "no". The recipe book generates, the taster recognises. Are they describing the same set of pithas? For context-free languages the recipe book is the grammar (CFG) and the taster is the pushdown automaton (PDA). Today we show they describe exactly the same languages, then see which PDAs compilers really use, and finally learn a table method, CYK, that checks any string against any grammar.

Recap: A CFG generates strings by replacing variables with rules. A PDA is a finite automaton with a stack; each move reads a symbol or nothing (ε), pops the top, and pushes a string, whose leftmost symbol becomes the new top. We trace PDAs with IDs (state, remaining input, stack). A PDA accepts if some path of moves reads all the input and accepts.

The big theorem: A language is context-free if and only if some PDA recognises it. "If and only if" means two directions. Direction 1: from any CFG we can build a PDA for the same language. Direction 2: from any PDA we can build a CFG. Together they say the generator and the recogniser have exactly equal power, just like regex and finite automata (Kleene's theorem) for regular languages.

CFG to PDA, the idea: The PDA simulates a leftmost derivation on its stack. The stack holds the part of the sentential form that is still to be matched. If a variable is on top, the PDA guesses a rule for it and replaces it with the rule's right side. If a terminal is on top, it must match the next input symbol, and then it is popped. If everything is matched and the bottom marker shows, accept.

The construction: Three states: q_start, q_loop, q_accept. First move: (ε, Z -> SZ), going to q_loop: push the start variable. In q_loop, for every rule A -> w, add (ε, A -> w): pop A, push w. For every terminal a, add (a, a -> ε): read a and pop a matching a. Finally (ε, Z -> Z) to q_accept. That is it: the number of transitions is the number of rules plus the number of terminals plus two.

Worked example: Grammar S -> aSb | ε. Trace on aabb, with the stack top on the left: (q_start, aabb, Z) |- (q_loop, aabb, SZ) |- (q_loop, aabb, aSbZ) |- (q_loop, abb, SbZ) |- (q_loop, abb, aSbbZ) |- (q_loop, bb, SbbZ) |- (q_loop, bb, bbZ) |- (q_loop, b, bZ) |- (q_loop, ε, Z) |- (q_accept, ε, Z). Read it: expand S with aSb, match a, expand S with aSb again, match a, expand S with ε, match b, match b, accept. At every moment, "input read so far" followed by "stack contents" (without Z) is exactly a sentential form of the leftmost derivation S => aSb => aaSbb => aabb. For example, after reading a the stack is SbZ, and a + Sb = aSb.

Why wrong guesses die: At the fourth row, (q_loop, abb, SbZ), the PDA could have chosen S -> ε instead. Then the stack becomes bZ while the input still starts with a; a terminal on top that does not match the input has no move, so that path dies. Nondeterminism tries all rule choices; only choices that agree with the actual input survive. That is why this construction needs a nondeterministic PDA.

PDA to CFG, the idea only: Going the other way is harder, so exams usually ask only the idea. First make the PDA tidy: one accept state, it empties its stack before accepting, and every move either pushes one symbol or pops one. Then create a variable A_pq for every pair of states p and q, meaning "all inputs that take the PDA from p with an empty stack to q with an empty stack". If the first push and the last pop match, A_pq -> a A_rs b. If the stack becomes empty somewhere in the middle at state r, A_pq -> A_pr A_rq. And A_pp -> ε. The start variable is A_start,accept.

Deterministic PDAs: A DPDA never has a choice. For every state, input symbol and stack top there is at most one move, and if an ε-move exists for some state and stack top, there is no input-reading move for that same state and top. The languages DPDAs accept (by final state) are called deterministic context-free languages, DCFLs.

Which languages are DCFLs: Our PDA for a^n b^n from lesson 16 never had a choice, so a^n b^n is a DCFL. The language { w c w^R } is a DCFL too: the middle marker c tells the machine exactly when to switch from pushing to popping. But { w w^R }, the same thing without the marker, is not a DCFL: no deterministic machine can know where the middle is. So, unlike DFA and NFA, the deterministic version is strictly weaker: regular languages are inside the DCFLs, which are inside the CFLs, and both containments are strict.

Useful facts about DCFLs: Every DCFL has an unambiguous grammar, so no DCFL is inherently ambiguous. DCFLs are closed under complement (flip accept and reject, with some care about ε-moves), while general CFLs are not, as lesson 18 will show. This gives a simple proof idea: if a CFL's complement is not context-free, the language cannot be a DCFL.

Why compilers want determinism: A nondeterministic PDA may need to follow many guesses, and a general parser for any CFG takes time that grows like n^3 for n tokens. A deterministic parser makes one move per step, so it runs in time proportional to n. For a 100,000-line program, that is the difference between instant and painful. So language designers write grammars that can be parsed deterministically.

LL and LR parsing, the idea: An LL(1) parser works top-down, like our CFG-to-PDA machine, but instead of guessing a rule it looks at the next one token (the lookahead) to choose. For S -> aSb | ε: if the next token is a, use S -> aSb; if it is b or the end, use S -> ε. No guessing at all. An LR parser works bottom-up: it shifts tokens onto a stack and, when the top of the stack matches a rule's right side, reduces it to the rule's variable. LR(1) is essentially a DPDA. Donald Knuth introduced LR parsing in 1965 and showed that LR(k) grammars describe exactly the DCFLs. Tools like Bison generate LR-style parsers; many compilers use hand-written top-down parsers in the LL style.

The membership question: Given any CFG G and a string w, is w in L(G)? Trying all derivations blindly can explode. In CNF we know a derivation of a length-n string has exactly 2n - 1 steps, so the search is finite, but still exponential. The CYK algorithm, found independently by Cocke, Younger and Kasami in the 1960s, answers in about n^3 steps using dynamic programming: solve small pieces first, store the answers, and build bigger answers from them.

How CYK works: The grammar must be in CNF (lesson 15). Make a triangle table. Cell (i, L) holds every variable that can derive the substring starting at position i with length L. Row L = 1: for each symbol, write the variables A with A -> that symbol. Row L > 1: split the substring into a left part of length k and a right part of length L - k, for every k from 1 to L - 1. If B is in the left cell, C is in the right cell, and there is a rule A -> BC, put A in the cell. Finally, w is in the language if the start variable is in the top cell (1, n).

Worked CYK on aabb: Grammar in CNF for { a^n b^n : n >= 1 }: S -> AB | AX, X -> SB, A -> a, B -> b. Row 1 (single letters): a {A}, a {A}, b {B}, b {B}. Row 2: aa: A then A, no rule has AA, so empty. ab: A then B, S -> AB, so {S}. bb: B then B, empty. Row 3: aab: split a|ab gives A then S, no rule AS; split aa|b gives empty then B. So empty. abb: split a|bb gives A then empty; split ab|b gives S then B, and X -> SB, so {X}. Row 4: aabb: split a|abb gives A then X, and S -> AX, so S. Splits aa|bb and aab|b give nothing. Top cell {S}: aabb is accepted.

CYK rejecting abab: Row 1: {A}, {B}, {A}, {B}. Row 2: ab {S}, ba empty, ab {S}. Row 3: aba: A with empty, or S with A, no rule SA: empty. bab: B with S, or empty with B: empty. Row 4: abab: A with empty; S with S, no rule SS; empty with B. Top cell empty: rejected. I checked both tables with a short program. Notice how the table itself shows why: the two halves ab and ab are each fine, but nothing glues S to S.

Cost of CYK: There are about n^2/2 cells, each tries up to n splits, and each split checks the rules. So time grows like n^3 times the grammar size. For n = 10 that is about a thousand basic steps, fine. For n = 100,000 tokens it is around 10^15, far too slow for a compiler. That is why compilers use deterministic LR or LL parsers, and CYK is used where grammars are naturally ambiguous and sentences are short, like parsing human language, where the table can even store all possible trees.

Real life example 1, a Bangla sentence: Grammar in CNF: বাক্য -> কর্তা ক্রিয়াপদ, ক্রিয়াপদ -> কর্ম ক্রিয়া, কর্তা -> আমি, কর্ম -> ভাত, ক্রিয়া -> খাই. CYK on "আমি ভাত খাই": row 1 gives কর্তা, কর্ম, ক্রিয়া. Row 2: "আমি ভাত" gives nothing; "ভাত খাই" gives ক্রিয়াপদ. Row 3: আমি + ভাত খাই = কর্তা then ক্রিয়াপদ, giving বাক্য. Accepted, and the table also tells you the structure: subject plus verb phrase. Where the analogy breaks: real Bangla allows "ভাত খাই আমি" and dropping the subject, which a real grammar must add rules for.

Real life example 2, an error message: When a compiler says "expected ';' before '}'", it is a deterministic parser that reached a state with no move for the current token, exactly like our PDA trace that got stuck on aab. Because the parser is deterministic, it knows precisely where it got stuck, which is why the error points to a specific line and token.

When to use what: To prove a language is context-free, either a CFG or a PDA is fine; pick the easier one (grammars for nesting shapes, PDAs for counting with a stack). For a real compiler, design an LL or LR grammar so the parser is deterministic and linear. For checking strings against an arbitrary, possibly ambiguous grammar, use CYK or a similar general algorithm. Do not use CYK for long inputs, and do not expect a DPDA to handle languages like ww^R.

Common mistakes: Running CYK on a grammar that is not in CNF. Forgetting some splits; every k from 1 to L - 1 must be tried. Mixing up the table indices; label cells with the actual substring to stay safe. In the CFG-to-PDA construction, pushing the right side in the wrong order; the leftmost symbol must be on top. Assuming DPDA equals NPDA as DFA equals NFA; it does not.

What exams ask: Convert a given CFG to a PDA and trace it on a string; explain the PDA-to-CFG idea; define a DPDA and give a language that is context-free but not deterministic (ww^R); fill a CYK table for a given CNF grammar and string and decide membership; state the running time of CYK and explain why compilers use LL or LR parsing instead.

Mental model: Picture the CFG-to-PDA machine as a person with a to-do stack of sticky notes. Each note is either "make a dish" (a variable) or "serve this exact item" (a terminal). When a "make" note is on top, they replace it with the recipe's steps; when a "serve" note is on top, the next guest must want exactly that item, or this plan fails. CYK is a different picture: a pyramid built from the bottom, where each brick records which variables can make that piece of the string, and the top brick answers the question for the whole string.

Recap and what is next: CFGs and PDAs describe exactly the same languages; CFG to PDA simulates leftmost derivations on the stack. DPDAs are strictly weaker than PDAs; their languages, DCFLs, are what LL and LR parsers handle in linear time. CYK decides membership for any CNF grammar in about n^3 time with a triangle table. Next lesson we prove that some languages, like a^n b^n c^n, are not context-free at all, and study closure properties.
key_points: A language is context-free if and only if some PDA recognises it.
CFG to PDA: push S; on a variable on top, replace it by a rule's right side; on a terminal on top, match and pop input.
Input read so far plus stack contents always equals the current leftmost sentential form.
PDA to CFG uses variables A_pq for 'go from p to q with empty stack'.
DPDAs are strictly weaker than PDAs: w c w^R is a DCFL but w w^R is not.
Compilers use deterministic LL or LR parsers that run in linear time; LR(k) grammars give exactly the DCFLs.
CYK fills a triangle table of variables for every substring using a CNF grammar; accept if S is in the top cell.
CYK takes about n^3 time, fine for short sentences, too slow for long programs.
lessons.tip: In a CYK table, write the actual substring next to each cell (like 'abb') before filling it. Most CYK mistakes are index mistakes, not grammar mistakes.
lessons.task: Using the CNF grammar S -> AB | AX, X -> SB, A -> a, B -> b, fill the CYK table for aaabbb on paper. Check that S appears in the top cell, then try aabbb and find the row where things go wrong.

quiz.q: In the CFG-to-PDA construction, what does the PDA do when a variable A is on top of the stack?
options: Replaces A with the right side of a rule for A, without reading input
quiz.explain: It guesses a rule A -> w and replaces A by w using an ε-move.

quiz.q: Which language is context-free but not deterministic context-free?
quiz.explain: Without a middle marker, no deterministic machine can know where to switch from pushing to popping.

quiz.q: In CYK for aabb with S -> AB | AX, X -> SB, A -> a, B -> b, which cell contains X?
quiz.explain: ab gives S, then S followed by B (the last b) gives X -> SB.

quiz.q: Why do compilers not use CYK to parse programs?
options: CYK only works on regular languages
Its time grows like n^3, while LL/LR parsers run in linear time
quiz.explain: For long programs n^3 is far too slow; deterministic parsers make one move per token.

quiz.q: What must the grammar look like before running CYK?
quiz.explain: CYK combines exactly two pieces per rule (A -> BC) and single letters (A -> a).

lessons.title: Pumping Lemma for CFLs and Closure Properties
lessons.content:
At a biye bari the manager wants three numbers to match: guests, plates and chairs. With one notebook where he can only add or erase the last line, he can match guests to plates: write a tick for each guest, erase one for each plate. But by the time the chairs arrive, the ticks are gone. That is exactly the weakness of one stack. Today we prove it properly: the language a^n b^n c^n is not context-free. Then we see which operations keep context-free languages context-free, and which do not.

Recap of the regular pumping lemma: In lesson 11, a DFA with p states reading a string of length p or more must visit some state twice (pigeonhole: more visits than states). The part read between the two visits is a loop, so it can be repeated or removed and the machine still accepts. That gave s = xyz with y pumpable. For context-free languages, the loop comes not from a DFA but from the parse tree.

Why parse trees must get tall: Put the grammar in Chomsky Normal Form (lesson 15), so every inner node has two children, except the last variable above each leaf, which has one terminal child. A binary tree that is short cannot have many leaves: if the longest root-to-leaf path has at most k variables, the tree yields at most 2^(k-1) letters. So if the string has length at least p = 2^|V|, where |V| is the number of variables, some path must have at least |V| + 1 variables.

Pigeonhole on the path: A path with |V| + 1 or more variable nodes, but only |V| different variables, must repeat some variable. Call it R. On that path there is an upper R and, below it, a lower R. Now cut the string into five pieces using these two subtrees. The lower R yields some piece x. The upper R yields a longer piece v x y: the part left of x is v, the part right of x is y. The rest of the string, left and right of the upper R's piece, is u and z. So s = u v x y z.

Pumping the tree: Since both nodes are labelled R, we can swap subtrees. Replace the lower R's subtree with a copy of the upper R's subtree: the tree is still valid, and it yields u v v x y y z. Do it again and you get u v^3 x y^3 z. Replace the upper R's subtree with the lower one: you get u x z. So u v^i x y^i z is in the language for every i >= 0. The two pieces v and y are pumped together, at the same time, which is the key difference from the regular lemma, where one piece is pumped.

The two size facts: First, |vy| >= 1: in CNF the upper R uses a rule R -> BC, and since CNF has no ε-rules (except at the start), both B and C yield something, so v and y cannot both be empty. Second, |vxy| <= p: pick the repeated pair among the lowest |V| + 1 variables of the longest path; then the upper R's subtree has paths of at most |V| + 1 variables, so it yields at most 2^|V| = p letters.

The formal statement: If L is a context-free language, there is a number p (the pumping length) such that every string s in L with |s| >= p can be written s = u v x y z where: one, |vy| >= 1; two, |vxy| <= p; three, u v^i x y^i z is in L for every i >= 0. Read it as a promise: every long string of a CFL has two nearby pieces that can be pumped together.

How to use it, the game: The lemma is used only to prove a language is NOT context-free, by contradiction. Think of it as a game against an opponent. The opponent picks p (you do not know it, so keep it as a letter). You pick a string s in L with |s| >= p. The opponent picks any split u v x y z obeying |vy| >= 1 and |vxy| <= p. You must then show some i for which u v^i x y^i z is not in L, for every split the opponent could choose. If you can always win, L is not context-free.

Proof that a^n b^n c^n is not context-free, setup: Let L = { a^n b^n c^n : n >= 0 }. Assume L is context-free, with pumping length p. Choose s = a^p b^p c^p. It is in L and longer than p. Now consider any split s = u v x y z with |vy| >= 1 and |vxy| <= p. The key observation: vxy is a window of at most p letters, and the block of b's alone is p long. So the window cannot touch both the a's and the c's. It lies within the a's and b's, or within the b's and c's.

Case 1, v and y each contain only one kind of letter: Then pumping up to i = 2 adds letters of at most two kinds, because the window touches at most two kinds. The third kind stays at p. Since |vy| >= 1, at least one count grows above p while one count stays at p, so the three counts are no longer equal. Concrete picture with p = 4: s = aaaabbbbcccc, and suppose u = aaa, v = a, x = b, y = b, z = bbcccc (window abb has length 3). Then u v^2 x y^2 z = a^5 b^5 c^4, not in L.

Case 2, v or y contains two kinds of letters: For example v = ab. Then v^2 = abab, so u v^2 x y^2 z contains a b followed by an a. Every string in L has all a's before all b's before all c's, so this string is not in L. The same happens if y = bc. In both cases i = 2 gives a string outside L, contradicting the lemma. So the assumption was wrong: a^n b^n c^n is not context-free. Pumping down, i = 0, would also work in case 1.

Other non-context-free languages: The same style proves that { a^(n^2) }, { a^p : p prime } and { w w : w in {a, b}* } (a string followed by an exact copy) are not context-free. Compare ww with w w^R: the reversed copy is context-free, because a stack gives things back in reverse order. The straight copy is not, because the first symbol stored would be needed first, but a stack gives it last. One stack is natural for mirror images, not for copies.

Common mistakes with the lemma: Choosing the split yourself; you must handle every split. Forgetting the |vxy| <= p rule, which is what limits the window to two kinds of letters. Picking a string shorter than p or not in L. Pumping v and y differently; they always get the same i. Using the lemma to prove a language IS context-free; passing the pumping test proves nothing, because some non-context-free languages pass it. For those, a stronger tool called Ogden's lemma exists, which lets you mark which positions must be pumped.

Closure under union, concatenation and star: Closure means: apply the operation to context-free languages and the result is still context-free. Take grammars G1 with start S1 and G2 with start S2, with different variable names. Union: new start S -> S1 | S2. Concatenation: S -> S1 S2. Star: S -> S S1 | ε. Each is one new rule, and it works because derivations of the two grammars never share variables. Reversal also works: reverse the right side of every rule. Example: a^n b^n union b^n a^n has the grammar S -> S1 | S2, S1 -> aS1b | ε, S2 -> bS2a | ε.

Not closed under intersection: Let L1 = { a^n b^n c^m } (equal a's and b's, any c's) and L2 = { a^m b^n c^n } (any a's, equal b's and c's). Both are context-free: L1 has S -> AC, A -> aAb | ε, C -> cC | ε, and L2 is similar. Their intersection has equal a's and b's AND equal b's and c's: that is exactly a^n b^n c^n, which we just proved is not context-free. So intersecting two CFLs can leave the family. One stack cannot check both at once.

Not closed under complement: Suppose CFLs were closed under complement. De Morgan's law says L1 ∩ L2 = complement( complement(L1) ∪ complement(L2) ). Complement, union, complement would all stay context-free, so intersection would too. But we just showed intersection fails. So complement must fail as well. A surprising fact: the complement of a^n b^n c^n actually is context-free; what fails is that complements of CFLs are not always CFLs. Compare with regular languages, closed under everything here, and DCFLs, closed under complement.

Intersection with a regular language works: If L is context-free and R is regular, L ∩ R is context-free. Run the PDA for L and the DFA for R side by side: the new states are pairs (PDA state, DFA state), each input symbol moves both, and only the PDA uses the stack. Accept when both accept. This is a great proof tool. Example: let E be all strings over {a, b, c} with equal numbers of a's, b's and c's. Is E context-free? Intersect with the regular language a*b*c*: you get a^n b^n c^n. If E were context-free, this intersection would be too. It is not, so E is not context-free, and we proved it without pumping at all.

Real life example 1, compilers' second check: "Every variable must be declared before it is used" is like checking ww: the name in the declaration must reappear later, in the same letter order. Lesson 13 said CFGs cannot express this; now you see why: it is copy-checking, beyond one stack. Compilers therefore parse with a grammar and then run a separate step with a symbol table, a lookup table of declared names. The same holds for a form like a national ID application asking you to type your mobile number twice: the "matches" check is done by code, not by a grammar.

Real life example 2, the biye bari manager again: He can match guests and plates with his erase-as-you-go notebook, like a PDA with a^n b^n. Adding chairs breaks it, like a^n b^n c^n. Where the analogy matches: one last-in-first-out memory can match one pair of counts. Where it breaks: a real manager can just write numbers down and compare them later, which is like having random access memory, more than a stack. Machines with that kind of memory come next, in Turing machines.

When to use which tool: To prove a language is not context-free, first try closure: intersect with a regular language or map it to a known non-CFL. If that fails, use the pumping lemma, choosing s so that the window |vxy| <= p cannot touch every part that must match. To prove a language is context-free, build a grammar or a PDA, or combine known CFLs with union, concatenation, star or intersection with a regular language. Never use complement or intersection of two CFLs in such a proof.

What exams ask: State the pumping lemma for CFLs and explain where p comes from (parse tree height and pigeonhole); prove a^n b^n c^n, ww or a^(n^2) is not context-free; show CFLs are closed under union, concatenation and star with grammar constructions; show they are not closed under intersection and complement, with the L1, L2 example and De Morgan; use intersection with a regular language to prove a language is not context-free.
