Mental model: Picture any very long string of a CFL hanging from a tall parse tree, like a long garland hanging from a tree in a decorated biye bari gate. Somewhere along one tall branch, the same variable appears twice, like a repeated knot. The section between the two knots can be copied any number of times or cut out, and the garland still hangs correctly: that is u v^i x y^i z. Because the copied section has a left part and a right part, two pieces stretch together. And because the knots are low on the branch, the stretched area is small, at most p letters wide. A language like a^n b^n c^n needs three areas to stretch together, far apart; a small window can only reach two.

Recap and what is next: Long strings of a CFL have a repeated variable in their parse tree, so s = uvxyz with |vy| >= 1, |vxy| <= p, and u v^i x y^i z in L for all i. Using s = a^p b^p c^p we proved a^n b^n c^n is not context-free. CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, star and reversal, and under intersection with regular languages, but not under intersection or complement. Next we finally break the one-stack barrier with Turing machines, which can handle a^n b^n c^n easily.
key_points: In CNF, a string of length at least p = 2^|V| has a parse-tree path with a repeated variable (pigeonhole).
Swapping the subtrees of the two copies gives u v^i x y^i z for all i >= 0: two pieces pump together.
CFL pumping lemma: s = uvxyz with |vy| >= 1, |vxy| <= p, and u v^i x y^i z in L for every i.
For a^p b^p c^p, the window vxy touches at most two kinds of letters, so pumping breaks equality or order.
The lemma only proves a language is not context-free; passing it proves nothing.
CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, star and reversal.
CFLs are not closed under intersection ({a^n b^n c^m} ∩ {a^m b^n c^n}) or complement (De Morgan).
CFL ∩ regular is context-free, a handy tool for non-CFL proofs.
lessons.tip: In pumping proofs, draw the string as three blocks and slide a small window of width p across it. Ask: which blocks can the window touch? Each answer is one case of your proof.
lessons.task: Prove on paper that { a^n b^n c^n d^n : n >= 0 } is not context-free using the pumping lemma with s = a^p b^p c^p d^p. Then prove the same result in two lines using intersection with a regular language and a fact you already know.

quiz.q: Where does the pumping length p come from in the CFL pumping lemma?
options: The number of states of a DFA
A long string's parse tree in CNF must be tall, so a variable repeats on some path
The length of the longest rule
quiz.explain: With p = 2^|V|, a tree yielding p or more letters has a path with more than |V| variables, so one repeats.

quiz.q: In the proof for a^n b^n c^n with s = a^p b^p c^p, why can vxy not contain both a's and c's?
options: Because v and y are always equal
Because |vxy| <= p and the b-block alone has length p
quiz.explain: A window of at most p letters cannot jump over p b's to reach both a's and c's.

quiz.q: Which pair of CFLs shows CFLs are not closed under intersection?
quiz.explain: Their intersection is a^n b^n c^n, which is not context-free.

quiz.q: What is true about L ∩ R when L is context-free and R is regular?
quiz.explain: Run the PDA and the DFA together with paired states; only the PDA needs the stack.

quiz.q: A language passes the CFL pumping lemma test for every long string. What can you conclude?
options: Nothing certain: the lemma is only a necessary condition
quiz.explain: Some non-context-free languages also satisfy the pumping conditions, so passing proves nothing.

lessons.title: Turing Machines
lessons.content:
Imagine you are sitting an exam with a long khata, a pencil and an eraser. You look at one box at a time, write in it, rub it out, and move one box left or right, keeping only a tiny note in your head like "now checking the b's". In 1936 Alan Turing turned exactly this picture into a pretend machine. The Turing machine is the strongest model in this course, and it is what computer scientists mean when they say "a computer can do this" or "no computer can ever do this".

Quick recap of what came before: A DFA (deterministic finite automaton) reads the input once, from left to right, and remembers only which state it is in. A PDA (pushdown automaton) adds a stack, a pile of plates where you can only touch the top one. A language is a set of strings; recognising it means saying yes to exactly those strings. In lesson 18 we proved that a^n b^n c^n (some a's, then the same number of b's, then the same number of c's) is not context-free, so no PDA can recognise it. One stack can match a's against b's, but then the count is used up before the c's.

The problem this lesson solves: We need a model with memory that is not trapped in a stack. We want to reread, change, and go back and forth freely. And we want one model that can do anything any computer can do. Turing's machine gives both.

What people did before: In 1936 the word "computer" meant a person. Human computers did long calculations by hand, following fixed rules. Around 1928 the mathematician David Hilbert asked a famous question, the Entscheidungsproblem (German for "decision problem"): is there a mechanical method that can decide whether any given mathematical statement is provable? To answer "no", someone first had to define "mechanical method" precisely. Turing did.

Turing's first-principles thinking: Turing asked, "What does a human computer actually do, at the smallest step?" She looks at a few symbols, is in some state of mind such as "carrying 1", may change a symbol, may shift attention to a nearby spot, and may change her state of mind. That is all. Her states of mind are limited, but her paper is not: she can always ask for another sheet. Turing then simplified further: looking at a few symbols can be done as looking at one symbol many times, and a page can be cut into one long strip. What remains is the Turing machine.

The four parts: First, the tape: an endless strip of cells going to the right, each cell holding one symbol. At the start the input sits in the leftmost cells and every other cell holds the blank symbol, written _. Second, the head: a pointer sitting on exactly one cell, which can read that cell, write into it, and move one cell left or right. Third, the state: a small label like q0 or q3, the machine's "state of mind", from a finite list. Fourth, the rules: a table saying, for each state and each symbol under the head, what to do.

One step of the machine: Each step: read the symbol under the head, look up the rule for (state, symbol), write the rule's symbol (maybe the same one), move the head one cell left (L) or right (R) and switch state. A rule is written like this: In q1 reading a: write X, move R, go to q2. Formally, δ(q1, a) = (q2, X, R). δ (delta) is the rule book.

The formal 7-tuple: A Turing machine is M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, q_accept, q_reject). Q is the finite set of states, Σ (sigma) the input alphabet, Γ (gamma) the tape alphabet (every symbol that may ever appear on the tape). Σ is inside Γ, and the blank _ is in Γ but not in Σ. Why? If blank could be part of the input, the machine could not tell where the input ends. δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R} is the rule book. q0 is the start state. q_accept and q_reject are two special states; the moment the machine enters one of them, it stops at once with that answer. If the head is on the leftmost cell and a rule says L, the head simply stays there, so it never falls off the tape.

How this differs from a DFA and a PDA: A DFA can only read; a Turing machine can write. A DFA moves only right; a Turing machine moves both ways. A PDA can only see the top of its stack; a Turing machine can walk to any cell. And a Turing machine may stop halfway through its input, the moment it enters q_accept or q_reject.

Configurations, the snapshot of a moment: To trace a machine we write its whole situation in one line called a configuration. We write the tape, and put the current state just before the cell the head is reading. So X a q1 b b c c means: the tape holds X a b b c c, the head is on the first b, and the state is q1. A run is a list of configurations, like the frames of a cartoon.

Three possible endings: A DFA always finishes, because the input runs out. A Turing machine has three possible endings. It may reach q_accept: it halts and says yes. It may reach q_reject: it halts and says no. Or it may never reach either and keep running forever, which we call looping. Looping is the price of unlimited tape and the freedom to move back: a machine that walks right forever looking for a symbol that never comes will loop. Lessons 21 and 22 are all about it.

Designing a machine for a^n b^n c^n: With a pencil, you would cross off one a, walk right and cross off one b, walk on and cross off one c, then walk back and repeat. When all a's are crossed, you check that no b or c is left. That zig-zag plan is the whole design. We use X to mark a crossed a, Y for a crossed b, Z for a crossed c.

The rule table: In q0 reading a: write X, move R, go to q1. In q0 reading Y: keep Y, move R, go to q4 (all a's are done, now check the rest). In q0 reading _: accept (the empty string, n = 0). In q1 reading a or Y: keep it, move R, stay q1 (skip to the first b). In q1 reading b: write Y, move R, go to q2. In q2 reading b or Z: keep it, move R, stay q2 (skip to the first c). In q2 reading c: write Z, move L, go to q3. In q3 reading a, b, Y or Z: keep it, move L, stay q3 (walk back). In q3 reading X: keep X, move R, go to q0. In q4 reading Y or Z: keep it, move R, stay q4. In q4 reading _: accept. Any situation not in the table means reject.

Trace on aabbcc, first round: q0 aabbcc. Read a, write X: X q1 abbcc. Skip a: Xa q1 bbcc. Cross the first b: XaY q2 bcc. Skip b: XaYb q2 cc. Cross the first c and turn back: XaY q3 bZc. Walk left: Xa q3 YbZc, then X q3 aYbZc, then q3 XaYbZc. Found X, step right: X q0 aYbZc. One a, one b and one c are now crossed. That took 9 steps.

Trace, second round and final check: X q0 aYbZc. Cross the a: XX q1 YbZc. Skip Y: XXY q1 bZc. Cross b: XXYY q2 Zc. Skip Z: XXYYZ q2 c. Cross c, turn: XXYY q3 ZZ. Walk left over Z, Y, Y until X: X q3 XYYZZ. Step right: XX q0 YYZZ. Now q0 sees Y, meaning no a is left, so go to q4 and check: XXY q4 YZZ, XXYY q4 ZZ, XXYYZ q4 Z, XXYYZZ q4 _. Blank found with nothing unchecked left, so accept. The whole run is 23 steps.

A rejecting trace on aabbc: The first round goes exactly as before and leaves X a Y b Z. The second round crosses the second a and the second b, giving XXYYZ q2 with the head on a blank. State q2 is looking for a c, but it reads _. There is no rule for (q2, _), so the machine rejects. Try abcc yourself: after one round you reach q4 reading the leftover c, and (q4, c) has no rule, so it rejects.

Turing machines can also compute answers: So far the machine only said yes or no. But a Turing machine can also leave an answer on the tape, which makes it a calculator of functions. Write numbers in unary, meaning the number n is written as n ones: 2 is 11 and 3 is 111. To add 2 + 3 we put 11+111 on the tape. Plan: turn the + into a 1, which gives one 1 too many, then go to the end and erase the last 1.

Rules and trace for 11+111: In q0 reading 1: keep, move R, stay q0. In q0 reading +: write 1, move R, go to q1. In q1 reading 1: keep, move R, stay q1. In q1 reading _: keep, move L, go to q2. In q2 reading 1: write _, then halt (accept). Trace: q0 11+111, 1 q0 1+111, 11 q0 +111, 111 q1 111, 1111 q1 11, 11111 q1 1, 111111 q1 _, 11111 q2 1, and finally the last 1 becomes blank. The tape now holds 11111, which is 5. Correct.

Why so slow? Our a^n b^n c^n machine walks back and forth about n times, and each walk is about n cells, so it takes roughly n^2 steps. A real laptop would check it in about n steps. That is fine: the model is built to be simple enough to reason about, not fast.

Real-life analogy, the government office clerk: Picture a land office clerk bound to a rule book. He looks at one line of a long register, checks the rule book, writes a stamp, moves to the next or previous line, and updates his mental note ("now checking signatures"), never using his own judgement. Where it matches: finite rule book, one spot at a time, read and write, no creativity. Where it breaks: a real clerk can flip straight to page 400, while a Turing machine must walk there cell by cell; and a real register has an end, while the tape never does.

Second example, your phone: Your phone's processor has a fixed instruction set (rule book), registers (state) and read-write memory. Anything it does, a Turing machine can do, just slower. The match breaks because the phone jumps to any memory address in one step and its memory is finite; the unlimited tape makes the model more generous on purpose, so no answer depends on hardware size.

When to use this model, and when not: Use Turing machines when the question is "can this be computed at all?" or "is this problem impossible for every computer?", and when you need to prove such things. Do not use it to write real software or to measure real speed; use a programming language and real algorithms for that. When a weaker model is enough, prefer it: a DFA always halts in one pass, so a lexer uses a DFA. Once a model can loop, we lose the guarantee of always getting an answer.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students forget that the blank is in Γ but not in Σ. They mix up reject and loop: rejecting is halting with "no", looping is never halting. In traces they forget to show the head position. Exams ask for the 7-tuple, a machine for a^n b^n c^n, ww or unary addition, and its configurations on an input like aabbcc.

The mental model to keep: Picture a long paper strip, a tiny robot standing on one box, and a small card in the robot's pocket showing its current state. Each tick, the robot looks down, checks the rule book with (card, symbol), writes, steps left or right, and swaps the card. The strip is all the memory, the card is all the "mood", the rule book never changes. To design one, ask "how would I do this with a pencil, one box at a time?" and write each move as a rule.

Recap and what comes next: A Turing machine is a finite rule book plus an infinite tape it can read, write and move along in both directions. It can accept, reject or loop, it beats PDAs on languages like a^n b^n c^n, and it can compute functions like addition. In lesson 20 we will try to make it stronger with more tapes, nondeterminism and other upgrades, discover that none of them add power, and meet the universal Turing machine that runs other machines, the idea behind every stored-program computer.
key_points: A Turing machine has a tape of cells, a head that reads, writes and moves L or R, a finite set of states and a rule table δ.
Formally M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, q_accept, q_reject); the blank _ is in Γ but never in Σ.
One step: read the symbol, look up (state, symbol), write, move one cell, change state.
A configuration like XaY q2 bcc shows the tape, the head position (just after the state) and the state.
Three outcomes: halt and accept, halt and reject, or loop forever.
a^n b^n c^n is decided by zig-zag crossing off with X, Y, Z; it needs about n^2 steps.
Turing machines can compute functions too, e.g. unary 11+111 becomes 11111.
Turing modelled a human computer with pencil and paper (1936); the model is about what is possible, not speed.
lessons.tip: When tracing, write one configuration per line with the state placed just before the cell under the head. Examiners mark each line, and you will spot a wrong move instantly.
lessons.task: On paper, trace the a^n b^n c^n machine from this lesson on abc (accept) and on aabcc (reject). Write every configuration and circle the step where a missing rule causes the reject.

quiz.q: Why is the blank symbol in the tape alphabet Γ but not in the input alphabet Σ?
options: Because blanks are not allowed on the tape
So the machine can tell where the input ends
Because Γ is smaller than Σ
Because the head cannot read blanks
quiz.explain: If the input could contain blanks, the machine could not know where the input stops and empty tape begins.

quiz.q: Which ability does a Turing machine have that a DFA does not?
options: Having a finite set of states
Writing on the tape and moving left
quiz.explain: A DFA only reads left to right. A Turing machine can write and move in both directions.

quiz.q: In the configuration XX q1 YbZc, where is the head?
quiz.explain: The state is written just before the cell being read, so the head is on Y.

quiz.q: What is the difference between rejecting and looping?
options: Looping means the machine accepted twice
Rejecting halts with "no"; looping never halts
Rejecting happens only on empty input
quiz.explain: Reject is a definite halting answer. Looping means no answer ever arrives.

quiz.q: On tape 11+111, the unary adder replaces + with 1 and then erases the last 1. Why erase one 1?
options: To mark the end of the tape
Because turning + into 1 adds one extra 1
Because unary numbers must be even
quiz.explain: 11+111 becomes 111111 (six ones), one too many, so removing the last one leaves 11111 = 5.

lessons.title: Turing Machine Variants and the Universal Machine
lessons.content:
Imagine you give a student one exam khata and ask her to do a long sum. Then you give another student three khatas, a friend who can guess, and a khata that goes on forever in both directions. Surely the second student can solve harder problems? Surprisingly, no. She will be faster, but every problem she can solve, the first student can also solve with one khata and patience. This lesson proves that for Turing machines, and then meets the most important machine of all: one machine that can run every other machine.

Quick recap: A Turing machine (lesson 19) has one tape of cells, a head that reads, writes and moves left or right, a finite set of states, and a rule table. A run can accept, reject, or loop forever. We say a model is "as powerful as" another if it recognises exactly the same languages (sets of strings). Speed does not count here, only what is possible.

Why we study variants: Turing's model is very bare. People naturally asked, "What if we give it more?" If some upgrade gave extra power, the idea of "computable" would depend on the details of the model, and theory would be shaky. If every reasonable upgrade gives the same power, then "computable" is a solid, natural idea. That is what happens, and this is the strongest evidence for the Church-Turing thesis of lesson 21.

The simulation argument: To show model B is no stronger than model A, we show that a machine of type A can imitate, step by step, any machine of type B. If A can copy everything B does, then any language B recognises, A recognises too. The reverse direction is usually easy, because the plain machine is a special case of the fancy one. Every proof in this lesson has this same shape, so learn the shape, not the details.

Small upgrade 1, stay-put moves: Let the head also choose S, "stay where you are". No new power: replace each S move by "move R, then move L" using one extra helper state. Two steps instead of one, same result.

Small upgrade 2, two-way infinite tape: Let the tape go on forever to the left as well. No new power: fold the tape at the starting cell, like folding a long paper strip in half. Now each cell of the one-way tape holds two symbols in two tracks, the upper track for the right half and the lower track for the left half. The state remembers which half the head is in. Moving left on the lower track is moving right on the folded tape.

Big upgrade 1, multi-tape machines: A k-tape machine has k tapes, each with its own head. The input starts on tape 1, the others are blank, and in one step the machine reads all k heads, then writes and moves each head independently. These are very handy. For a^n b^n, a 2-tape machine copies the a's onto tape 2, then moves forward over the b's on tape 1 while moving backward over the copied a's on tape 2. That takes about 2n steps, while the single-tape zig-zag needs about n^2.

How one tape imitates k tapes: Write all k tapes on one tape, separated by #, like # a a b # X _ # 1 0 #. Put a dot on the symbol each virtual head is reading. To imitate one step of the k-tape machine, the single head scans the whole tape once to see the k dotted symbols, remembering them in its states, then scans again to write the new symbols and shift the dots left or right. If a virtual tape needs more room, shift everything after it one cell right. So it is the same power, only slower: if the k-tape machine takes t steps, the copy takes about t^2 steps.

Big upgrade 2, nondeterministic Turing machines: In a nondeterministic Turing machine (NTM), a state and symbol may have several rules, and the machine may follow any of them, like the NFAs of lesson 6. Its runs form a tree of possibilities. It accepts if at least one branch reaches q_accept. Think of it as a machine that magically guesses right. Example: to check whether a number like 15 is composite (not prime), an NTM guesses a divisor between 2 and 14, then divides. The branch that guesses 3 finds remainder 0 and accepts.

How a normal machine imitates guessing: A deterministic machine explores the tree of choices level by level: all branches of length 1, then all of length 2, and so on, called breadth-first search. It keeps a third tape holding the "address" of the branch it is trying, such as 2-1-3, meaning take choice 2, then 1, then 3. If any branch accepts, it will be found at some depth and the simulation accepts. Why not go deep first? Because one branch might loop forever, and a depth-first search would get stuck there and never try the accepting branch. Same power again, but the cost can be exponential: with b choices per step and an accepting branch at depth d, up to about b^d branches may be tried.

Enumerators, machines that print: An enumerator is a Turing machine with a printer and no input. It runs and prints strings, maybe in any order, maybe with repeats, maybe forever. The language it enumerates is the set of everything it ever prints. Fact: a language is Turing-recognisable (some Turing machine accepts exactly its strings, possibly looping on others) exactly when some enumerator prints it.

Why the enumerator fact is true: From enumerator to recogniser: on input w, run the enumerator and compare every printed string with w; accept on a match. If w is never printed, we wait forever, which is fine for a recogniser. From recogniser M to enumerator: list all strings in order s1, s2, s3, ... (shortest first). The naive plan "run M on s1, then on s2" fails, because M might loop on s1 and we never reach s2. The fix is dovetailing: for i = 1, 2, 3, ..., run M for i steps on each of s1 to si and print any that accept. Every accepted string gets enough steps eventually, and no single loop can block the others.

Other models that turned out equal: In the same year 1936, Alonzo Church defined computation with lambda calculus, a system of rewriting functions, and it turned out equal in power to Turing machines. So do general recursive functions, Post systems, a PDA with two stacks, and every ordinary programming language like C, Java or Python if you pretend memory is unlimited. A system as powerful as a Turing machine is called Turing-complete.

Encoding a machine as a string: Here is a key trick. A Turing machine is a finite object: finite states, finite symbols, finite rules. So we can write any machine M as a string, written <M>. One simple code: number the states q1, q2, q3 as 0, 00, 000, the symbols 0, 1, _ as 0, 00, 000, and the moves L, R as 0, 00. The rule "In q1 reading 1: write 0, move R, go to q2", that is δ(q1, 1) = (q2, 0, R), becomes 0 1 00 1 00 1 0 1 00, that is 010010010100. Separate rules with 11 and you have the whole machine as one binary string. Now a machine can be input to another machine.

The universal Turing machine: Turing showed there is one machine U that takes <M, w> (a machine's code plus an input) and does exactly what M would do on w. U uses three tapes: tape 1 holds <M>, tape 2 holds M's tape contents, tape 3 holds M's current state. Each round, U reads M's state from tape 3 and the symbol under M's head from tape 2, searches tape 1 for the matching rule, then updates tapes 2 and 3. If M accepts, U accepts. If M rejects, U rejects. If M loops, U loops too. U's own rule book is fixed; only the input changes.

Why the universal machine changed the world: Early electronic machines such as ENIAC (1945) were set up for a new job by changing cables and switches by hand, which could take days. The stored-program idea, described in John von Neumann's 1945 report on the EDVAC design, keeps the program in memory as data, next to the data it works on. That is exactly the universal machine's trick: the machine is fixed, the program is just input. The Manchester Baby ran the first stored program in 1948. Every laptop and phone since then is a universal machine.

Real-life example 1, a cook and recipes: A good cook (the universal machine) can follow any recipe written in a book (the encoded machine) to make any dish (the output) from the bazar items (the input). You do not build a new cook for biryani and another for khichuri. Where it matches: the recipe is just data the cook reads step by step. Where it breaks: a real cook uses judgement and taste, while U follows rules with zero judgement, and a recipe never runs forever, while some encoded machines do.

Real-life example 2, apps on your phone: When you install the bKash app or a game, no wires inside your phone change. The app is a file of instructions, a string, and the phone's processor runs it. A Python interpreter is a universal machine for Python programs, and an emulator that runs old console games on a PC is a universal machine for that console's programs. Downloading an app is like handing U a new <M>.

When to use the variants: In proofs and designs, use whichever version makes your life easier. Multi-tape machines make constructions short. Nondeterministic machines make "guess and check" ideas easy to describe. Then the simulation theorems say the result holds for the plain machine too. When not to: do not use the equivalence to claim the variants are equally fast. Multi-tape to one tape costs a square, which is mild, but nondeterministic to deterministic, as far as anyone knows, can cost exponential time. Whether that blow-up can be avoided is the P vs NP question of lesson 25.

What does reduce power: Not every change keeps full power. A Turing machine that may never write and only moves right is just a DFA. A machine whose only memory is one stack is a PDA. A machine limited to the cells holding the input is a linear bounded automaton, which we meet in lesson 24. Power comes from unlimited read-write memory that can be revisited; take that away and you fall down the ladder.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Thinking NTMs recognise more languages than deterministic ones: they do not. Thinking simulation keeps the same speed: it does not. Forgetting that the deterministic simulation of an NTM must be breadth-first. Forgetting that an enumerator may print in any order with repeats. Thinking U decides whether M accepts w: it only recognises, since it loops when M loops. Exams ask: prove multi-tape equals single-tape, describe the NTM simulation and why BFS, prove the enumerator theorem, and describe the universal machine and string encoding.

The mental model to keep: Picture a ladder of machines. At the top stands one plain Turing machine with one tape. Around it float fancy versions: many tapes, guessing, two-way tape, printers. Draw an arrow from each fancy version to the plain one labelled "can be simulated, slower". All arrows land on the same spot, so they share one power level. Then picture U holding a printed page with <M> on it: programs are data, and one fixed machine can run them all.

Recap and what comes next: Stay-put moves, two-way tapes, many tapes and nondeterminism add speed or convenience, not power, because the plain machine can simulate each of them. Enumerators describe exactly the recognisable languages. Any machine can be written as a string, and the universal machine runs such strings, which is the root of stored-program computers. In lesson 21 we turn this "all models agree" fact into the Church-Turing thesis and start sorting problems into decidable and undecidable.
key_points: Two models have equal power if they recognise the same languages; speed is ignored.
Proof pattern: show the plain machine can simulate the fancy one step by step.
Stay-put, two-way infinite tape and multi-tape machines add no power; k tapes cost about a square in time.
An NTM is simulated deterministically by breadth-first search of its choice tree, possibly with exponential slowdown.
A language is recognisable exactly when some enumerator prints it; dovetailing avoids getting stuck on one loop.
Any Turing machine can be encoded as a string <M>, e.g. with blocks of 0s separated by 1s.
The universal machine U runs <M, w>: it accepts, rejects or loops exactly as M does on w.
Stored-program computers use the same idea: the machine is fixed and the program is just data in memory.
lessons.tip: For every equivalence proof, first say in one line who simulates whom, then describe how one step of the fancy machine is imitated. That two-part answer earns most of the marks.
lessons.task: Using the code in this lesson (states 0, 00, 000; symbols 0, 00, 000 for 0, 1, _; moves 0, 00), encode the rule "In q2 reading _: write 1, move L, go to q3". Then decode 001010100100 back into a rule. (Check: the first is 001000100010010; the second says "In q2 reading 0: write 1, move R, go to q1".)

quiz.q: Why must the deterministic simulation of an NTM search its choice tree breadth-first?
options: Depth-first could get stuck forever in a looping branch
Depth-first cannot be done on a Turing machine
NTMs only branch at the start
quiz.explain: A looping branch would trap a depth-first search, so an accepting branch elsewhere might never be tried.

quiz.q: A 2-tape machine runs in t steps. About how long does the single-tape simulation take?
quiz.explain: Each simulated step scans the whole used tape, which can be about t cells long, giving roughly t^2.

quiz.q: What does the universal machine U do on <M, w> if M loops on w?
quiz.explain: U simply imitates M, so it keeps running forever when M does.

quiz.q: Which change DOES reduce a Turing machine to a weaker model?
options: Allowing it only to read and move right
Making the tape infinite in both directions
quiz.explain: Read-only, right-moving machines are exactly DFAs. The other changes keep full Turing power.

quiz.q: Why does the enumerator built from a recogniser M use dovetailing?
options: To print strings in alphabetical order
Because M might loop on an early string and block the rest
quiz.explain: Giving every string a growing step budget means no single loop can stop later strings from being checked.

lessons.title: The Church-Turing Thesis and Decidability
lessons.content:
Suppose you send a complaint to a mobile banking helpline. Helpline A always replies within a day, either "yes, refunded" or "no, not eligible". Helpline B says "If your refund is approved, we will SMS you." If the answer is yes, the SMS comes. If the answer is no, you hear nothing, ever. While waiting, you can never tell "not yet" from "never". Helpline A is a decider. Helpline B is a recogniser. This lesson is about that difference, and about the bold claim that Turing machines capture what "algorithm" means.

Quick recap: A Turing machine reads and writes on an endless tape and can accept, reject, or loop forever (lesson 19). Adding tapes or nondeterminism gives no extra power (lesson 20). A language is a set of strings, and a decision problem ("is this number prime?") is the same as asking whether a string belongs to a language (lesson 2). Any object, a DFA, a grammar, even a Turing machine, can be written as a string; we write <B, w> for the string encoding a DFA B together with an input w.

The problem: what is an algorithm? People used algorithms for thousands of years: Euclid's method for the greatest common divisor, long division taught in class 4. But "algorithm" was an intuitive idea: "a finite list of clear steps a person could follow mechanically." In 1900 David Hilbert listed 23 big problems. His 10th problem asked for a process to decide whether a polynomial equation with integer coefficients, like x^2 + y^2 = 25, has a whole number solution. Nobody could prove such a process cannot exist without first pinning down exactly what a "process" is.

The Church-Turing thesis: In 1936 Alonzo Church (with lambda calculus) and Alan Turing (with his machines) each gave a precise definition, and the two were soon shown to be equal. The Church-Turing thesis says: every intuitive algorithm can be carried out by a Turing machine, and vice versa. In short, algorithm = Turing machine that always halts. With this definition, Yuri Matiyasevich proved in 1970, building on work by Martin Davis, Hilary Putnam and Julia Robinson, that no algorithm solves Hilbert's 10th problem.

Why a thesis and not a theorem: A theorem is proved from exact definitions. But one side of the claim, "intuitive algorithm", is not an exact mathematical object, so it cannot be proved. It is like proving "every delicious food uses salt": "delicious" is not defined. The thesis is supported by strong evidence: every model anyone has proposed (lambda calculus, recursive functions, multi-tape machines, real programming languages) turned out equal to Turing machines, and nobody has found an intuitive algorithm a Turing machine cannot run. It could in principle be challenged by some new physical computing device, but none has done so.

Deciders: A decider is a Turing machine that halts on every input, always ending in accept or reject. A language is decidable (also called recursive) if some decider accepts exactly its strings. Decidable means: fully, always answerable by a computer. This is helpline A.

Recognisers: A language is Turing-recognisable (also called recursively enumerable, or semi-decidable) if some Turing machine accepts exactly its strings. On strings outside the language, that machine may reject or may loop forever. That is helpline B: yes answers always arrive, no answers may never arrive.

A recognisable example: Take one-variable polynomials with integer coefficients and ask, "does p have an integer root?" A recogniser: try x = 0, 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, ... and accept when p(x) = 0. If a root exists you reach it in finite time. If not, you search forever. For one variable we can do better: any integer root must divide the constant term (the number without x), so only finitely many candidates need checking. For x^2 - 5x + 6 the candidates are ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6, and testing finds 2 and 3. With many variables no such bound exists, and Matiyasevich's theorem says no decider exists at all.

Co-recognisable languages: A language is co-recognisable if its complement (all strings not in it) is recognisable. Now a key fact: a language is decidable exactly when it is both recognisable and co-recognisable. Why? If decidable, flip the decider's answer to recognise the complement. Conversely, take recogniser M1 for L and recogniser M2 for its complement. On input w, run them side by side, one step of M1, then one step of M2, alternating. Every w is either in L or not, so one of them must accept eventually. If M1 accepts, accept; if M2 accepts, reject. This always halts. Note that we must alternate: running M1 to the end first could loop forever.

Decidable problem 1, A_DFA: A_DFA = { <B, w> : DFA B accepts string w }. Decider: check the input is a valid encoding, then simulate B on w, one symbol at a time, tracking the current state. When w ends, accept if the state is an accept state, else reject. It always halts, because w is finite and each symbol is one step. The same works for NFAs: first convert to a DFA by subset construction (lesson 7), then run this decider. For regular expressions, convert to an NFA first (lesson 10).

Decidable problem 2, E_DFA (is the language empty?): E_DFA = { <A> : L(A) is empty }. Simulating on all strings is impossible, there are infinitely many. Think instead: the language is non-empty exactly when some accept state can be reached from the start state. So mark the start state, then repeatedly mark any state with an arrow from a marked state, until nothing new gets marked. If no accept state is marked, accept (empty); otherwise reject. Example: states A (start), B, C (accept). A on 0 goes to A, on 1 to B; B on 0 and 1 goes to B; C on 0 and 1 stays in C. Marking gives A, then B, and stops. C is unmarked, so the language is empty. Change B on 1 to go to C, and now C gets marked; the string 11 is a witness.

Decidable problem 3, EQ_DFA (do two DFAs accept the same language?): Build a DFA C that accepts strings accepted by exactly one of A and B, using complement and the product construction (lesson 5). C's language is empty exactly when A and B agree on every string. Run the E_DFA decider on C. This is a beautiful habit: solve a new problem by turning it into one you already solved. Lesson 23 uses the same habit to prove impossibility.

Decidable problem 4, A_CFG: A_CFG = { <G, w> : grammar G generates w }. Trying all derivations fails, because a grammar can have infinitely many. Fix: first convert G to Chomsky Normal Form (lesson 15), where any string of length n ≥ 1 needs exactly 2n - 1 steps to derive. Now only finitely many derivations of that length exist, so list and check them all. Example: S → AB, A → a, B → b and w = ab. Here n = 2, so we check derivations of 3 steps and find S ⇒ AB ⇒ aB ⇒ ab. The CYK algorithm (lesson 17) does the same job far faster.

Decidable problem 5, E_CFG: Does grammar G generate any string at all? Mark every terminal symbol. Then repeatedly mark a variable if it has a rule whose right side is all marked symbols. Stop when nothing changes. If the start variable S is marked, some string can be generated, so reject; otherwise accept. Note a surprise: EQ_CFG, "do two grammars generate the same language?", is undecidable. The DFA trick fails because context-free languages are not closed under complement or intersection (lesson 18).

The containment picture: Every context-free language is decidable: for a fixed grammar G, a decider just runs the A_CFG procedure with G built in. So the picture is: regular inside context-free inside decidable inside recognisable inside all languages. Each step is a strict jump. a^n b^n is context-free but not regular. a^n b^n c^n is decidable but not context-free. In lesson 22 we see A_TM is recognisable but not decidable.

Why some languages have no machine at all: Every Turing machine is a finite string, so we can list all machines one by one: they are countable. But the set of all languages over {0, 1} is uncountable, as the diagonal argument of lesson 3 shows. There are far more languages than machines, so most languages have no recogniser at all. Lesson 22 shows that a famous complement of A_TM is one of them.

Real-life example 1, the compiler: When you press "compile", the compiler first checks whether your code follows the language's grammar. That is a membership question about a context-free language, so it is decidable, and real parsers always finish with "OK" or "syntax error". But the compiler cannot promise your program will finish running. That question is about Turing machines and lives in the next lesson.

Real-life example 2, a search party: Imagine searching an endless list of phone numbers for your lost friend's number. If it is there, you will find it eventually: recognisable. If it is not, you never get to say "it is not there": no decider. If the list were sorted, you could stop as soon as you passed where it should be: decidable. Where the analogy breaks: real lists are finite, while recognisers face genuinely infinite searches.

When to aim for a decider and when a recogniser is enough: Aim for a decider whenever you want a guaranteed answer, as in a compiler, a bank's fraud rule or an exam grader. Settle for a recogniser when the "yes" case is what matters and no decider exists, as in a theorem-proving program that searches for proofs: if a proof exists it finds it, otherwise it may run forever. In practice people add a time limit, which turns "loop" into "don't know", not into "no".

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Calling the Church-Turing thesis a theorem. Thinking recognisable means decidable. Thinking E_DFA is decided by trying strings one by one: it is decided by reachability. Forgetting the CNF bound 2n - 1 when proving A_CFG decidable. Running two recognisers one after the other instead of alternating. Exams ask: define decidable and recognisable, prove A_DFA, E_DFA, EQ_DFA and A_CFG decidable, prove "decidable iff recognisable and co-recognisable", and explain why the thesis cannot be proved.

The mental model to keep: Picture nested boxes. Smallest, regular: machines with no notebook. Next, context-free: one stack. Next, decidable: Turing machines that always come back with an answer. Next, recognisable: machines that come back if the answer is yes. Outside everything, the huge dark space of languages with no machine. For any problem ask two questions: "does a machine exist that says yes when it should?" and "does one exist that also always says no when it should?" The answers place the problem in the right box.

Recap and what comes next: The Church-Turing thesis identifies algorithms with Turing machines that always halt; it is a thesis because "algorithm" is informal. Decidable languages have deciders, recognisable ones have machines that confirm yes, and decidable means recognisable plus co-recognisable. Problems about DFAs and grammars such as A_DFA, E_DFA, EQ_DFA, A_CFG and E_CFG are decidable. In lesson 22 we ask the same question about Turing machines themselves and meet the first problem no computer can ever solve: the halting problem.
key_points: Church-Turing thesis: every intuitive algorithm can be run by a Turing machine; it is a thesis because "algorithm" is informal.
Decider: halts on every input. Decidable (recursive) language: some decider accepts exactly its strings.
Recognisable (semi-decidable, r.e.): some TM accepts exactly its strings but may loop on others.
Decidable exactly when recognisable and co-recognisable: run both recognisers alternately.
A_DFA by simulation, E_DFA by marking reachable states, EQ_DFA by emptiness of the symmetric difference.
A_CFG is decidable using CNF (derivations of exactly 2n - 1 steps) or CYK; every CFL is decidable.
Regular inside context-free inside decidable inside recognisable inside all languages; most languages have no machine.
lessons.tip: For every "is this decidable?" proof, write the decider as numbered steps and add one line explaining why it always halts. The halting reason is where most marks are lost.
lessons.task: Draw a 4-state DFA of your choice over {0, 1}. Run the E_DFA marking procedure by hand, colouring states as they get marked. Then change one arrow so that the answer flips, and write down a witness string.

quiz.q: Why is the Church-Turing thesis not a proven theorem?
options: Nobody has tried to prove it
"Intuitive algorithm" is not a precise mathematical notion
quiz.explain: You cannot prove an equality between a precise object and an informal idea; you can only collect evidence.

quiz.q: A machine accepts every string in L but loops on some strings not in L. L is at least...
quiz.explain: Accepting exactly the members, possibly looping on others, is the definition of recognisable.

quiz.q: How is E_DFA decided?
options: Try every string up to length 100
Check whether any accept state is reachable from the start state
Convert the DFA to a grammar
quiz.explain: The language is non-empty exactly when some accept state can be reached, which marking checks in finitely many steps.

quiz.q: Why does the A_CFG decider convert the grammar to Chomsky Normal Form first?
options: In CNF a string of length n needs exactly 2n - 1 steps, so only finitely many derivations need checking
quiz.explain: The fixed derivation length turns an endless search into a finite one, so the machine always halts.

quiz.q: L is recognisable and its complement is recognisable. What follows?
quiz.explain: Run both recognisers alternately; one must accept, so we always get an answer.

lessons.title: The Halting Problem
lessons.content:
Your phone freezes and a box pops up: "App isn't responding. Wait or close?" Why does the phone ask you? Why can't it just look at the app and know whether it is stuck forever or only slow? This is not laziness by the phone makers. In 1936 Alan Turing proved that no program can ever look at every other program and correctly say whether it will finish. This lesson rebuilds that proof one small step at a time, so that by the end you could have discovered it yourself.

Quick recap: A decider is a Turing machine that halts on every input with accept or reject; a recogniser may loop on "no" inputs (lesson 21). Any Turing machine M can be written as a string <M>, and the universal machine U runs <M, w> exactly as M would run on w (lesson 20). By the Church-Turing thesis, "no Turing machine can do it" means "no algorithm, in any language, on any computer, can do it".

The question: Define A_TM = { <M, w> : M is a Turing machine and M accepts w }. A close cousin is HALT_TM = { <M, w> : M halts on w }, halting meaning it stops with accept or reject. A decider for these would be a dream tool: a perfect bug checker that tells you, before running anything, whether your program ever gets stuck in an endless loop.

Half of the dream is easy: A_TM is recognisable. On input <M, w>, run U. If M accepts w, U accepts. If M rejects, U rejects. If M loops, U loops, and that is allowed for a recogniser. The trouble is only the "loops" case: to be a decider, we would need to say "no" about a run that never ends, without waiting for it.

Warm-up, feeding a program to itself: This sounds strange, but it is normal. A word-counting program can count the words in its own source code. A C compiler is often written in C and compiles itself. A program is just a string, and any string can be input. So asking "what does machine M do on its own description <M>?" is a perfectly fair question. It is the key move of the proof.

Warm-up, the fortune teller: A jyotishi in the bazar claims he can predict anything you will do. You say: "Predict whether I will raise my hand. Whatever you predict, I will do the opposite." If he says "you will raise it", you keep it down. If he says "you won't", you raise it. Whatever he says is wrong. The problem is not that he is a bad fortune teller. The problem is that a person who reads the prediction and does the opposite exists. The halting proof builds exactly such a person.

Step 1, assume the tool exists: Suppose, for contradiction (lesson 3), there is a decider H for A_TM. Given <M, w>, H always halts, and accepts if M accepts w, and rejects if M does not accept w (whether M rejects or loops). We do not know how H works inside. We just assume it works.

Step 2, ask machines about themselves: Since H takes any machine and any input, we can give it a machine together with that machine's own description: H on <M, <M>>. This asks, "Does M accept its own code?" H answers this for every M, because H answers everything.

Step 3, build the contrarian D: Using H as a part, build a new machine D. On input <M>: first run H on <M, <M>>. If H accepts, D rejects. If H rejects, D accepts. In short, D does the opposite of what M does on its own code. D always halts, because H always halts and D only adds one flip. D is the person who hears the prediction and does the opposite.

Step 4, run D on itself: D is a Turing machine, so it has a description <D>. Feed it to D. Case one: suppose D accepts <D>. Then by D's rule, H must have rejected <D, <D>>, which by H's promise means D does not accept <D>. But we supposed it does. Contradiction. Case two: suppose D rejects <D>. Then H must have accepted <D, <D>>, which means D accepts <D>. Contradiction again. D halts on every input, so these are the only two cases, and both are impossible.

Step 5, find the guilty assumption: Every step after Step 1 was a safe construction: running a machine as a subroutine, flipping an answer, feeding a string. The only unproven thing was the existence of H. So H cannot exist. A_TM is undecidable: no algorithm decides, for every machine and input, whether the machine accepts.

The same proof as a table (diagonalization): List all Turing machines as rows M1, M2, M3, ... and all descriptions as columns <M1>, <M2>, <M3>, .... In each cell put H's answer: does row machine accept column string? For example, row M1: acc, rej, acc; row M2: rej, rej, acc; row M3: acc, acc, acc. The diagonal reads acc, rej, acc. D is built to flip the diagonal: rej, acc, rej. So D differs from M1 in column 1, from M2 in column 2, from every Mk in column k. But D is a Turing machine, so D is some row. The row that must disagree with itself on its own diagonal cell is the contradiction. This is Cantor's diagonal trick from lesson 3, applied to machines.

The same proof in code: Suppose someone writes a function halts(p, x) that returns True if program p halts on input x and False otherwise, always correctly and always quickly. Write trouble(p): if halts(p, p) is True, run while True: pass, a loop that never ends; else return. Now call trouble(trouble). If halts says it halts, it loops forever. If halts says it loops, it returns at once. halts is wrong about trouble either way, so no correct halts function can be written, in Python, C or any language. This version proves HALT_TM undecidable directly.

A language that is not even recognisable: The complement of A_TM, the pairs <M, w> where M does not accept w, is not recognisable. Lesson 21 showed: decidable means recognisable and co-recognisable. A_TM is recognisable. If its complement were recognisable too, A_TM would be decidable, which we just disproved. So no machine can even confirm "M does not accept w" in all cases.

Where the impossibility really comes from: It is not about slow hardware, small memory or clever enough programmers. A faster computer would face the same D. The impossibility comes from two things together: machines can read descriptions of machines, and H claims a total, always-correct answer. Combine them and a contrarian machine can always be built to beat H.

What it does NOT say: It does not say we can never tell whether a particular program halts. "for i in range(10): print(i)" obviously halts, and tools prove such facts every day. It says no single method works for every program-input pair. Also, a real computer with a fixed finite memory has only finitely many possible configurations, so in principle a repeat could be spotted, but the number of configurations is astronomically huge, so this is useless in practice. The clean impossibility is for the idealised machine with unlimited tape.

Real consequence, open maths problems: Look at this tiny program: given n, while n is not 1, if n is even set n = n / 2, else set n = 3n + 1. For 6 it goes 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 and stops. Does it stop for every starting n? That is the Collatz conjecture, unsolved for decades. A perfect halting decider could settle it by asking about a program that searches for a counterexample. The fact that such simple loops resist analysis shows the halting problem is not just a trick, it is real.

Real-life example 1, "not responding" dialogs: Your phone or computer cannot know whether a frozen app is stuck forever or about to finish. So it uses a time limit: if the app does not respond within a few seconds, it asks you. A time limit turns "maybe never" into "don't know yet", which is exactly the honest answer a recogniser can give. Where it matches: the OS can confirm "it finished" but never "it will never finish". Where it differs: a phone has finite memory, but as we saw, that does not help in practice.

Real-life example 2, virus scanners and bug finders: A perfect virus detector would answer "will this program ever do something harmful?" for every program, which runs into the same wall; lesson 23 makes this precise with Rice's theorem. So real antivirus tools use known patterns and heuristics, and accept two kinds of errors: false alarms and missed viruses. Static analysis tools that warn "this loop may never end" are designed to be sometimes wrong or to say "unknown" instead of claiming perfection.

When to use this knowledge, and when not: Use it when someone promises a perfect, fully automatic analysis of all programs: be suspicious, and ask what it does when it cannot tell. Use it to switch your goal from "perfect" to "useful": time limits, test cases, restricted languages where analysis is decidable, tools that may answer "don't know". Do not use it as an excuse to skip testing or proving your own code. Specific programs can usually be analysed.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Saying "the halting problem is undecidable because programs can be very long". Forgetting that D must be built to always halt, using H. Mixing up "undecidable" (no decider) with "unrecognisable" (no recogniser). Thinking it means no program's halting can ever be decided. Exams ask: state A_TM and HALT_TM, prove A_TM undecidable using D, explain the diagonal table, show A_TM is recognisable, and prove its complement is not recognisable.

The mental model to keep: Picture a judge H who claims to predict every machine's behaviour on every input. Next to him stands a mischievous boy D, who asks H about himself and then does the opposite. The moment D asks H "what will I do on my own code?", H is trapped: any answer becomes false. Whenever you meet a claim of a perfect program analyser, imagine that boy standing beside it.

Recap and what comes next: A_TM and HALT_TM are recognisable but undecidable. The proof assumes a decider H, builds a contrarian D that runs H on <M, <M>> and flips the answer, then runs D on <D> to get a contradiction, the diagonal trick. The complement of A_TM is not even recognisable. Practical tools survive by using time limits and approximations. In lesson 23 we learn reductions, a way to spread this one impossibility to many other problems, and Rice's theorem, which says almost every question about what a program does is undecidable.
key_points: A_TM = { <M, w> : M accepts w } and HALT_TM = { <M, w> : M halts on w } are both undecidable.
A_TM is recognisable: the universal machine U accepts when M accepts.
Proof: assume decider H, build D(<M>) = opposite of H(<M, <M>>), then D on <D> contradicts itself.
This is diagonalization: D differs from every machine on the diagonal of the acceptance table.
Since A_TM is recognisable but undecidable, its complement is not recognisable.
It forbids one method for all programs, not analysis of particular programs; hardware speed does not matter.
Consequences: no perfect loop detector, virus detector or bug checker; real tools use time limits and approximations.
lessons.tip: Practise writing the proof in exactly five labelled steps: assume H, ask about <M, <M>>, build D, run D on <D>, conclude. Examiners look for each step and especially the two-case contradiction.
lessons.task: Write the halts / trouble argument in your own words as a 6 to 8 line dialogue between a friend who claims to have a perfect "infinite loop checker" app and you. Then run the Collatz loop by hand for n = 7 and count how many steps it takes to reach 1.

quiz.q: In the proof, what does machine D do on input <M>?
options: Runs M on an empty tape
Runs H on <M, <M>> and does the opposite of its answer
quiz.explain: D is the contrarian: it flips H's prediction about M on its own description.

quiz.q: Why is A_TM recognisable?
options: The universal machine U accepts exactly when M accepts w
quiz.explain: U simulates M on w; if M accepts, U accepts, and looping on other inputs is allowed for a recogniser.

quiz.q: Which language is NOT Turing-recognisable?
options: The set of strings a^n b^n
quiz.explain: If the complement of A_TM were recognisable, A_TM would be decidable, which is false.

quiz.q: What does the halting problem result actually forbid?
options: Knowing whether any specific program halts
One algorithm that correctly answers halting for every program and input
quiz.explain: Specific cases can be analysed; what is impossible is a single method that is always correct for all cases.

quiz.q: Why does building D require H to always halt?
options: So that D always halts and only accept/reject cases are possible for D on <D>
So that D uses less tape
quiz.explain: Because H halts, D halts too, so D on <D> must accept or reject, and both cases lead to contradiction.

lessons.title: Reductions and Rice's Theorem
lessons.content:
Your friend boasts, "I can solve every class 10 maths problem." You know a trick that rewrites any class 8 problem as a class 10 problem. Then your friend can also solve every class 8 problem: just rewrite it and hand it over. Now suppose you know one class 8 problem that nobody can ever solve. Then your friend's boast must be false. That simple chain of thinking is called a reduction, and it is the main tool for proving that a problem is impossible for computers.

Quick recap: A language is decidable if some Turing machine always halts and answers correctly, and recognisable if some machine accepts exactly its members, possibly looping on others (lesson 21). In lesson 22 we proved A_TM = { <M, w> : M accepts w } is undecidable with a diagonal argument. <M> means a machine written as a string.

The problem reductions solve: The diagonal proof was clever and hard to invent. Doing a fresh one for every new problem would be exhausting. Instead, we take A_TM as our one "known impossible" problem and show that a new problem B is at least as hard: if B could be solved, A_TM could be solved too. This is like the class 8 trick: one impossible problem spreads its impossibility to others.

What a reduction is: A reduces to B, written A ≤ B, means: if you had a solver for B, you could build a solver for A using it as a subroutine. Two things follow. If B is decidable, A is decidable. And the flipped form, the one we use for impossibility: if A is undecidable, B is undecidable. The arrow of hardness points from A to B: B is at least as hard as A.

The direction trap: To prove B undecidable, you reduce a KNOWN undecidable problem (like A_TM) TO B. You assume a decider for B and build a decider for A_TM. Doing it the other way, reducing B to A_TM, proves nothing about B, just as "class 10 problems can be turned into PhD problems" tells you nothing about how hard class 10 is. This is the most common exam mistake in this whole topic.

Mapping reductions: A more precise kind is the mapping reduction. A ≤m B if there is a computable function f, a machine that always halts and turns strings into strings, such that w is in A exactly when f(w) is in B. The solver for A just computes f(w) and asks B's solver. Example: A_NFA ≤m A_DFA, where f turns <N, w> into <D, w> using the subset construction (lesson 7). Mapping reductions also carry recognisability: if A ≤m B and B is recognisable, so is A.

Proof 1, HALT_TM is undecidable: HALT_TM = { <M, w> : M halts on w }. Assume a decider R for it. Build S for A_TM. On input <M, w>: run R on <M, w>. If R rejects, M loops on w, so M does not accept: reject. If R accepts, M halts, so it is now safe to run M on w to the end. If M accepts, accept; if it rejects, reject. S always halts and decides A_TM, which is impossible. So R cannot exist. Notice the cause and effect: R's one job is to remove the danger of looping, and that is exactly the part A_TM could not do.

Proof 2, E_TM is undecidable: E_TM = { <M> : L(M) is empty }. Here is a cleverer move. Given <M, w>, we do not run M. We write down the description of a new machine M1: "On input x: if x is not w, reject. If x is w, run M on w and accept if M accepts." Think about M1's language. If M accepts w, M1 accepts exactly one string, w. If M does not accept w, M1 accepts nothing. So L(M1) is empty exactly when M does not accept w. Now if a decider E for E_TM existed, build S for A_TM: on <M, w>, write <M1>, run E on it, and give the opposite answer. Contradiction, so E_TM is undecidable.

The key idea in Proof 2: S never runs M1. It only builds M1's description, which takes finite time, like writing a recipe without cooking it. All the danger of looping sits inside M1, and the imaginary decider E is the one who would have to deal with it. This "build a machine whose language depends on whether M accepts w" trick is the engine behind almost every undecidability proof.

Proof 3, REGULAR_TM is undecidable: Is L(M) a regular language? Given <M, w>, describe M2: "On input x: if x has the form 0^n 1^n, accept. Otherwise run M on w and accept x if M accepts w." If M accepts w, M2 accepts everything, Σ*, which is regular. If not, M2 accepts only 0^n 1^n, which is not regular (lesson 11). So a decider for REGULAR_TM would tell us whether M accepts w. Undecidable.

Proof 4, EQ_TM is undecidable: Do two machines accept the same language? Reduce E_TM to it: let M_none be a machine that rejects every input. Then L(M) is empty exactly when <M, M_none> is in EQ_TM. A decider for EQ_TM would decide E_TM, so none exists. Compare with EQ_DFA, which was decidable in lesson 21: more power means fewer questions we can answer about the machines.

The Post Correspondence Problem: Undecidability is not only about machines. Emil Post described this puzzle in 1946. You get domino types, each with a string on top and a string on the bottom, and unlimited copies of each. Can you line up some dominoes (at least one, repeats allowed) so that the top string equals the bottom string? Example types: d1 = [b / ca], d2 = [a / ab], d3 = [ca / a], d4 = [abc / c]. Try d2, d1, d3, d2, d4. Top: a + b + ca + a + abc = abcaaabc. Bottom: ab + ca + a + ab + c = abcaaabc. A match! A verifier checks a proposed answer easily, but Post proved no algorithm can decide, for every set of dominoes, whether a match exists. The proof reduces A_TM to PCP using dominoes that spell out a machine's run. PCP is then used to prove problems like "is this context-free grammar ambiguous?" undecidable.

Rice's theorem: Proving undecidability one problem at a time still takes effort. Henry Rice proved in the early 1950s a theorem that handles a whole family at once. Let P be a property of the language a Turing machine recognises. Call P nontrivial if some machine's language has it and some machine's language does not. Rice's theorem: for every nontrivial property P, the problem "given <M>, does L(M) have property P?" is undecidable.

Why Rice's theorem is true: It is Proof 2, generalised. Assume the empty language does not have P (otherwise work with "not P"). Because P is nontrivial, some machine T has a language with P. Given <M, w>, describe Mw: "On input x: run M on w; if M accepts, run T on x and accept if T accepts." If M accepts w, L(Mw) = L(T), which has P. If not, L(Mw) is empty, which lacks P. A decider for P would decide A_TM. So none exists.

Using Rice step by step: To apply it, check two things. First, is the question about the language, meaning which inputs get accepted, rather than about the code's shape? Second, is it nontrivial, true for some machines and false for others? If both, you are done: undecidable. Examples: Is L(M) finite? Does M accept the string "bkash"? Is L(M) equal to Σ*? Does L(M) contain at least two strings? All four are about the language and nontrivial, so all four are undecidable.

What Rice does NOT say: It says nothing about properties of the machine's code. "Does M have more than 5 states?" is decidable: read <M> and count. "Does M halt on input ε within 100 steps?" is decidable: simulate 100 steps. Trivial properties like "L(M) is recognisable" are decidable, because the answer is always yes. Rice is about Turing machines only; for DFAs, emptiness and equality are decidable. And it says nothing about recognisability: "L(M) is non-empty" is undecidable but still recognisable, by dovetailing over inputs.

Real-life example 1, programming judges: When you submit code to an online judge or an assignment auto-grader, the checker would ideally ask: "does this program produce the same output as the reference solution for every input?" That is an equivalence question about behaviour, undecidable in general. So judges run a finite set of test cases with time limits. Where the analogy fits: the judge is a practical substitute for an impossible decider. Where it breaks: test cases can miss bugs, which is why passing all tests is strong evidence, not proof.

Real-life example 2, app review for safety: An app store would love an automatic check: "will this app ever send your OTP to a stranger?" That is a question about behaviour, and arguments just like Rice's show no checker can be perfect for all apps. So reviewers combine permission checks, known malware patterns, running apps in a sandbox for a while, and human review, accepting some misses and some false alarms.

When to use these tools, and when not: Use a reduction whenever you suspect a problem is impossible: pick a known undecidable problem and show that solving yours would solve it. Use Rice for quick verdicts on questions about what a general program accepts. Do not use Rice for questions about code structure, step-limited behaviour, or weaker models like DFAs and grammars. And remember undecidable is not the end in practice: restrict the programs, add time limits, or accept "don't know" answers.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Reducing in the wrong direction. Running the constructed machine M1 inside the reduction instead of only building it. Applying Rice to "M has 5 states". Forgetting to check nontriviality. Thinking PCP is undecidable for each specific domino set: a given set may be easy, the impossibility is for all sets. Exams ask: define reduction and mapping reduction, prove HALT_TM, E_TM or REGULAR_TM undecidable, state and apply Rice's theorem, and solve or explain a small PCP instance.

The mental model to keep: Picture a row of dominoes standing on the floor, A_TM at the front. Every reduction is a domino placed so that if it could stand forever (be decidable), A_TM would stand too. Since A_TM must fall, every domino behind it falls: HALT_TM, E_TM, REGULAR_TM, EQ_TM, PCP. Rice's theorem is a giant push that knocks down every nontrivial question about what a program's language is, in one go.

Recap and what comes next: A ≤ B means a solver for B would give a solver for A, so undecidability flows from A to B. We proved HALT_TM, E_TM, REGULAR_TM and EQ_TM undecidable by building machines whose language depends on whether M accepts w, met PCP as an undecidable puzzle, and learned Rice's theorem with its limits. In lesson 24 we step back and organise everything with the Chomsky hierarchy: four kinds of grammars, four kinds of machines, and the full containment picture.
key_points: A ≤ B: a solver for B can be used to build a solver for A; then A undecidable implies B undecidable.
To prove B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable problem (like A_TM) TO B, never the other way.
Mapping reduction: computable f with w in A exactly when f(w) in B.
HALT_TM, E_TM, REGULAR_TM and EQ_TM are undecidable; the trick is to build (not run) a machine whose language depends on whether M accepts w.
PCP (domino matching) is undecidable in general, though a given instance like abcaaabc may be easy to check.
Rice's theorem: every nontrivial property of the language L(M) is undecidable.
Rice does not cover code properties (number of states), step-bounded behaviour, trivial properties or DFAs/CFGs.
lessons.tip: Before writing any reduction proof, write one line at the top: "Assume a decider for B. I will build a decider for A_TM." It locks in the right direction and earns the first marks.
lessons.task: Use Rice's checklist on these questions and decide which are undecidable: (a) Does L(M) contain 01? (b) Does M have exactly 7 states? (c) Is L(M) infinite? (d) Does M make at least 50 moves on input 1? Then try to find a match for the dominoes [a / aa], [aab / b] or explain why none exists.

quiz.q: To prove a new problem B undecidable, what should you show?
options: A decider for B would give a decider for A_TM
quiz.explain: Reduce the known undecidable A_TM to B: if B were decidable, A_TM would be too.

quiz.q: In the E_TM proof, why is it safe for S to use M1?
options: S only writes M1's description and never runs it
quiz.explain: Building a description takes finite time; the looping danger stays inside M1 and is the imaginary decider's problem.

quiz.q: Which question is decidable?
options: Does M have more than 5 states?
quiz.explain: Counting states is a property of the code, not the language, so Rice does not apply; just read <M>.

quiz.q: For dominoes d1 = [b/ca], d2 = [a/ab], d3 = [ca/a], d4 = [abc/c], which sequence is a match?
quiz.explain: Top: a b ca a abc = abcaaabc; bottom: ab ca a ab c = abcaaabc.

quiz.q: What does "nontrivial" mean in Rice's theorem?
options: The property is hard to compute
Some machines' languages have it and some do not
The property mentions at least two strings
quiz.explain: A trivial property is true for all or for no recognisable languages, and those are trivially decidable.

lessons.title: The Chomsky Hierarchy
lessons.content:
Imagine four students in an exam hall, each with different paper. Student 1 has no paper at all, only her memory of a few moods. Student 2 has a stack of loose sheets, and may only look at the top sheet. Student 3 has a khata with exactly as many lines as the question is long. Student 4 has a khata that never runs out. Give them harder and harder questions and they drop out one by one. That ladder of students is the Chomsky hierarchy, the map that ties together every model in this course.

Why we need a map: Over 23 lessons we met DFAs, NFAs, regular expressions, grammars, PDAs and Turing machines, and classes like regular, context-free, decidable and recognisable. It is easy to lose track of who beats whom. The Chomsky hierarchy puts them in one picture: four kinds of grammars, four kinds of machines, each level strictly stronger than the one below.

Where it came from: In 1956 the linguist Noam Chomsky was studying how human languages build sentences. He asked: what kinds of grammar rules are needed to describe a language? He sorted grammars into four types by how free their rules are. Computer scientists then found that each type matches exactly one kind of machine. A tool for describing English became the backbone of compilers and computation theory.

Grammar recap: A grammar has variables (capital letters, like S, A, B), terminals (small letters, the actual symbols of strings), a start variable S, and rules of the form left → right. A derivation starts at S and keeps replacing a part matching some rule's left side with its right side, until only terminals remain. The four types differ only in what shapes of rules are allowed.

Type 3, regular grammars: Every rule looks like A → aB, A → a, or A → ε: one terminal, optionally followed by one variable at the end. Example for strings over {a, b} ending in b: S → aS | bS | b. Derive aab: S ⇒ aS ⇒ aaS ⇒ aab. Why this matches finite automata: treat each variable as a state. The rule A → aB says "in state A, reading a, go to state B". A rule A → a means "reading a, you may finish". The grammar never needs to remember anything except the current variable, just like a DFA remembers only its state. Machine: finite automaton. Memory: none beyond the state.

Type 2, context-free grammars: Every rule has a single variable on the left and anything on the right: A → γ. The variable can be replaced no matter what surrounds it, hence "context-free". Example: S → aSb | ε gives a^n b^n. Machine: nondeterministic pushdown automaton (lesson 17). Memory: one stack. The stack is what lets it match nested pairs.

Type 1, context-sensitive grammars: Rules look like αAβ → αγβ, where γ is not empty. The variable A may be replaced by γ only when it sits between α and β, its context. An equivalent and easier form: noncontracting grammars, where every rule's right side is at least as long as its left side, |left| ≤ |right| (with one special allowance for S → ε if the empty string is needed). Key consequence: a derivation never shrinks. So to derive a string of length n, every intermediate string has length at most n. Remember this fact; it is why membership is decidable at this level.

A context-sensitive grammar for a^n b^n c^n: Rules: S → aSBC | aBC, CB → BC, aB → ab, bB → bb, bC → bc, cC → cc. Derive aabbcc step by step: S ⇒ aSBC ⇒ aaBCBC (using S → aBC) ⇒ aaBBCC (swap CB to BC) ⇒ aabBCC (aB → ab) ⇒ aabbCC (bB → bb) ⇒ aabbcC (bC → bc) ⇒ aabbcc (cC → cc). Checking all derivations by computer up to length 9 gives only abc, aabbcc and aaabbbccc, exactly as hoped.

Why those rules work: The first rule plants n a's and n copies of B and C, but mixed up. CB → BC works like bubble sort, moving every B in front of every C. Then the context rules turn variables into letters only in the right place: B becomes b only right after a or b, and C becomes c only right after b or c. If you turn a B into b too early, a later B gets stuck behind a c and no rule can ever finish the string. Context is what lets the grammar check order, which a context-free grammar could not do (lesson 18).

Linear bounded automata: The machine for Type 1 is the linear bounded automaton (LBA): a nondeterministic Turing machine whose head may never leave the cells holding the input. End markers on both sides stop it. Memory grows only in proportion to the input length, like student 3's khata. Sige-Yuki Kuroda showed in 1964 that context-sensitive languages are exactly the languages of LBAs. Whether deterministic LBAs are as powerful as nondeterministic ones is still an open question.

Why LBA membership is decidable, from first principles: An LBA on input of length n has q states, n head positions, and g^n possible tape contents if the tape alphabet has g symbols. So it has at most q × n × g^n different configurations. With q = 5, g = 4, n = 3 that is 5 × 3 × 64 = 960. If a deterministic run lasts longer than that, some configuration has repeated, and a repeated configuration means it will repeat forever: a loop. So a decider can simulate with a step counter and reject once the count passes the limit. For the nondeterministic case, search all reachable configurations, of which there are finitely many. Either way, every context-sensitive language is decidable.

Type 0, unrestricted grammars: Any rule α → β is allowed, as long as α is not empty. Rules may even shrink strings. Machine: Turing machine. Languages: exactly the Turing-recognisable languages. Because derivations may shrink and grow, there is no length bound, and membership becomes undecidable; this follows from A_TM being undecidable (lesson 22).

The containment picture: regular inside context-free inside context-sensitive inside decidable inside recognisable (Type 0) inside all languages. Each inclusion is strict. Witnesses: a^n b^n is context-free but not regular; a^n b^n c^n is context-sensitive but not context-free; there exist decidable languages that are not context-sensitive (shown by diagonalization over all LBAs); A_TM is recognisable but not decidable; the complement of A_TM is not recognisable at all. Note that "decidable" is not one of Chomsky's four types; it sits between Type 1 and Type 0.

Comparison by level, in rows: Type 3: rules A → aB or A → a; machine finite automaton; memory just the state; example strings ending in b. Type 2: rules A → anything; machine PDA; memory one stack; example a^n b^n, balanced brackets. Type 1: rules never shrink; machine LBA; memory as long as the input; example a^n b^n c^n. Type 0: any rules; machine Turing machine; memory unlimited; example A_TM.

Closure properties by level: Regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation and star. Context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation and star, but not intersection or complement (lesson 18). Context-sensitive languages are closed under all five, including complement, which was proved independently by Neil Immerman and Róbert Szelepcsényi in 1987. Decidable languages are closed under all five too. Recognisable languages are closed under union, intersection, concatenation and star, but not complement, since A_TM is recognisable and its complement is not.

Decision problems by level: Membership ("is w in L?"): decidable for Types 3, 2 and 1, undecidable for Type 0. Emptiness ("is L empty?"): decidable for Types 3 and 2, undecidable for Types 1 and 0. Equivalence ("do two grammars give the same language?"): decidable only for Type 3. Notice the cause and effect: every step up the ladder adds expressive power, and every step up takes away guaranteed answers about the machines. Power and predictability trade against each other.

Real-life example 1, a compiler's pipeline: A compiler first splits code into tokens like names, numbers and operators. Tokens are regular, so a DFA built from regular expressions does this. Next, it checks structure, nested brackets and if-else blocks, using a context-free grammar and a parser. But some rules, like "a variable must be declared before it is used", need to match a name with an earlier name, much like the non-context-free language ww. Compilers handle these in a later stage, semantic analysis, with ordinary code and a symbol table. And the program being compiled can be any Turing machine, so the compiler cannot promise it halts.

Real-life example 2, human language: Chomsky's original question was about sentences. Nested phrases like "the boy that the girl that I know likes sings" need stack-like memory, beyond regular. Linguists later found rare patterns, such as certain word orders in Swiss German studied by Stuart Shieber in 1985, that are not even context-free. Where the analogy to programming fits: both use grammars to describe structure. Where it breaks: human language is full of ambiguity and meaning that no grammar type captures fully.

When to use which level: Pick the weakest level that can describe your problem. Validating a Bangladeshi phone number like 01712345678: regular expression. Checking balanced brackets or JSON structure: context-free grammar and parser. Do not use a regex to parse nested HTML, because nesting needs a stack. Use full programming power only when you truly need it, because then you lose guarantees like "always terminates".

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Thinking decidable is one of Chomsky's types. Forgetting the γ non-empty condition in Type 1 rules. Thinking every Type 3 rule can have the variable on either side: one grammar must be consistently right-linear (or consistently left-linear). Forgetting that context-sensitive languages are closed under complement while context-free ones are not. Exams ask: list the four types with rule shapes, matching machines and examples; draw the containment picture; write a context-sensitive grammar for a^n b^n c^n and derive a string; and explain why LBA membership is decidable.

The mental model to keep: Picture a staircase with four steps.
