On each step stands a machine holding its memory: a finite automaton with empty hands, a PDA holding a stack of plates, an LBA holding a khata exactly as long as the question, a Turing machine with an endless roll of paper. Next to each step, a grammar with its rule shape. Climbing up, you can describe more languages, but each step leaves some guaranteed answers behind on the floor below.

Recap and what comes next: The Chomsky hierarchy has four levels: regular (Type 3, finite automata), context-free (Type 2, PDAs), context-sensitive (Type 1, LBAs) and recursively enumerable (Type 0, Turing machines), each strictly containing the one below, with decidable languages between Types 1 and 0. Closure and decision properties weaken as power grows. In the final lesson we stop asking "can it be computed?" and ask "how fast?", meeting P, NP and NP-completeness, then wrap up the whole course.
key_points: Type 3 regular grammars (A → aB, A → a) match finite automata; memory is only the state.
Type 2 context-free grammars (A → γ) match nondeterministic PDAs; memory is one stack.
Type 1 context-sensitive (noncontracting) grammars match linear bounded automata; memory is as long as the input.
Type 0 unrestricted grammars match Turing machines and give the recognisable languages.
Regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ decidable ⊂ recognisable, all strict; decidable is not a Chomsky type.
LBA membership is decidable because there are at most q × n × g^n configurations.
Context-sensitive languages are closed under complement (Immerman-Szelepcsényi), context-free ones are not.
More power means fewer decidable questions: emptiness is undecidable from Type 1 up, equivalence from Type 2 up.
lessons.tip: Memorise nothing loose: build one table with columns Type, Rule shape, Machine, Memory, Example, Closed under complement?, Emptiness decidable?. If you can redraw it from reasoning, you can answer almost every hierarchy question.
lessons.task: Using the grammar S → aSBC | aBC, CB → BC, aB → ab, bB → bb, bC → bc, cC → cc, derive aaabbbccc step by step. Then try turning a B into b too early in another attempt and see where the derivation gets stuck.

quiz.q: Which machine matches context-sensitive grammars?
quiz.explain: Context-sensitive languages are exactly those of LBAs, Turing machines limited to the input cells.

quiz.q: Why is membership decidable for context-sensitive languages?
options: Derivations never shrink, so an LBA has only finitely many configurations to check
quiz.explain: Bounded memory means at most q × n × g^n configurations, so loops can be detected and the search ends.

quiz.q: Which class is closed under complement?
quiz.explain: Immerman and Szelepcsényi proved closure under complement for context-sensitive languages in 1987.

quiz.q: Where does the class of decidable languages fit?
quiz.explain: Every context-sensitive language is decidable, every decidable language is recognisable, and both inclusions are strict.

quiz.q: Which grammar rule is NOT allowed in a regular (Type 3) grammar?
quiz.explain: A right side with two variables needs a stack-like memory; regular rules allow at most one variable at the end.

lessons.title: P, NP, NP-Completeness and Course Wrap-up
lessons.content:
Your school needs an exam routine: 12 subjects, 3 time slots a day, and no student may have two of their exams at the same time. If a teacher hands you a finished routine, checking it takes minutes: look at each student's subjects and see that none clash. But making a good routine from scratch can take days of trial and error. Checking is easy, finding is hard. Is that gap real, or have we just not found the clever method yet? That question, P versus NP, is the most famous open problem in computer science, and it is where this course ends.

From "can" to "how fast": Lessons 19 to 24 asked whether a problem can be solved at all. But a decidable problem that needs 10^30 steps is useless in practice. Complexity theory asks how many steps a problem needs as the input grows. We still use Turing machines, because they let us count steps honestly.

Measuring time: The running time of a decider is a function t(n): the largest number of steps it takes on any input of length n (the worst case). We ignore constant factors and small terms using big-O: 3n^2 + 5n + 7 is O(n^2). Example from lesson 19: the single-tape zig-zag machine for a^n b^n c^n takes O(n^2) steps; the 2-tape copying idea from lesson 20 does a^n b^n in O(n).

Polynomial versus exponential: Compare n^2 with 2^n. For n = 10: 100 versus 1,024. For n = 20: 400 versus about a million. For n = 50: 2,500 versus about 1.1 × 10^15. For n = 100: 10,000 versus about 1.3 × 10^30. A computer doing a billion steps per second needs about 13 days for 2^50 steps and far longer than the age of the universe for 2^100. Polynomial growth stays manageable; exponential growth explodes. So the line between them is the line between "practical in principle" and "hopeless for large inputs".

The class P: P is the set of languages decided by a deterministic single-tape Turing machine in polynomial time, O(n^k) for some fixed k. Why polynomial, and not "fast" in some other sense? Because it is robust. Switching from multi-tape to single-tape at most squares the time (lesson 20), and a square of a polynomial is still a polynomial. Running one polynomial algorithm inside another keeps it polynomial. So P does not depend on model details. Honest caveat: n^100 is polynomial but useless; luckily, most natural problems in P have small exponents.

Problems in P: PATH, "is there a route from s to t in this graph?", is solved by breadth-first search, marking reachable nodes, much like E_DFA in lesson 21. Sorting, shortest paths (Dijkstra's algorithm), checking whether a graph can be 2-coloured, and even primality testing, shown to be in P by Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena in 2002, are all in P.

The verifier view of NP: For many problems, finding an answer seems hard, but checking a proposed answer is easy. The proposed answer is called a certificate. A verifier is an algorithm that takes the input plus a certificate and checks it in polynomial time. NP is the class of problems where every yes-instance has a certificate that a polynomial-time verifier accepts, and no-instances have none. Equivalently, NP is what a nondeterministic Turing machine decides in polynomial time: guess the certificate, then check it. NP stands for "nondeterministic polynomial", not "not polynomial". Every problem in P is in NP, since the verifier can ignore the certificate and solve it directly. So P is inside NP.

Example 1, SAT: A Boolean formula uses variables that are true or false, joined by AND (∧), OR (∨) and NOT (¬). SAT asks: can the variables be set to make the formula true? Take (x ∨ y) ∧ (¬x ∨ z) ∧ (¬y ∨ ¬z). Certificate: x = true, y = false, z = true. Verify: clause 1, x is true, OK. Clause 2, z is true, OK. Clause 3, ¬y is true, OK. All clauses true, so the formula is satisfiable. Checking took one pass. Finding it blindly could mean trying all 2^n assignments, 8 here, but over 10^30 with 100 variables.

Example 2, Hamiltonian path: A Pathao rider must visit each of n drop points exactly once, using only the roads that exist. Does such a route exist? Certificate: the order of points. Verify: every point appears exactly once and each consecutive pair is joined by a road, easy in polynomial time. Finding it by trying every order means up to n! orders: 10! is 3,628,800, and 20! is about 2.4 × 10^18.

Example 3, subset sum: Given the numbers {3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2}, is there a subset adding to 9? Certificate: {4, 5}. Verify: 4 + 5 = 9, done ({3, 4, 2} also works). Blind search tries up to 2^6 = 64 subsets here, which doubles with every extra number.

Polynomial-time reductions: Lesson 23's reductions, now with a speed limit. A ≤p B if a polynomial-time function f turns every instance w of A into an instance f(w) of B with the same yes/no answer. Then a fast solver for B gives a fast solver for A: compute f(w) quickly, then solve. Direction rule as before: to show B is hard, reduce a known hard problem TO B.

NP-complete: A problem B is NP-complete if B is in NP, and every problem in NP reduces to B in polynomial time. So NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP. Cause and effect: if any single NP-complete problem had a polynomial algorithm, then every NP problem would, through the reductions, and P would equal NP.

The Cook-Levin theorem: Stephen Cook in 1971, and Leonid Levin independently around 1973, proved that SAT is NP-complete. The idea, from first principles: take any NP problem and its polynomial-time verifier, a Turing machine. Its whole run fits in a table, one row per step, one column per tape cell, polynomial in size. Each small window of the table must obey the machine's rules, a local check, which can be written as a small formula. AND all these together with "the run accepts" and you get one formula that is satisfiable exactly when some certificate makes the verifier accept. So every NP problem turns into SAT.

The family grows: Once SAT was known NP-complete, others followed by reduction. Richard Karp in 1972 showed 21 problems NP-complete. Famous members: 3-SAT, CLIQUE, vertex cover, Hamiltonian path, subset sum, graph 3-colouring and Sudoku generalised to n^2 × n^2 grids. To prove a new problem B NP-complete, do two things: show B is in NP (give a verifier), and reduce a known NP-complete problem to B.

NP-hard: A problem is NP-hard if every NP problem reduces to it, whether or not it is in NP itself. NP-complete = NP-hard and in NP. Some NP-hard problems are not in NP: the optimisation version "find the shortest tour through all cities" is not a yes/no question, and the halting problem is NP-hard but not even decidable.

P versus NP, open: Is P equal to NP? Nobody knows. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems, with a one million dollar prize, announced in 2000. Most experts believe P ≠ NP, but there is no proof. If P = NP with a practical algorithm, much of today's public-key cryptography, which protects online banking and mobile payments, would be in serious trouble, and many scheduling and design problems would become easy. If P ≠ NP, the picture is: P inside NP, NP-complete problems inside NP but outside P.

How people cope with NP-complete problems: NP-complete does not mean "give up". Approximation: for vertex cover, a simple algorithm guarantees an answer at most twice the best. Heuristics: modern SAT solvers handle many industrial formulas with millions of variables, though no guarantee exists for all inputs. Special cases: 2-SAT, with two literals per clause, is in P. Small inputs: exact search is fine for small n. Pseudo-polynomial methods: subset sum by dynamic programming is fast when the target number is small.

Real-life example, the exam routine again: Make each subject a dot, and join two dots if some student takes both subjects. Time slots are colours, and joined dots need different colours. That is graph colouring, NP-complete for 3 or more colours. Schools use greedy rules like "schedule the subject with most clashes first", which usually work well. Where it matches: checking a routine is easy, finding one is hard. Where it breaks: real schools add soft wishes like "no two hard exams in a row", which makes it even harder.

When to use this knowledge, and when not: When you meet a new problem, ask whether it looks like a known NP-complete problem before spending weeks hunting for a perfect fast algorithm. If it is, switch to approximation, heuristics or special structure. Do not conclude "NP-complete, so impossible": your inputs may be small or special. And do not say NP means "not polynomial".

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Saying NP = non-polynomial. Thinking NP-complete problems are undecidable: they are decidable, just possibly slow. Reducing in the wrong direction. Forgetting to show membership in NP when proving NP-completeness. Claiming P ≠ NP is proved. Exams ask: define P, NP, NP-complete and NP-hard, verify a certificate for SAT or Hamiltonian path, state Cook-Levin, and draw the P, NP, NP-complete picture assuming P ≠ NP.

Course recap, part 1, automata: We started with yes/no problems as languages. DFAs and NFAs, equal in power, recognise regular languages, the same as regular expressions; the pumping lemma shows limits like a^n b^n. Context-free grammars and PDAs add a stack and capture nesting; the CFL pumping lemma shows limits like a^n b^n c^n.

Course recap, part 2, computability and complexity: Turing machines add a read-write tape and capture every algorithm, by the Church-Turing thesis. Variants add no power, and a universal machine runs them all. Some problems are decidable, some only recognisable, and the halting problem is undecidable, spreading through reductions and Rice's theorem. The Chomsky hierarchy ties grammars to machines. Finally, among decidable problems, P is the efficient ones, NP the efficiently checkable ones, and whether they are equal is open.

The mental model for the whole course: Picture nested boxes: regular, context-free, context-sensitive, decidable, recognisable, and the dark space of everything else. Each box holds a machine with a certain kind of memory. Now place a ruler of time inside the decidable box: P near the start, NP around it, NP-complete at NP's outer edge. For any new problem, ask: which box, which machine, and how fast?

What to study next: Compiler Design uses this course directly: lexers are DFAs built from regular expressions, and parsers are CFG and PDA ideas made deterministic as LL and LR parsing. Algorithms deepens P, NP, reductions, approximation and dynamic programming. Cryptography builds on problems believed hard. Formal verification uses automata to check hardware and software. Keep practising by tracing machines by hand: if you can simulate it on paper, you understand it.
key_points: Running time t(n) counts worst-case Turing machine steps on inputs of length n, using big-O.
P: decidable in polynomial time by a deterministic TM; robust across reasonable models.
NP: yes-answers have certificates checkable in polynomial time; NP means nondeterministic polynomial, and P is inside NP.
SAT, Hamiltonian path and subset sum are easy to verify, e.g. x = T, y = F, z = T satisfies (x ∨ y) ∧ (¬x ∨ z) ∧ (¬y ∨ ¬z).
NP-complete: in NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time; Cook-Levin (1971/1973) showed SAT is NP-complete.
NP-hard problems need not be in NP; the halting problem is NP-hard and undecidable.
P vs NP is open; coping methods are approximation, heuristics, special cases and exact search for small inputs.
Course map: regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ decidable ⊂ recognisable, with P ⊆ NP inside decidable.
lessons.tip: For any NP question, first write the certificate and how to check it in one or two lines. If you can do that, you have shown membership in NP, which is half of every NP-completeness proof.
lessons.task: Write a Boolean formula with 3 variables and 4 clauses. Swap with a friend: each tries to find a satisfying assignment, timing it, then each checks the other's answer, timing that too. Compare finding time with checking time.

quiz.q: What does NP stand for?
quiz.explain: NP is what a nondeterministic TM decides in polynomial time, equivalently what a polynomial verifier can check.

quiz.q: Why is every problem in P also in NP?
options: A verifier can ignore the certificate and solve the problem directly in polynomial time
Because P problems have no certificates
quiz.explain: Solving in polynomial time is a valid polynomial-time verification that needs no certificate.

quiz.q: What did the Cook-Levin theorem show?
options: The halting problem is in NP
quiz.explain: Any NP verifier's run can be described by a formula that is satisfiable exactly when a certificate exists.

quiz.q: If someone found a polynomial algorithm for one NP-complete problem, what would follow?
options: Nothing, because NP-complete problems are undecidable
Every NP problem would be in P, so P = NP
quiz.explain: Every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time, so all of them would get polynomial algorithms.

quiz.q: Which statement about NP-hard is correct?
options: Every NP-hard problem is in NP
An NP-hard problem may lie outside NP, like the halting problem
NP-hard means solvable in polynomial time
NP-hard and P are the same
quiz.explain: NP-hard only requires that every NP problem reduces to it; NP-complete additionally requires membership in NP.
